checks.label: Explain
checks.meaning: Say what it does and when to use it, in plain words, with no notes.

checks.label: Write
checks.meaning: Write the query from a blank page, then run it to check.

checks.label: Predict
checks.meaning: Read a query and say which rows it returns before you run it.

checks.label: Edge cases
checks.meaning: Say what happens with NULLs, ties, duplicates or no rows at all, and fix it.

confidentRule: A topic is finished when you pass all four checks, not when you have read it. Be strict: if you had to look at the notes, it is not ticked yet.
howToStudy: Go in order. Each phase uses the ones before it, and the practice database stays the same all the way through.
Open "The practice database" once and look at the six tables. Every example uses them, so you will soon know the rows by heart — that is what lets you check answers by eye.
Type every example yourself before you look at the result. Press "Try it", change something small, and run it again. Reading SQL is not the same as writing it.
Before you run any query, say out loud what you expect it to return. That is the Predict check, and it is the fastest way to find gaps.
The notes on every topic are enough on their own. The free resources are a second explanation and extra practice.
Phases 0–3 are the core: most real work and most interview questions use only these. Phases 4–5 (subqueries, CTEs, window functions) are what separates a pass from a strong pass.
Interview soon? Learn every "Must know" topic, then do Phase 8 twice: once with the hints, once from a blank page. Use Revise mode the night before.

cheatSheet.title: The order you write a query in
cheatSheet.code:
SELECT    columns, aggregates
FROM      table
JOIN      other_table ON key = key
WHERE     row filter
GROUP BY  columns
HAVING    group filter
ORDER BY  columns
LIMIT     n;

cheatSheet.title: The order the database runs it in
cheatSheet.code:
1 FROM / JOIN   build the rows
2 WHERE         keep some rows
3 GROUP BY      make groups
4 HAVING        keep some groups
5 SELECT        work out the columns (and window functions)
6 DISTINCT      drop duplicate rows
7 ORDER BY      sort
8 LIMIT         cut

cheatSheet.title: Joins in one line each
cheatSheet.code:
INNER JOIN   only rows that match on both sides
LEFT JOIN    every left row; NULLs where the right has no match
FULL JOIN    every row from both sides
CROSS JOIN   every left row paired with every right row
anti-join    LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL  (or NOT EXISTS)

cheatSheet.title: NULL rules
cheatSheet.code:
x = NULL            never true: use x IS NULL
NULL + 1            NULL
COUNT(*)            counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs
SUM / AVG / MIN / MAX   skip NULLs
COALESCE(x, 0)      first value that is not NULL
x NOT IN (…, NULL)  returns no rows: use NOT EXISTS

cheatSheet.title: Top N per group
Window function shapes
cheatSheet.code:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x)   1,2,3,4
RANK()       …                                 1,2,2,4
DENSE_RANK() …                                 1,2,2,3
LAG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)                        previous row
SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)                        running total
AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS 2 PRECEDING)      3-row moving average

phases.title: Start here: databases, tables and SQL
phases.goal: Know what a database is, what a table, a row and a key are, and the six practice tables you will use in every lesson.
phases.bigPicture: Almost every app keeps its data in a relational database, and SQL is how you ask it questions. Learn the shape of the data first — tables, rows, keys — and every later topic is just a new way of asking.

topics.name: What a database, a table and SQL are
topics.definition: A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns, and SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language you use to ask it questions and to change what it holds.
topics.problem: A spreadsheet works for a few hundred rows and one person. An app with thousands of users needs data that many people can read and change at the same time, safely, without losing anything, and fast enough to answer in milliseconds. A database does that job, and SQL is how you talk to it.
topics.idea: A database is an organised store of data, run by a program called a DBMS (database management system), such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server or SQLite. The data lives in tables. A table is like one sheet in a spreadsheet: each row is one thing (one employee, one order) and each column is one fact about it (name, salary). You never open the files yourself. You send the database a query — a request written in SQL — and it sends back rows.
topics.analogy: A library with a librarian. The shelves are the tables, each book is a row, and the details on its catalogue card (title, author, year) are the columns. You don't walk the shelves yourself: you hand the librarian a request slip — "every book by this author, newest first" — and they bring back exactly those books.
topics.breaks: A librarian fetches books one by one, in the order you asked. SQL is declarative: you describe what you want, not how to get it, and the database picks its own way. That is why the order you write a query in is not the order it runs in.
howItWorks: You write a query in SQL, for example: give me the name and salary of everyone in department 1.
You send it to the database, from a SQL editor, a Python script, or your app's backend.
The database checks the query makes sense: do these tables and columns exist?
Its query planner picks the fastest way to find the rows, for example by using an index.
It runs that plan and returns the result: a new, temporary table of rows and columns.
Reading never changes the stored tables. A SELECT is always safe to run.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR Y["You or your app"] -->|"1 a SQL query"| P["Database (DBMS)
checks and plans it"] P -->|"2 reads"| T[("Tables
rows and columns")] T --> P P -->|"3 the result: a new table"| Y
diagram.caption: Follow the numbers. You send a query, the database works out how to answer it and reads its tables, and you get back a result — which is itself a small table.

examples.title: Your first query
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 1
ORDER BY name;
examples.note: Read it like English: select the name and salary, from the employees table, where the department is 1, sorted by name. The answer is a small table of four rows.

keyPoints: A table holds one kind of thing. A row is one of them; a column is one fact about each.
SQL is declarative: you say what you want, and the database decides how to get it.
The result of a query is itself a table. That is why a query can be put inside another query.
SQL keywords are not case-sensitive (`select` works), but writing them in capitals makes a query easier to read.
Every major database speaks SQL. The core is the same everywhere; small details such as dates and LIMIT differ, and these notes point them out.
How databases scale — SQL versus NoSQL, replication, sharding — is in the System Design tab, Phase 3.
mistakes: Thinking SQL runs top to bottom like Python. It doesn't: the database reads FROM first and SELECT near the end.
Thinking a database is just a big spreadsheet. It also enforces rules, handles many users at once and survives crashes.
Forgetting the semicolon between two statements. One statement on its own usually runs without it.
dialects: This page runs SQLite, a small database that lives inside one file — here, inside your browser. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server run as servers, but the SQL you learn here is the same for almost everything you will write.
topics.interviewAnswer: A relational database stores data in tables, where each row is one record and each column is one attribute, and the tables are linked through keys. SQL is the declarative language for querying and changing that data: I describe the result I want, and the database's optimiser decides how to get it. That separation is why the same query can become much faster just by adding an index.

followUps.q: What is the difference between a database and a DBMS?
followUps.a: The database is the data itself. The DBMS is the software that stores it and answers queries: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, SQLite.

followUps.q: What does "declarative" mean?
followUps.a: You describe the result you want, not the steps to get it. The database chooses the steps, which is called its query plan.

followUps.q: When would you not use a relational database?
followUps.a: When the data has no fixed shape, or one simple lookup by key must scale across many machines — a key-value or document store can fit better. For most products, a relational database is the right default.

explain.answer:
A table is one sheet in a spreadsheet. The employees table is a sheet with one line per person.

A row is one line: one employee, such as Asha with her id, department, manager, salary and hire date.

A column is one heading, one fact that every row has: name, salary, hire_date.

A query is a question you write down in SQL, such as "give me the name and salary of everyone in department 1". You don't scroll and filter by hand like in Excel: you send the question, and the database sends back just the rows and columns you asked for.

write.answer: Pick the two columns, name the table, keep department 2, and sort. Dara and Eli are the two people in Sales.

query.sql:
SELECT name, hire_date
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 2
ORDER BY name;

predict.answer:
4 rows: Asha (95,000), Ben (70,000), Chen (70,000) and Hana (80,000).

Dara earns exactly 60,000, and `>` means strictly more than, so she is left out. Use `>=` to include her.

The query has no ORDER BY, so the database may return the 4 names in any order. The query below adds ORDER BY name and the salary, so you can check.

query.sql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 60000
ORDER BY name;

edge.answer:
With `WHERE dept_id = 1`: no. Gus's dept_id is NULL (unknown), and `NULL = 1` is not true, it is unknown. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true, so Gus is dropped.

With no WHERE at all: yes. Nothing filters the rows, so all 8 employees come back, Gus included.

The query below shows the test for every row. Gus gets NULL, not 0 (false): that is why he is in neither "department 1" nor "not department 1".

topics.name: Meet the practice database
topics.definition: Six small tables — departments, employees, customers, orders, products and order_items — that every example and exercise in this course uses.
topics.problem: Learning SQL on a different made-up table in every lesson means learning new data each time. With one small database you get to know the rows by heart, so you can check any result by eye. That habit is what catches wrong queries, at work and in interviews.
topics.idea: There are two small worlds. The company: departments, and employees who belong to a department and report to a manager. The shop: customers place orders, each order contains products, and order_items records which products are in which order, and how many. A few awkward cases are planted on purpose, because real data always has them: an employee with no department, a customer with no orders, two people on the same salary, and an order with no amount.
topics.analogy: A training kitchen with a fixed pantry. Every recipe (query) uses the same ingredients, so you learn how each one behaves, and you notice straight away when a dish comes out wrong.
topics.breaks: Real databases have hundreds of tables and millions of rows, so you can't check results by eye there. That is exactly why it pays to practise on data small enough that you can, and to build the habit of testing a query on a few known rows.
howItWorks: departments (4 rows): Engineering, Sales, Marketing and HR. HR has no employees yet.
employees (8 rows): each has a dept_id that points at departments, and a manager_id that points at another employee. Asha runs the company, so her manager_id is NULL. Gus has no department.
customers (6 rows): Tom signed up twice with the same email. Omar has never ordered. Zoe didn't give a city.
orders (10 rows), from January to March 2024: each has a customer_id. Order 106 was cancelled and has no amount.
products (7 rows): nobody has bought the phone case.
order_items (14 rows): one row per product in an order, with the quantity. An order's amount is the sum of quantity × price over its items.

examples.title: The departments table
examples.note: `SELECT *` means every column. Use it to look at a table; in real queries, name the columns you need.

examples.title: The employees table
examples.note: Spot the planted cases: Asha's manager_id is NULL, Gus's dept_id is NULL, Ben and Chen both earn 70000, and Hana (80000) earns more than her manager Ben.

examples.title: The orders table
examples.note: Customer 1 (Priya) placed five orders, three of them on consecutive days. Order 106 has no amount.

keyPoints: employees.dept_id points at departments.dept_id; employees.manager_id points at employees.emp_id — the same table.
orders.customer_id points at customers.customer_id.
order_items links orders and products: one row per product in an order.
Dates are stored as text in YYYY-MM-DD form, so sorting them as text also sorts them by date.
Amounts and prices are whole pounds, to keep the sums easy to check by hand.
mistakes: Assuming every employee has a department, or every customer has an order. NULLs and missing rows are where most wrong answers come from.
Assuming ids are in date order. Here they happen to be; in real data, always sort by the date column.
Writing a query before knowing the grain of each table — what one row means.
topics.interviewAnswer: Before writing any SQL in an interview, I look at the tables: what one row means in each, which columns are keys, and how the tables join. Then I ask about the awkward cases — can this be NULL, can there be duplicates, can a customer have no orders — because those decide whether I need a LEFT JOIN, a DISTINCT or a COALESCE. Two minutes of that saves a wrong answer.

followUps.q: Why look at the data before writing the query?
followUps.a: To learn the grain, the keys, and the awkward cases — NULLs, duplicates, missing matches — that change the answer.

followUps.q: What is the grain of a table?
followUps.a: What one row represents. One row of orders is one order; one row of order_items is one product within one order. Mixing grains is how totals get counted twice.

explain.answer:
One row of order_items is one line on a receipt: "order X contains this many of product Y". For example, (102, 4, 2) means order 102 contains 2 of product 4, the desk lamp.

order_id points to a row in orders (who bought it, when, the total). product_id points to a row in products (its name and price). So order_items is the link between the two: one order can hold many products, and one product can appear in many orders.

write.answer: `SELECT *` means every column. ORDER BY customer_id puts them in id order, so you can see the two Tom rows (2 and 6) and Zoe's missing city.

predict.answer:
2 rows: product 4 (the desk lamp, 2 of them) and product 5 (the backpack, 1).

Check it against orders: 2 × £25 + 1 × £30 = £80, which is exactly order 102's amount. (ORDER BY product_id is added below so the order is fixed.)

query.sql:
SELECT *
FROM order_items
WHERE order_id = 102
ORDER BY product_id;

edge.answer:
• No manager: Asha (manager_id is NULL; she is the boss).
• No department: Gus (dept_id is NULL).
• No orders: Omar. (The second Tom sign-up, customer 6, has none either; Tom's orders are all under id 2.)
• Never sold: the phone case (product 7).
• No amount: order 106, which was cancelled.

The others worth knowing: HR has no employees, Ben and Chen earn the same, Hana earns more than her manager Ben, Tom signed up twice with the same email, Zoe has no city, and Priya ordered three days in a row.

topics.name: Keys and relationships: primary keys, foreign keys, one-to-many, many-to-many
topics.definition: A primary key is a column whose value identifies exactly one row; a foreign key is a column that holds another table's primary key, and those links are how tables relate: one-to-many, many-to-many or one-to-one.
topics.problem: If every order repeated the customer's name, email and city, changing an email would mean editing every one of their orders — and one missed row would leave two different emails. Splitting data into tables linked by keys stores each fact once. Keys are also what joins use to put the rows back together.
topics.idea: Every table has a primary key: a column, like emp_id, that is never empty and never repeats, so it points at exactly one row. A foreign key is a column in another table that stores those ids, like orders.customer_id: it says "this order belongs to customer 1". The database can enforce it, so you can't add an order for a customer who doesn't exist. Relationships come in three shapes. One-to-many: one customer, many orders — the foreign key sits on the "many" side. Many-to-many: an order has many products and a product is in many orders, so a link table (order_items) holds pairs of keys. One-to-one: one row matches at most one row, such as a user and their settings.
topics.analogy: Passport numbers. Your passport number is your primary key: one per person, never shared. When a hotel writes your passport number on its booking, that is a foreign key: the booking doesn't copy your whole life story, it just points at you.
topics.breaks: A passport number means something in the real world. Good primary keys usually mean nothing at all — just a counter like 1, 2, 3, called a surrogate key — because real-world values like emails can change, and a key should never change.
howItWorks: customers.customer_id is the primary key: the values 1 to 6, each used once.
orders.customer_id is a foreign key: order 101 holds 1, which means "Priya placed this".
One customer can appear in many orders (Priya is in five), but each order points at exactly one customer. That is one-to-many.
order_items has a composite primary key: the pair (order_id, product_id). One order holds many products and one product is in many orders. That is many-to-many, and order_items is the link table.
employees.manager_id is a foreign key into its own table: Ben's manager_id is 1, which is Asha's emp_id. This is a self-reference, and it is how org charts and folder trees are stored.

examples.title: Follow a foreign key by hand
examples.sql:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1
ORDER BY order_id;
examples.note: All five orders hold customer_id 1, so all five belong to Priya. In Phase 3, a JOIN will fetch her name for you.

examples.title: Many-to-many through the link table
examples.sql:
SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity
FROM order_items
WHERE product_id = 6
ORDER BY order_id;
examples.note: Headphones (product 6) appear in three different orders, and order 105 also contains a backpack. Neither column is unique on its own; the pair is.

keyPoints: A primary key is unique and never NULL. A table has exactly one, though it may span several columns.
A foreign key holds values of another table's primary key — or NULL, if the column allows it.
One-to-many: the foreign key goes on the "many" side (orders.customer_id), never a list of ids on the "one" side.
Many-to-many needs a link table with two foreign keys (order_items).
A natural key is a real-world value (an email); a surrogate key is a meaningless counter (customer_id). Prefer surrogate keys as primary keys.
mistakes: Putting the foreign key on the wrong side, such as a column of order ids stored inside customers.
Using a value that can change, like an email or a phone number, as the primary key.
Thinking a foreign key must always be filled in. It can be NULL unless it is also NOT NULL: employees.dept_id is NULL for Gus.
dialects: SQLite only checks foreign keys after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;` (the practice database switches it on). PostgreSQL, MySQL (InnoDB) and SQL Server always check them.
topics.interviewAnswer: A primary key uniquely identifies each row: it is unique and never NULL, and I usually make it a meaningless surrogate id. A foreign key is a column that references another table's primary key; it defines the relationship and lets the database reject links to rows that don't exist. One-to-many puts the foreign key on the many side; many-to-many needs a junction table with two foreign keys, usually with the pair as its composite primary key.

followUps.q: Primary key or unique key — what is the difference?
followUps.a: Both forbid duplicates. A table has one primary key, and it can't be NULL. It can have many unique constraints, and in most databases a unique column may still hold NULLs.

followUps.q: What is a composite key?
followUps.a: A key made of two or more columns together, like (order_id, product_id) in order_items. Neither column is unique on its own, but the pair is.

followUps.q: What happens if you delete a customer who has orders?
followUps.a: With a foreign key, the database refuses by default. You can choose ON DELETE CASCADE (delete their orders too) or ON DELETE SET NULL instead.

explain.answer:
A primary key is the column that names exactly one row. In customers it is customer_id: 1 is Priya and nobody else, ever.

A foreign key is a column that holds another table's primary key, to point at that row. orders.customer_id is a foreign key: order 104 has customer_id 2, so it belongs to Tom. One customer can have many orders, so that is one-to-many.

A link table joins two tables that are many-to-many. One order can hold many products, and one product can be in many orders, so neither table can hold the other's key. order_items sits in the middle: each row holds one order_id and one product_id.

write.answer: Order 103 has two lines: 1 notebook (product 2) and 5 mugs (product 3). That is 1 × £5 + 5 × £8 = £45, order 103's amount.

query.sql:
SELECT *
FROM order_items
WHERE order_id = 103
ORDER BY product_id;

predict.answer:
Ben, Chen, Dara and Fatima: the four people who report straight to Asha (emp_id 1).

Hana is not in the list: her manager is Ben (2). Eli and Gus report to Dara (4). Asha has no manager at all.

query.sql:
SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE manager_id = 1
ORDER BY name;

edge.answer:
The primary key of order_items is the pair (order_id, product_id), so only the pair must be unique.

• Same order_id: yes. Order 102 has two rows, one for the lamp and one for the backpack.
• Same product_id: yes. Product 6, the headphones, is in orders 101, 104 and 105.
• Both at once: no. That would be the same product listed twice in one order. You change the quantity instead.

Try to add a second desk-lamp row to order 102 and the database refuses:

query.sql: INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (102, 4, 1);

topics.name: Data types: numbers, text, dates and true/false
topics.definition: Every column has a data type — such as INTEGER, a decimal number, TEXT, a date or a boolean — which decides what values it can hold and how they compare, sort and calculate.
topics.problem: The same value acts differently by type. The text '10' sorts before '9', because text compares letter by letter. Integer 7 divided by integer 2 gives 3, not 3.5. Knowing the types explains a whole class of "why is my answer wrong?" bugs.
topics.idea: Common types: INTEGER for whole numbers (counts, ids), DECIMAL or NUMERIC for exact money values, REAL or FLOAT for approximate numbers, TEXT or VARCHAR for words, DATE and TIMESTAMP for dates and times, and BOOLEAN for true or false. You can convert between types with CAST. NULL is not a type: it is the marker for "no value", and any column can hold it unless it is declared NOT NULL.
topics.analogy: Containers in a kitchen. A measuring jug (a number column) lets you add and divide; a label maker (text) lets you join and cut words; a calendar (dates) lets you count days. Put the right thing in the right container, or the tools stop working properly.
topics.breaks: In a kitchen, a jug simply refuses a label. SQLite is relaxed and lets almost any value into any column, while PostgreSQL rejects the wrong type outright. Don't lean on SQLite's flexibility — write SQL as if every database were strict.
topics.syntax:
CAST(value AS INTEGER)
CAST(value AS REAL)
CAST(value AS TEXT)
howItWorks: An integer divided by an integer gives an integer: `7 / 2` is 3. The part after the point is thrown away.
Make one side a decimal and you get the exact answer: `7 / 2.0` or `CAST(7 AS REAL) / 2` is 3.5.
Text compares character by character, so '10' < '9' as text. Store numbers in number columns.
Dates written as YYYY-MM-DD text sort correctly, because the biggest unit (year) comes first.
A boolean expression such as `salary > 60000` is true or false — or unknown when salary is NULL.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD V["A value"] --> N["Number
INTEGER, DECIMAL, REAL"] V --> T["Text
TEXT, VARCHAR"] V --> D["Date and time
DATE, TIMESTAMP"] V --> B["True or false
BOOLEAN"] N --> N1["add, divide, SUM, AVG"] T --> T1["join, cut, LIKE"] D --> D1["compare, count days"] B --> B1["WHERE conditions"]
diagram.caption: The type decides what you can do with a value. Numbers calculate, text joins and matches patterns, dates compare and count days, and true/false values drive WHERE.

examples.title: Integer division, and how to avoid it
examples.note: This bites in interviews when you compute a percentage: `delivered / total` gives 0. Multiply by 100.0 first.

examples.title: Dates as YYYY-MM-DD text compare correctly
examples.sql:
SELECT name, hire_date
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2022-01-01'
ORDER BY hire_date;
examples.note: Text in single quotes is a string; the comparison works because the year comes first.

keyPoints: INTEGER ÷ INTEGER = INTEGER in SQLite, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. Use 100.0 or CAST to get decimals.
Use DECIMAL or NUMERIC for money: REAL and FLOAT are approximate and can show 0.30000000000000004.
Text values go in single quotes: 'London'. Double quotes are for names of tables or columns.
Store dates in date columns (or YYYY-MM-DD text), never as '06/01/2024', which sorts wrongly.
NULL means "no value" and can appear in any column that isn't NOT NULL.
mistakes: Computing a ratio with two integers and getting 0.
Storing numbers as text and getting '10' sorted before '9'.
Using double quotes for text values. In PostgreSQL, "London" means a column called London.
dialects: MySQL is the odd one out: `7 / 2` returns 3.5000, and `DIV` does whole division.
SQLite has no real DATE or BOOLEAN type: dates are text and true/false are 1 and 0. PostgreSQL has DATE, TIMESTAMP and BOOLEAN types.
`VARCHAR(50)` caps text at 50 characters in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server; SQLite ignores the limit.
topics.interviewAnswer: Data types decide how values compare and calculate. The classic traps are integer division — 7 / 2 is 3 in most databases, so for percentages I multiply by 100.0 first — and storing numbers or dates as text, which makes them sort wrongly. For money I use DECIMAL rather than FLOAT, because floating point can't represent most decimals exactly.

followUps.q: CHAR or VARCHAR?
followUps.a: `CHAR(n)` is fixed length and pads with spaces; `VARCHAR(n)` stores only what you give it, up to n. VARCHAR is the usual choice.

followUps.q: Why not FLOAT for money?
followUps.a: Floating point stores numbers in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. DECIMAL stores exact decimal digits.

explain.answer:
7 and 2 are both whole numbers (integers), and integer divided by integer gives an integer: the part after the point is thrown away, so 7 / 2 is 3. It is not rounded; it is cut off.

Two ways to get 3.5:
• Make one side a decimal: `7 / 2.0` or `7 * 1.0 / 2`.
• Convert it: `CAST(7 AS REAL) / 2`.

The same trap hits averages and percentages built by dividing two integer columns.

write.answer: Divide by 12.0, not 12. One decimal side is enough to make the whole division exact. (To show pounds and pence, wrap it in `ROUND(salary / 12.0, 2)`, from the built-in functions lesson.)

predict.answer:
0, then 0.333…, then 0 (false).

• `1 / 3`: two integers, so the fraction is cut off: 0.
• `1.0 / 3`: one decimal, so the answer is exact: 0.3333333333333333.
• `'5' < '40'`: these are text, so they compare letter by letter, like words in a dictionary. The first characters are 5 and 4, and 5 comes after 4, so '5' is bigger. The answer is false, which SQLite shows as 0.

edge.answer:
Sorting text compares character by character, so you get '10', '100', '9'. The 1s come before the 9.

The quick fix is to sort by the number: `ORDER BY CAST(price AS INTEGER)`. The real fix is to store prices in a number column (INTEGER, or DECIMAL for pence), so they sort, compare and add up correctly everywhere.

Below, WITH just makes a tiny three-row table to test on (you meet it in Phase 4). Change the ORDER BY to plain `price` to see the wrong order.

query.sql:
WITH prices(price) AS (VALUES ('9'), ('10'), ('100'))
SELECT price
FROM prices
ORDER BY CAST(price AS INTEGER);

phases.title: Reading data: SELECT, WHERE and sorting
phases.goal: Pick the columns you want, keep only the rows you want, sort them, and handle the missing values that trip everyone up.
phases.bigPicture: Most queries you will ever write are a SELECT with a WHERE and an ORDER BY. Get these, plus NULL, completely solid, and the rest of SQL is built on top of them.

topics.name: SELECT and FROM: choosing columns
topics.definition: SELECT lists the columns (or calculations) you want in the result, and FROM names the table they come from.
topics.problem: A table can have dozens of columns, and you usually need two or three. You also often need values that are not stored at all — a salary after a raise, a name and city joined into one label. SELECT lets you choose and calculate exactly the columns you need.
topics.idea: After SELECT you write a list, separated by commas. Each item can be a column name (`salary`), a calculation (`salary + 5000`), or a fixed value (`'hello'`). AS gives an item a new name in the result, called an alias. `SELECT *` means every column, in table order. The rows come from the table named after FROM, and every row of that table is used, because there is no filter yet.
topics.analogy: Ordering a set menu but saying "just the starter and the dessert, please". FROM is the menu you are ordering from; SELECT is the courses you want on your plate, in the order you name them.
topics.breaks: A waiter can only bring what is on the menu. SELECT can also bring things that don't exist in the table, because it can calculate new values from the columns on the fly.
topics.syntax:
SELECT column, expression AS new_name
FROM table_name;
howItWorks: The database reads FROM first: it takes every row of employees.
For each row, it works out every item in the SELECT list: name, salary, and salary + 5000.
AS after_raise names the calculated column; without it, the column would be called "salary + 5000".
The result has one row for every row of the table, with just these columns.
Nothing is saved. The calculated column exists only in this result.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR T["employees
emp_id, name, dept_id,
manager_id, salary, hire_date"] -->|"FROM: every row"| S["SELECT name, salary,
salary + 5000 AS after_raise"] S --> R["result
name, salary, after_raise"]
diagram.caption: FROM supplies all six columns of every row; SELECT keeps two of them and calculates a third. The result has the same number of rows but only the columns you asked for.

examples.title: Choose columns and calculate a new one
examples.note: after_raise is calculated for every row and named with AS. The employees table itself is unchanged.

examples.title: Join text together with ||
examples.note: `||` glues strings together. The text in single quotes, ' in ', is a fixed value added to every row.

keyPoints: SELECT chooses and calculates columns; FROM says which table the rows come from.
Separate items with commas — and no comma after the last one.
AS gives a column an alias. Use one for every calculated column, so the result has a readable name.
`SELECT *` is fine for looking at a table, but in real queries name the columns you need: it is clearer, and faster on wide tables.
Without a WHERE, every row of the table is in the result.
mistakes: A trailing comma before FROM: `SELECT name, salary, FROM employees` is a syntax error.
Using double quotes for text. 'London' is text; "London" means a column called London in PostgreSQL.
Using an alias in WHERE in the same query. WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet (Phase 2 explains why).
dialects: Joining text: PostgreSQL and SQLite use `||`; MySQL uses `CONCAT(a, b)`; SQL Server uses `+` or `CONCAT`. `CONCAT` works almost everywhere.
AS is optional for column aliases in every major database (`salary + 5000 after_raise` works), but writing AS is clearer.
topics.interviewAnswer: SELECT defines the columns of the result — stored columns, expressions, or constants — and FROM names the source table. I alias every calculated column with AS so the output is readable, and I avoid SELECT star in production queries: naming columns is clearer, it reads less data, and the query doesn't silently change when someone adds a column.

followUps.q: Why avoid SELECT * in production code?
followUps.a: It reads columns you don't need, can stop the database using a covering index, and the result changes shape when a column is added — which can break the code that reads it.

followUps.q: Can you SELECT without FROM?
followUps.a: Yes in SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server: `SELECT 2 + 3;` returns 5. Oracle needs `FROM dual`.

explain.answer:
FROM says which table to read: `FROM employees` means "look at the employees sheet".

SELECT says which columns to give back, and in what order: `SELECT name, salary` returns just those two, even though the table has six. It can also work things out, such as `salary + 5000`.

AS gives a column a new name in the result: `salary + 5000 AS after_raise`. Without it, the column would be called "salary + 5000". AS only renames the result; the table itself does not change.

write.answer: Work out the new column in SELECT and name it with AS. Every product comes back, because there is no WHERE.

predict.answer: 8 rows and 2 columns. There is no WHERE, so you get one row per employee. SELECT returns exactly what you list, and you listed name twice, so both columns are the same name. Asking for a column twice is allowed; it is just pointless.

edge.answer:
NULL. NULL means "unknown", and unknown plus 5000 is still unknown. There is no error and no 5000: the NULL quietly spreads through the sum.

If a missing salary should count as 0, say so: `COALESCE(salary, 0) + 5000`.

query.sql: SELECT NULL + 5000;

topics.name: WHERE: keeping only the rows you want
topics.definition: WHERE keeps only the rows for which a condition is true, using comparisons such as =, <>, <, > and the words AND, OR and NOT.
topics.problem: Tables hold every row ever stored, and you almost always want a slice: one department, orders over £100, everyone hired this year. WHERE is how you say which rows count.
topics.idea: A condition is a statement about a row that is either true or false, like `salary > 60000`. The database checks it against every row and keeps the rows where it is true. You can combine conditions: AND needs both to be true, OR needs at least one, and NOT flips true and false. Comparisons are `=`, `<>` (not equal; `!=` also works), `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Text values go in single quotes.
topics.analogy: A bouncer with a list of rules. Every row walks up to the door; if it passes the rules, it gets in. "Over 18 AND on the guest list" is stricter than "over 18 OR on the guest list".
topics.breaks: A bouncer answers yes or no. SQL has a third answer, unknown, which comes from NULL — and WHERE treats unknown the same as no. The NULL lesson next in this phase shows why that matters.
howItWorks: FROM takes every row of employees.
WHERE checks the condition `dept_id = 1 AND salary < 90000` on each row.
Asha: department 1 is true, but 95000 < 90000 is false. Both must be true for AND, so Asha is dropped.
Ben, Chen and Hana pass both tests, so they are kept. Everyone outside department 1 fails the first test.
SELECT then picks the columns from the rows that are left.
AND is worked out before OR, just as × comes before + in maths. Use brackets whenever you mix them.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR R["every row of employees"] --> C{"dept_id = 1
AND salary under 90000?"} C -->|"true"| K["kept:
Ben, Chen, Hana"] C -->|"false or unknown"| D["dropped:
Asha and the rest"]
diagram.caption: WHERE is a filter: each row is tested one at a time. Only rows where the condition is true go through. False and unknown are both dropped.

examples.title: Two conditions with AND
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 1 AND salary < 90000
ORDER BY name;
examples.note: Asha is in department 1 but fails the salary test, and AND needs both tests to pass.

examples.title: OR inside brackets
examples.sql:
SELECT name, dept_id, salary
FROM employees
WHERE (dept_id = 2 OR dept_id = 3) AND salary > 50000
ORDER BY name;
examples.note: Read it as: in department 2 or 3, and also earning over 50000. Eli is in department 2 but earns 45000.

examples.title: The same query without brackets — a different answer
examples.sql:
SELECT name, dept_id, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 2 OR dept_id = 3 AND salary > 50000
ORDER BY name;
examples.note: AND is worked out first, so this means: department 2 (any salary), or department 3 with a salary over 50000. Eli sneaks in. Brackets remove the doubt.

keyPoints: WHERE runs on each row, before any grouping, and keeps only rows where the condition is true.
Comparisons: =, <> (or !=), <, <=, >, >=. One = sign, not two.
AND needs both sides true; OR needs at least one; NOT flips the answer.
AND binds tighter than OR. Put brackets around every OR that is mixed with AND.
Text goes in single quotes and must match exactly: 'Sales' is not 'sales' in most databases.
mistakes: Mixing AND and OR without brackets, and getting extra rows.
Writing `==`. SQL uses a single `=` for comparing.
Writing `WHERE dept_id = 2 OR 3`. Each side of OR must be a full condition: `dept_id = 2 OR dept_id = 3`, or better, `dept_id IN (2, 3)`.
dialects: Text comparison: PostgreSQL is case-sensitive ('Sales' ≠ 'sales'); MySQL and SQL Server usually are not, depending on settings; in SQLite `=` is case-sensitive but LIKE is not.
topics.interviewAnswer: WHERE filters rows before any grouping: the database evaluates the condition for each row and keeps only those where it is true — false and unknown are both dropped. I combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT, and because AND has higher precedence than OR, I always bracket OR conditions when mixing them, so the query says exactly what I mean.

followUps.q: Which is evaluated first, AND or OR?
followUps.a: AND. `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`. Brackets make it explicit.

followUps.q: Can WHERE use a column alias from SELECT?
followUps.a: No in standard SQL, because WHERE runs before SELECT. Repeat the expression, or wrap the query in a subquery or CTE. (SQLite and MySQL are lenient about this; don't rely on it.)

explain.answer:
AND needs both conditions to be true. OR needs at least one.

`WHERE status = 'delivered' AND amount > 100` returns orders that are both delivered and over £100: just 101 and 104.

`WHERE status = 'delivered' OR amount > 100` returns orders that are either: all 7 delivered orders, plus 105, which is only shipped but is over £100. That makes 8.

So AND makes the result smaller, and OR makes it bigger.

write.answer: "At least £75" includes £75, so use `>=`. Order 108 is exactly £75; with `>` it would be missed.

query.sql:
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'delivered' AND amount >= 75
ORDER BY order_id;

predict.answer:
Dara, Eli and Fatima. Gus is not in the list.

Gus's dept_id is NULL. `dept_id = 1` is unknown for him, and NOT unknown is still unknown, not true. WHERE keeps only true rows, so he is dropped. To include him, add `OR dept_id IS NULL`.

query.sql:
SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE NOT dept_id = 1
ORDER BY name;

edge.answer:
Add brackets around the OR: `WHERE (status = 'shipped' OR status = 'pending') AND amount > 40`.

AND is worked out before OR, so the original really meant "shipped (any amount), or pending and over £40".

Here both versions return only order 105. That is luck: the only shipped order is £150, and the only pending one (110) is £33. If a shipped order were £20, the original would wrongly include it. The brackets make the query say what you mean, whatever the data.

query.sql:
SELECT order_id, status, amount
FROM orders
WHERE (status = 'shipped' OR status = 'pending') AND amount > 40
ORDER BY order_id;

topics.name: IN, BETWEEN and LIKE: shorter conditions
topics.definition: IN checks a value against a list, BETWEEN checks a range (both ends included), and LIKE matches text against a pattern with % (any number of characters) and _ (exactly one).
topics.problem: `status = 'shipped' OR status = 'pending' OR status = 'cancelled'` is long and easy to get wrong. Questions like "names starting with P" or "orders in February" come up all the time. These three words make such conditions short and readable.
topics.idea: IN: `status IN ('shipped', 'pending')` is true when status equals any value in the list. BETWEEN: `amount BETWEEN 50 AND 100` means `amount >= 50 AND amount <= 100`, ends included. LIKE: `product_name LIKE 'P%'` matches text starting with P; `%` stands for any number of characters (even none) and `_` for exactly one. Put NOT in front of any of them to flip it: NOT IN, NOT BETWEEN, NOT LIKE.
topics.analogy: IN is a guest list: is your name on it? BETWEEN is a height limit at a fair ride: between 1.2 m and 1.9 m, both ends allowed. LIKE is a crossword clue with blanks: "P _ _" fits Pen.
topics.breaks: A guest list doesn't care about missing names, but SQL does: if the list after NOT IN contains a NULL, nothing matches at all. Phase 4 shows this trap.
topics.syntax:
WHERE column IN (value1, value2)
WHERE column BETWEEN low AND high
WHERE text_column LIKE 'pattern%'
howItWorks: `status IN ('shipped', 'pending')` is checked against each order: shipped matches, pending matches, delivered doesn't.
`order_date BETWEEN '2024-02-01' AND '2024-02-29'` keeps every date from the 1st to the 29th of February, both days included.
`product_name LIKE 'P%'` keeps Pen and Phone case: P, then anything.
`LIKE '%s'` keeps names ending in s: Headphones.
`LIKE '_en'` means exactly one character, then "en": Pen matches, but Phone case doesn't.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD V["a value in a row"] --> I["IN (a, b, c)
equal to any one of them?"] V --> B["BETWEEN low AND high
low or more, and high or less?"] V --> L["LIKE pattern
% any run of characters
_ exactly one character"]
diagram.caption: Three shortcuts for common conditions: IN for a list of values, BETWEEN for a range with both ends included, and LIKE for a text pattern.

examples.title: IN: one of a list
examples.sql:
SELECT order_id, status
FROM orders
WHERE status IN ('shipped', 'pending')
ORDER BY order_id;
examples.note: The same as `status = 'shipped' OR status = 'pending'`, but shorter and harder to get wrong.

examples.title: BETWEEN: a range of dates
examples.sql:
SELECT order_id, order_date, amount
FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-02-01' AND '2024-02-29'
ORDER BY order_date;
examples.note: Both ends are included. This works because the dates are YYYY-MM-DD text; with real timestamps, see the mistakes below.

examples.title: LIKE: text patterns
examples.sql:
SELECT product_name
FROM products
WHERE product_name LIKE 'P%' OR product_name LIKE '%s'
ORDER BY product_name;
examples.note: 'P%' finds names starting with P; '%s' finds names ending in s.

keyPoints: `x IN (a, b)` means `x = a OR x = b`.
`x BETWEEN a AND b` means `x >= a AND x <= b` — both ends included, and a must be the smaller value.
LIKE wildcards: `%` is any number of characters (including none); `_` is exactly one character.
NOT IN, NOT BETWEEN and NOT LIKE flip each test.
A LIKE pattern that starts with % ('%son') can't use a normal index, so it is slow on big tables.
mistakes: Using BETWEEN on timestamps: `BETWEEN '2024-02-01' AND '2024-02-29'` misses everything after midnight on the 29th. Use `>= '2024-02-01' AND < '2024-03-01'` instead.
Writing BETWEEN with the bigger value first: `BETWEEN 100 AND 50` returns nothing.
Forgetting the % in LIKE: `LIKE 'P'` only matches the exact text P.
dialects: Case: LIKE ignores case in SQLite and usually in MySQL and SQL Server, but is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL, which has ILIKE for case-insensitive matching.
SQL Server also allows `[abc]` sets in LIKE patterns; PostgreSQL has full regular expressions with `~`.
topics.interviewAnswer: IN tests membership in a list and is shorthand for several ORs; BETWEEN tests an inclusive range; LIKE matches text patterns, where percent is any sequence of characters and underscore is exactly one. Two cautions: for timestamps I use a half-open range — greater-or-equal the start and less-than the next day — rather than BETWEEN, and a leading-wildcard LIKE can't use a B-tree index.

followUps.q: Is BETWEEN inclusive?
followUps.a: Yes, at both ends. `BETWEEN 1 AND 5` includes 1 and 5.

followUps.q: How would you find names containing an actual % sign?
followUps.a: Escape it: `LIKE '%!%%' ESCAPE '!'`. The ESCAPE character says the next % is a real percent sign.

followUps.q: Why is `LIKE '%term%'` slow?
followUps.a: An index is sorted from the first character, so a pattern that can start anywhere forces a scan of every row. Full-text search indexes solve that.

explain.answer:
% means "any number of characters, including none". `LIKE 'P%'` matches anything starting with P: Pen and Phone case.

_ means "exactly one character". `LIKE '_en'` matches three-letter words ending in "en": Pen, but not "Phone case" or "en".

Without % or _, LIKE is just an exact match. In SQLite, LIKE ignores upper and lower case for plain English letters; in PostgreSQL it doesn't (use ILIKE there).

query.sql:
SELECT product_name
FROM products
WHERE product_name LIKE '_en' OR product_name LIKE 'P%'
ORDER BY product_name;

write.answer: BETWEEN includes both ends, so run from the first day of 2020 to the last day of 2021. Dates stored as YYYY-MM-DD text compare correctly as text.

query.sql:
SELECT name, hire_date
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date BETWEEN '2020-01-01' AND '2021-12-31'
ORDER BY hire_date;

predict.answer: Headphones, Notebook and Phone case: every name with an "o" anywhere in it. %o% means "anything, then an o, then anything". Pen, Mug, Desk lamp and Backpack have no o.

query.sql:
SELECT product_name
FROM products
WHERE product_name LIKE '%o%'
ORDER BY product_name;

edge.answer:
Neither returns it.

`NULL BETWEEN 0 AND 1000` is unknown, because you can't say whether an unknown number is in the range. `NOT BETWEEN` is NOT unknown, which is still unknown. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true, so order 106 falls through both.

That means "in range" plus "not in range" does not add up to every row when there are NULLs. The query below shows both tests for customer 3's orders.

query.sql:
SELECT order_id, amount,
       amount BETWEEN 0 AND 1000 AS in_range,
       amount NOT BETWEEN 0 AND 1000 AS out_of_range
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 3
ORDER BY order_id;

topics.name: NULL: the missing value
topics.definition: NULL means "no value" or "unknown"; any comparison with it — even `NULL = NULL` — is unknown rather than true, so you test for it with IS NULL and replace it with COALESCE.
topics.problem: Real data has gaps: an employee with no manager, an order with no amount. NULL causes more wrong answers than anything else in SQL, because it doesn't behave like a normal value. Rows quietly vanish from filters, and sums and averages change, without any error message.
topics.idea: NULL is not zero and not empty text; it means "we don't know". So SQL uses three-valued logic: a condition can be true, false or unknown. `manager_id = NULL` is unknown for every row — even a NULL one, because "is this unknown thing equal to that unknown thing?" is itself unknown. WHERE keeps only true, so the query returns nothing. To test for NULL, use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL (`10 + NULL` is NULL). `COALESCE(a, b, …)` returns the first value that isn't NULL, which is how you put in a default.
topics.analogy: A form with a blank box for "age". Is a blank age over 30? You can't say yes, and you can't say no — you just don't know. Are two blank ages equal? You don't know that either.
topics.breaks: A person looking at two blank boxes might say "they're both blank, so they match". SQL never does that with `=`. Only IS NULL, IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, and grouping (GROUP BY puts all NULLs together) treat NULLs as alike.
topics.syntax:
WHERE column IS NULL
WHERE column IS NOT NULL
COALESCE(column, default_value)
howItWorks: `WHERE manager_id = NULL`: for Asha, NULL = NULL is unknown; for everyone else, 1 = NULL is unknown. Nothing is true, so no rows come back.
`WHERE manager_id IS NULL`: true for Asha only. IS NULL is a real test that answers yes or no.
`WHERE dept_id <> 1`: for Gus, NULL <> 1 is unknown, so Gus is dropped — even though he is clearly not in department 1.
To keep him, say so: `WHERE dept_id <> 1 OR dept_id IS NULL`.
`COALESCE(amount, 0)` turns order 106's NULL into 0 and leaves the other amounts alone.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["a condition
on one row"] --> T["true"] C --> F["false"] C --> U["unknown
anything compared with NULL"] T -->|"WHERE keeps"| K["kept"] F -->|"WHERE drops"| D["dropped"] U -->|"WHERE drops"| D
diagram.caption: SQL has three answers, not two. Any comparison with NULL is unknown, and WHERE only keeps rows whose answer is true — so rows with NULLs quietly disappear.

examples.title: = NULL never matches
examples.note: No error, and no rows — the most dangerous kind of bug. Asha has a NULL manager_id, but NULL = NULL is unknown, not true.

examples.title: IS NULL is the right test
NULL quietly drops a row from "not equal"
examples.sql:
SELECT name, dept_id
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id <> 1
ORDER BY name;
examples.note: Gus is missing. His department is unknown, so "not 1" is unknown, and WHERE drops him. Add `OR dept_id IS NULL` to keep him.

examples.title: COALESCE puts in a default
examples.sql:
SELECT order_id, amount, COALESCE(amount, 0) AS amount_or_zero
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 3
ORDER BY order_id;
examples.note: COALESCE returns its first argument that isn't NULL. Choose the default carefully: 0 is right for "nothing paid", but wrong if it means "we don't know".

keyPoints: NULL means unknown or missing. It is not 0 and not ''.
Never write `= NULL` or `<> NULL`. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.
Any comparison with NULL is unknown, and WHERE drops unknown rows — including from `<>` and NOT IN.
Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: `10 + NULL` is NULL.
`COALESCE(a, b, c)` returns the first non-NULL value. `NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL when a = b — handy to avoid dividing by zero.
Aggregates (SUM, AVG, COUNT of a column) skip NULLs — Phase 2 covers this.
mistakes: Writing `WHERE manager_id = NULL` and getting no rows, with no error.
Forgetting that `<>` drops NULL rows: "everyone not in Sales" silently loses people with no department.
Replacing NULL with 0 in an average, which changes the answer. Decide what the gap really means first.
dialects: NULL-safe equality: PostgreSQL and SQLite have `a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b` (true when both are NULL); MySQL has `a <=> b`.
COALESCE works everywhere. MySQL also has `IFNULL(a, b)`, SQL Server has `ISNULL(a, b)`, and Oracle has `NVL(a, b)` — all for two arguments.
In Oracle, empty text '' is treated as NULL. No other major database does this.
topics.interviewAnswer: NULL represents a missing or unknown value, and SQL uses three-valued logic: comparisons with NULL return unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows that are true. So I never compare with equals NULL — I use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL — and I watch for filters like not-equal or NOT IN silently dropping NULL rows. When I need a default I use COALESCE, but only after deciding whether the gap really means zero.

followUps.q: What does NULL = NULL return?
followUps.a: NULL (unknown), not true. Use IS NULL, or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM to compare two values that might both be NULL.

followUps.q: Does `COUNT(*)` count NULLs?
followUps.a: `COUNT(*)` counts rows, so yes. `COUNT(column)` counts only the rows where that column is not NULL.

followUps.q: How do you avoid dividing by zero?
followUps.a: Wrap the divisor in NULLIF: `a / NULLIF(b, 0)` returns NULL instead of an error when b is 0.

explain.answer:
In SQL a condition can be true, false or unknown. That is three-valued logic. Any comparison with NULL is unknown, because you can't compare against a value nobody knows.

`WHERE manager_id = NULL` asks "is manager_id equal to unknown?" for each row. The answer is unknown every time, even for Asha, whose manager_id really is NULL. WHERE keeps only rows that are true, so no rows come back.

To find missing values, ask a different question: `WHERE manager_id IS NULL`. IS NULL is always true or false, never unknown.

write.answer: Use IS NULL, never `= NULL`. Only Zoe has no city.

predict.answer:
NULL, 1 (true), NULL, 7.

• `NULL = NULL`: two unknowns can't be called equal, so it is unknown: NULL.
• `NULL IS NULL`: true, which SQLite shows as 1.
• `5 + NULL`: any sum with NULL is NULL.
• `COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 7)`: the first value that is not NULL, which is 7.

query.sql: SELECT NULL = NULL, NULL IS NULL, 5 + NULL, COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 7);

edge.answer:
`dept_id <> 1` alone misses Gus, because `NULL <> 1` is unknown. Add the NULL case on purpose with `OR dept_id IS NULL`.

Other ways that also work: `COALESCE(dept_id, 0) <> 1`, or `dept_id IS NOT 1` in SQLite (`IS DISTINCT FROM 1` in PostgreSQL).

query.sql:
SELECT name, dept_id
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id <> 1 OR dept_id IS NULL
ORDER BY name;

topics.name: ORDER BY, LIMIT and OFFSET: sorting and top N
topics.definition: ORDER BY sorts the result by one or more columns (ASC for smallest first, DESC for largest first), and LIMIT keeps only the first n rows, with OFFSET to skip some first.
topics.problem: "The 3 highest salaries", "the newest orders first", "page 2 of the results" — order matters to people. And without ORDER BY, the database may return rows in any order it likes, which can change from one run to the next.
topics.idea: ORDER BY salary DESC sorts biggest first. Add more columns to break ties: `ORDER BY salary DESC, name` sorts by salary, and people with the same salary by name. ASC (smallest first) is the default. LIMIT 3 keeps the first 3 rows after sorting. OFFSET 3 skips 3 rows first, which is how page 2 works when there are 3 rows per page. Without an ORDER BY, LIMIT just takes whichever rows come first — an arbitrary choice.
topics.analogy: A race. ORDER BY lines the runners up by finishing time; LIMIT 3 hands out gold, silver and bronze. OFFSET 3 LIMIT 3 is "who came 4th, 5th and 6th?".
topics.breaks: In a race, two runners on the same time share a place. LIMIT doesn't: it cuts at exactly n rows, so if 3rd and 4th place tie, one of them is dropped without warning. Phase 5 (RANK) handles ties properly.
topics.syntax:
SELECT columns
FROM table_name
ORDER BY column1 DESC, column2 ASC
LIMIT n OFFSET skip;
howItWorks: The database finds all the rows first (FROM, then WHERE).
ORDER BY salary DESC puts the highest salary first: Asha 95000, Hana 80000, then Ben and Chen on 70000…
Ben and Chen tie on salary, so the second sort column, name, decides: Ben before Chen.
LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows: Asha, Hana, Ben. Chen is cut off even though he earns the same as Ben.
OFFSET 3 LIMIT 3 would skip those three and return the next three.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["rows in any order"] -->|"ORDER BY salary DESC, name"| B["1 Asha 95000
2 Hana 80000
3 Ben 70000
4 Chen 70000
5 Dara 60000 …"] B -->|"LIMIT 3"| C["Asha, Hana, Ben"]
diagram.caption: First sort, then cut. Ben and Chen tie on 70000, so the second sort column decides who comes first — and LIMIT 3 silently drops Chen.

examples.title: Sort by salary, then by name
examples.note: DESC applies only to salary. name has no direction, so it is ASC (A to Z).

examples.title: Top 3 with LIMIT — and the tie it hides
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, name
LIMIT 3;
examples.note: Chen earns the same as Ben but is cut off. If the question is "the top 3 salaries", say the tie out loud in an interview.

examples.title: Page 2, three rows per page
examples.sql:
SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;
examples.note: OFFSET 3 skips the first page (orders 101–103). For page n, use OFFSET (n − 1) × page size.

examples.title: Where do NULLs go?
examples.note: SQLite and MySQL put NULLs first when sorting A to Z; PostgreSQL puts them last. Write NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST to be sure.

keyPoints: Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed — even if it looks sorted today.
ASC (default) is smallest first; DESC is largest first. Each column gets its own direction.
Add a second sort column to break ties, so the order is the same every time.
LIMIT cuts after sorting. It ignores ties.
OFFSET skips rows; it is fine for small pages but slow for deep pages, because the skipped rows are still read.
mistakes: Using LIMIT without ORDER BY and expecting the "top" rows.
Writing `ORDER BY salary, name DESC` and expecting both to be descending. DESC applies only to the column right before it.
Answering "top 3 salaries" with LIMIT 3 when there are ties.
dialects: SQL Server uses `SELECT TOP 3 …`, or `OFFSET 3 ROWS FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY`. Oracle and the SQL standard use `FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY`. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite use LIMIT.
NULL position: PostgreSQL and Oracle put NULLs last for ASC; SQLite, MySQL and SQL Server put them first. PostgreSQL and SQLite accept NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST.
topics.interviewAnswer: ORDER BY sorts the final result, with ASC or DESC per column, and I always add a tiebreaker column so the order is deterministic. LIMIT and OFFSET then cut the sorted result. I point out two caveats: LIMIT ignores ties, so "top 3" may need RANK instead; and large OFFSETs are slow, so for deep pagination I use keyset pagination — WHERE id greater than the last id seen.

followUps.q: Is the order of rows guaranteed without ORDER BY?
followUps.a: No. The database returns rows in whatever order is cheapest, and it can change with indexes, data or version.

followUps.q: What is keyset pagination?
followUps.a: Instead of OFFSET, remember the last value you showed and ask for `WHERE order_id > 106 ORDER BY order_id LIMIT 3`. It uses the index, so page 1000 is as fast as page 1.

followUps.q: Can you ORDER BY a column you didn't SELECT?
followUps.a: Yes, in most cases. The exception is with DISTINCT, where you can only sort by selected columns.

practice.write: Write a query for the 2 most expensive products, showing product_name and price.

explain.answer:
Because of a tie. Asha (95,000) and Hana (80,000) are first and second, and Ben and Chen both earn 70,000, so they share third place.

`ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3` must cut one of them, and which one depends on the tie-breaker. With no tie-breaker it is whichever the database happens to return first. Either way you leave out someone who is just as highly paid.

So first ask: should ties be included? If yes, the answer has 4 people. Use RANK or DENSE_RANK (Phase 5), or `WHERE salary >= ` the third-highest salary. If no, say how you break the tie, for example `ORDER BY salary DESC, name`.

write.answer: Sort from most expensive and keep 2. The next product is the £25 desk lamp, so there is no tie to worry about here (but always check for one).

query.sql:
SELECT product_name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 2;

predict.answer: Gus, then Hana: the two most recent hires. DESC puts the latest date first. Gus joined on 2023-04-03 and Hana on 2022-11-30. Dates in YYYY-MM-DD form sort correctly even though they are text.

query.sql:
SELECT name, hire_date
FROM employees
ORDER BY hire_date DESC
LIMIT 2;

edge.answer:
SQLite puts NULLs first when sorting A to Z, so Zoe would come first. Sort by "is the city missing?" first: `city IS NULL` is 0 for a real city and 1 for NULL, so the missing one goes last.

SQLite and PostgreSQL also accept `ORDER BY city NULLS LAST, name`, which gives the same rows. The `IS NULL` trick also works in MySQL, which has no NULLS LAST.

topics.name: DISTINCT: removing duplicate rows
topics.definition: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result, where two rows are duplicates only if every selected column is the same.
topics.problem: "Which cities do our departments sit in?" lists London twice. "Which customers ordered in January?" lists Priya three times. DISTINCT gives each answer once.
topics.idea: DISTINCT goes straight after SELECT and applies to the whole row you selected, not to one column. `SELECT DISTINCT location` compares only location, so London appears once. `SELECT DISTINCT name, customer_id` compares both, so two Toms with different ids are both kept. For DISTINCT, NULLs count as equal to each other, so many NULLs become one.
topics.analogy: Collecting football stickers: when you sort your pile, you keep one of each and put the swaps aside. Two stickers count as the same only if they are completely identical.
topics.breaks: With stickers you can choose which copy to keep. DISTINCT can't: it keeps one row of each and throws the rest away, without remembering how many there were. If you need the count, use GROUP BY.
topics.syntax:
SELECT DISTINCT column1, column2
FROM table_name;
howItWorks: The database builds the rows with just the selected columns.
It compares whole rows: two rows are duplicates only if every selected column matches.
It keeps one copy of each distinct row.
ORDER BY then sorts what is left.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["London
Manchester
London
Leeds"] -->|"DISTINCT"| B["Leeds
London
Manchester"]
diagram.caption: DISTINCT collapses identical rows into one. Here the second London disappears, and ORDER BY sorts what is left.

examples.title: One column
examples.note: Engineering and Marketing are both in London, but London appears once.

examples.title: Several columns: the whole row must match
examples.note: Tom's two sign-ups have the same name and email, so they collapse into one row.

examples.title: Add a column that differs, and the duplicates come back
examples.note: The ids differ, so both Toms stay. DISTINCT works on the row, not on one column.

keyPoints: DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row, never to just one column.
Adding a unique column (like an id) to a DISTINCT query makes it do nothing.
NULLs count as equal for DISTINCT: many NULLs become one.
`COUNT(DISTINCT column)` counts the different values — Phase 2.
DISTINCT has to compare every row, which costs time on big results.
mistakes: Writing `SELECT DISTINCT(name), email` and thinking only name is distinct. The brackets do nothing; the whole row is compared.
Using DISTINCT to hide duplicates caused by a wrong join. Fix the join instead (Phase 3).
Using DISTINCT when you actually need a count per value. That is GROUP BY.
dialects: PostgreSQL has `DISTINCT ON (column)`, which keeps the first row for each value of that column — handy for "latest order per customer". Elsewhere, use ROW_NUMBER (Phase 5).
topics.interviewAnswer: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result, comparing all the selected columns together, with NULLs treated as equal. I use it for lists of unique values, but if I find myself adding DISTINCT to fix unexpected duplicates, I go back and check the join, because DISTINCT can hide a fan-out that also breaks sums and counts.

followUps.q: DISTINCT or GROUP BY?
followUps.a: For a plain list of unique values they give the same result. Use GROUP BY when you also need aggregates per value, such as counts.

followUps.q: Does DISTINCT apply to one column or the whole row?
followUps.a: The whole row of selected columns, always.

practice.write: Write a query for the list of customer ids who have placed at least one order, each id once, sorted.

explain.answer:
DISTINCT removes a row only when every selected column matches another row. Tom has two sign-ups, with customer_id 2 and 6. So the rows are (2, Tom) and (6, Tom): the names match, but the ids don't, so they are different rows and both stay.

Drop customer_id and select just name, and the two Toms become one.

write.answer: orders has one row per order, so customer 1 appears five times. DISTINCT keeps each id once. Customers 4 (Omar) and 6 (the second Tom) never ordered, so they are not in orders at all.

predict.answer: 4 rows: cancelled, delivered, pending and shipped. There are 10 orders but only four different statuses. (ORDER BY is added below so the order is fixed.)

edge.answer:
4 rows: 1, 2, 3 and NULL. Yes, the NULL counts.

DISTINCT treats all NULLs as one group, even though `NULL = NULL` is not true in a WHERE. Gus's missing department gives one NULL row. Department 4 (HR) is not in the list, because nobody works there.

topics.name: CASE WHEN: if-then logic inside a query
topics.definition: CASE WHEN condition THEN value … ELSE value END returns a value chosen by the first condition that is true, so a query can label, group or tidy values row by row.
topics.problem: Data often needs sorting into buckets — salary bands, "open" or "closed" orders, "new" or "returning" customers — and those labels aren't stored anywhere. CASE builds them inside the query. It is also the key to counting several things in one pass (Phase 2) and to pivoting.
topics.idea: CASE is SQL's if-else. For each row, it checks the WHEN conditions from top to bottom and returns the THEN value of the first one that is true. If none is true, it returns the ELSE value — or NULL if there is no ELSE. CASE is an expression, so it can go anywhere a value can: in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, or inside SUM and COUNT. The short form, `CASE status WHEN 'shipped' THEN …`, compares one column with several values.
topics.analogy: Sorting post into pigeonholes. You read the address, check the first rule ("London?"), then the next ("Leeds?"), and drop the letter into the first hole that fits. Anything that fits no rule goes into "other" — that is ELSE.
topics.breaks: A postal worker can put one letter in two holes by mistake. CASE never does: it stops at the first true WHEN, so the order of the WHENs matters. Put the strictest test first.
topics.syntax:
CASE
  WHEN condition1 THEN value1
  WHEN condition2 THEN value2
  ELSE other_value
END AS new_column
howItWorks: For Asha (95000): `salary >= 80000` is true, so the band is 'high', and CASE stops.
For Ben (70000): the first test is false; `salary >= 50000` is true, so 'medium'.
For Eli (45000): both tests are false, so ELSE gives 'low'.
If the tests were in the other order (>= 50000 first), Asha would wrongly get 'medium'. Order matters.
END closes the CASE, and AS names the new column.

diagram.caption: CASE checks its WHEN conditions in order and returns the first match. A row that matches nothing gets the ELSE value — or NULL if there is no ELSE.

examples.title: Salary bands
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE
         WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'high'
         WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'medium'
         ELSE 'low'
       END AS band
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, name;

examples.title: The short form: compare one column
examples.sql:
SELECT order_id, status,
       CASE status
         WHEN 'delivered' THEN 'closed'
         WHEN 'cancelled' THEN 'closed'
         ELSE 'open'
       END AS state
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1
ORDER BY order_id;

examples.title: No ELSE means NULL
examples.sql:
SELECT name, CASE WHEN dept_id = 1 THEN 'engineering' END AS team
FROM employees
WHERE salary <= 70000
ORDER BY name;
examples.note: Rows that match no WHEN get NULL. Add an ELSE whenever NULL isn't what you want.

keyPoints: CASE returns the THEN value of the first true WHEN, then stops.
No ELSE means NULL for rows that match nothing.
Always finish with END, and name the result with AS.
CASE is an expression: it works in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY and inside aggregates.
Every THEN should return the same type — all text, or all numbers.
mistakes: Putting the loose condition first (`>= 50000` before `>= 80000`), so the strict one is never reached.
Forgetting END, which gives a syntax error.
Writing `CASE status WHEN NULL THEN …`. The short form uses =, so it never matches NULL. Use `CASE WHEN status IS NULL THEN …`.
dialects: MySQL and SQLite also have `IF(condition, a, b)` / `IIF(condition, a, b)`, and SQL Server has IIF. CASE works everywhere, so learn CASE.
topics.interviewAnswer: CASE is SQL's conditional expression: it evaluates WHEN conditions in order and returns the first matching THEN value, or the ELSE value, or NULL if there is no ELSE. Because it is an expression it works anywhere — I use it to bucket values, to sort in a custom order, and most of all inside aggregates, like SUM of CASE WHEN status equals delivered THEN 1, to count several categories in a single pass.

followUps.q: What happens when no WHEN matches and there is no ELSE?
followUps.a: CASE returns NULL.

followUps.q: How would you sort orders with pending first, then shipped, then the rest?
followUps.a: `ORDER BY CASE status WHEN 'pending' THEN 1 WHEN 'shipped' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END`.

practice.write: Write a query that labels each product as 'cheap' (under £10), 'mid' (£10 to £29) or 'premium' (£30 and up), sorted by price.
practice.predict: What `state` does each of Tom's orders get in the short-form example? (Change customer_id to 2 in your head.)
