explain.answer:
CASE checks the WHEN lines from top to bottom and stops at the first one that is true. So the most specific test must come first.

The right order is `WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'high'`, then `WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'medium'`, then ELSE 'low'.

Swap the first two lines and Asha (95,000) meets `>= 50000` first. That is true, so she becomes 'medium', and the 'high' line is never reached for anyone. The query below has the lines swapped: nobody is high.

query.sql:
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE
         WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'medium'
         WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'high'
         ELSE 'low'
       END AS band
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, name;

write.answer: Test the cheapest band first; then each line only needs an upper limit. "Under £10" is `< 10`, and "£10 to £29" is `< 30` once the first line has taken the cheap ones.

query.sql:
SELECT product_name, price,
       CASE
         WHEN price < 10 THEN 'cheap'
         WHEN price < 30 THEN 'mid'
         ELSE 'premium'
       END AS price_band
FROM products
ORDER BY price;

predict.answer: Tom (customer 2) has two orders, 104 and 108. Both are delivered, so both are 'closed'.

query.sql:
SELECT order_id, status,
       CASE status
         WHEN 'delivered' THEN 'closed'
         WHEN 'cancelled' THEN 'closed'
         ELSE 'open'
       END AS state
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 2
ORDER BY order_id;

edge.answer: Test for NULL first. If you don't, `NULL > 100` is unknown, not true, so order 106 falls through to ELSE and is wrongly labelled 'small'.

query.sql:
SELECT order_id, amount,
       CASE
         WHEN amount IS NULL THEN 'unknown'
         WHEN amount > 100 THEN 'big'
         ELSE 'small'
       END AS size
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_id;

topics.name: Built-in functions for text, numbers and dates
topics.definition: Functions such as UPPER, LENGTH, SUBSTR, ROUND and the date functions transform a value inside a query — one value in, one value out, for each row.
topics.problem: Data rarely arrives in the shape you need: names in mixed case, prices that need rounding, dates you want as "2024-03" or as "how many days ago". Functions do these small transformations inside the query.
topics.idea: A function takes values in brackets and returns one value. Text: UPPER and LOWER change case, LENGTH counts characters, `SUBSTR(text, start, length)` cuts out a piece (counting from 1), TRIM removes spaces at the ends, and REPLACE swaps text. Numbers: `ROUND(x, 2)` rounds to 2 decimal places, ABS removes the minus sign. Dates are where databases differ most: SQLite uses strftime and julianday; PostgreSQL uses DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT and date subtraction. These run once per row — unlike aggregate functions, which turn many rows into one (Phase 2).
topics.analogy: Kitchen tools. A peeler (TRIM), a slicer (SUBSTR), a measuring spoon (ROUND). Each one takes one ingredient and gives back a changed version of it.
topics.breaks: Kitchen tools are the same in every kitchen. Date functions are not the same in every database — so in an interview, say which database you are assuming, and the interviewer will usually accept any reasonable syntax.
topics.syntax:
UPPER(text)   LENGTH(text)   SUBSTR(text, start, length)
ROUND(number, places)
strftime('%Y-%m', date)   -- SQLite: the year and month
howItWorks: `UPPER('Dara')` is 'DARA'; `LENGTH('Dara')` is 4; `SUBSTR('Dara', 1, 3)` is 'Dar' (start at character 1, take 3).
salary / 12.0 gives a long decimal; `ROUND(…, 2)` keeps 2 decimal places.
`strftime('%Y-%m', '2024-01-21')` is '2024-01': the year and month, ready to group by.
julianday turns a date into a day number, so subtracting two of them gives the days between.
Functions can be nested: `UPPER(SUBSTR(name, 1, 1))` is the first letter in capitals.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["one value per row
Dara · 52000 · 2024-01-21"] --> F["a function
UPPER · ROUND · strftime"] --> B["one new value per row
DARA · 4333.33 · 2024-01"]
diagram.caption: A row function changes each value on its own: one value in, one value out, for every row. Aggregate functions in Phase 2 do the opposite and squash many rows into one.

examples.title: Text functions
examples.sql:
SELECT name, UPPER(name) AS shout, LENGTH(name) AS letters, SUBSTR(name, 1, 3) AS first_three
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 2
ORDER BY name;

examples.title: Rounding
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary, ROUND(salary / 12.0, 2) AS monthly
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 3 OR dept_id IS NULL
ORDER BY name;
examples.note: Dividing by 12.0, not 12, avoids integer division. ROUND then keeps two decimal places.

examples.title: Dates: the month, and days between
examples.sql:
SELECT order_id, order_date,
       strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
       julianday('2024-03-31') - julianday(order_date) AS days_before_end_of_march
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 2
ORDER BY order_id;
examples.note: This is SQLite's way. The notes below give the PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server versions.

keyPoints: A row function runs once per row and returns one value; an aggregate function squashes many rows into one.
Text positions start at 1, not 0: `SUBSTR('Dara', 1, 3)` is 'Dar'.
`ROUND(x, 2)` for display; divide by a decimal (12.0) to avoid integer division first.
Date functions differ the most between databases. Know your target database's month-truncation and date-difference functions.
Wrapping a column in a function inside WHERE (`WHERE UPPER(name) = …`) stops a normal index on that column being used.
mistakes: Counting text positions from 0, as in Python.
Rounding before summing, which adds up rounding errors. Sum first, round at the end.
Comparing dates stored as '06/01/2024' text — they compare as text, not as dates.
dialects: Month of a date: PostgreSQL `DATE_TRUNC('month', d)` or `TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY-MM')`; MySQL `DATE_FORMAT(d, '%Y-%m')`; SQL Server `FORMAT(d, 'yyyy-MM')`; SQLite `strftime('%Y-%m', d)`.
Days between: PostgreSQL `d2 - d1` (dates); MySQL `DATEDIFF(d2, d1)`; SQL Server `DATEDIFF(day, d1, d2)`; SQLite `julianday(d2) - julianday(d1)`.
Year of a date: `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)` in PostgreSQL and MySQL; `YEAR(d)` in MySQL and SQL Server; `strftime('%Y', d)` in SQLite.
Text length is `LENGTH` in most databases but `LEN` in SQL Server.
topics.interviewAnswer: Scalar functions transform one value per row: string functions like UPPER, SUBSTRING and TRIM, numeric ones like ROUND, and date functions for truncating to a month or finding the days between two dates. Date syntax is the least portable part of SQL, so in an interview I name the dialect I am assuming — usually PostgreSQL, with DATE_TRUNC and date subtraction — and I avoid wrapping indexed columns in functions inside WHERE, because that blocks the index.

followUps.q: What is the difference between a scalar function and an aggregate function?
followUps.a: A scalar function returns one value per row (UPPER, ROUND). An aggregate returns one value per group of rows (SUM, COUNT).

followUps.q: How do you group orders by month in PostgreSQL?
followUps.a: `GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)`, which turns every date into the first day of its month.

practice.explain: Explain the difference between a row function like UPPER and an aggregate like SUM.
practice.write: Write a query that shows each customer's name and the part of their email before the @. (Hint: `INSTR(email, '@')` gives the position of the @.)
practice.predict: What does `SELECT SUBSTR('Headphones', 5, 5), LENGTH(TRIM('  Pen  ')), ROUND(2.675, 1);` return?
practice.edge: How many days passed between each employee's hire_date and '2024-01-01'? What happens if one of the dates is NULL?

resources.title: SQLite docs — Date And Time Functions
PostgreSQL docs — Date/Time Functions and Operators
SQLZoo — SELECT from WORLD: string functions

explain.answer:
A row function such as UPPER works on one value from one row and gives one value back. 8 employees in, 8 rows out, each with its own upper-case name.

An aggregate such as SUM reads a whole column across many rows and gives back one value for the group. 8 salaries in, one total out. The rows collapse.

That is why you can write `SELECT name, UPPER(name)`, but not `SELECT name, SUM(salary)` without GROUP BY: one name per row can't sit next to one total for all rows.

write.answer: `INSTR(email, '@')` finds where the @ is. Take the characters from position 1 up to one before it. For priya@mail.com the @ is at position 6, so take 5 characters.

predict.answer:
'phone', 3 and 2.7.

• `SUBSTR('Headphones', 5, 5)`: start at character 5 (counting from 1: H-e-a-d-p, so it starts at the p) and take 5 characters: "phone".
• `TRIM` removes the spaces at both ends, leaving "Pen", which has 3 letters.
• `ROUND(2.675, 1)` keeps one decimal place: 2.7.

query.sql: SELECT SUBSTR('Headphones', 5, 5), LENGTH(TRIM('  Pen  ')), ROUND(2.675, 1);

edge.answer:
Subtract the julianday numbers: each date becomes a count of days, so the difference is days between. Asha had been there 1,767 days by 1 January 2024.

If either date is NULL, julianday gives NULL, and the subtraction gives NULL for that row. There is no error, just a blank. Decide what you want: drop those rows with `WHERE hire_date IS NOT NULL`, or show a default with COALESCE. (In SQLite, `SELECT julianday('2024-01-01') - julianday(NULL);` returns NULL.)

query.sql:
SELECT name, hire_date,
       julianday('2024-01-01') - julianday(hire_date) AS days_to_2024
FROM employees
ORDER BY emp_id;

phases.title: Summarising data: aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING
phases.goal: Turn many rows into answers — totals, averages, counts per group — and know exactly which rows each number is built from.
phases.bigPicture: Questions like "how many orders per customer?" or "average salary per department?" are the heart of analytics and of SQL interviews. They all use the same three tools: an aggregate function, GROUP BY to make the groups, and HAVING to filter them.

topics.name: Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
topics.definition: An aggregate function turns many rows into one value — COUNT counts, SUM adds, AVG averages, MIN and MAX find the smallest and largest — and every one except `COUNT(*)` skips NULLs.
topics.problem: Nobody wants to read 10 million orders. They want "how many?", "how much in total?", "what is the average?". Aggregates answer those in one line — but the NULL rules quietly change the answers if you don't know them.
topics.idea: Without GROUP BY, an aggregate squashes the whole table (after WHERE) into one row. `COUNT(*)` counts rows. `COUNT(column)` counts rows where that column is not NULL. `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` counts the different non-NULL values. SUM and AVG add and average the non-NULL values. MIN and MAX work on numbers, text (alphabetical) and dates. Because AVG skips NULLs, the average of order amounts is the total divided by 9 orders, not 10.
topics.analogy: A cashier at the end of the day. They don't list every sale; they count the receipts (COUNT), add up the takings (SUM), and note the biggest and smallest sale (MAX, MIN). A receipt with the amount torn off still counts as a receipt, but it adds nothing to the takings.
topics.breaks: A cashier would notice the torn receipt and ask about it. SQL doesn't: it silently leaves NULLs out of SUM and AVG, so you have to decide yourself whether a missing value should count as zero.
howItWorks: FROM and WHERE decide which rows are in play — here all 10 orders.
`COUNT(*)` counts the rows: 10.
`COUNT(amount)` counts rows whose amount is not NULL: 9, because order 106 has none.
`SUM(amount)` adds the 9 amounts: 793. `AVG(amount)` is 793 ÷ 9 = 88.11, not 793 ÷ 10.
If the question means "average per order, counting the missing one as zero", divide SUM by `COUNT(*)` instead: 79.3.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["10 order rows
120, 80, 45, 200, 150,
NULL, 60, 75, 30, 33"] --> C["COUNT(*) = 10"] A --> N["COUNT(amount) = 9
NULL skipped"] A --> S["SUM(amount) = 793"] A --> V["AVG(amount) = 793 / 9"]
diagram.caption: Many rows go in and one number comes out. COUNT(*) counts every row; COUNT, SUM and AVG of a column skip the NULL — so AVG divides by 9, not 10.

examples.title: One summary row for the whole table
examples.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS employees,
       SUM(salary) AS total_pay,
       AVG(salary) AS average_pay,
       MIN(salary) AS lowest,
       MAX(salary) AS highest
FROM employees;

examples.title: Three different counts
examples.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows,
       COUNT(dept_id) AS with_a_department,
       COUNT(DISTINCT dept_id) AS different_departments
FROM employees;
examples.note: Gus has no department, so `COUNT(dept_id)` is 7. The 7 non-NULL values are only 1, 2 and 3, so `COUNT(DISTINCT dept_id)` is 3.

examples.title: How NULL changes an average
examples.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders,
       COUNT(amount) AS with_amount,
       SUM(amount) AS total,
       ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) AS avg_of_known,
       ROUND(SUM(amount) * 1.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS avg_over_all
FROM orders;
examples.note: Both averages are "right" — they answer different questions. Say which one you mean.

keyPoints: `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values; `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts different non-NULL values.
SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX ignore NULLs.
SUM of no rows (or only NULLs) is NULL, not 0. Wrap it: `COALESCE(SUM(x), 0)`.
Without GROUP BY, an aggregate query returns exactly one row — even from an empty table.
MIN and MAX work on text and dates too.
mistakes: Using `COUNT(column)` when you mean "how many rows", and getting a smaller number because of NULLs.
Mixing a plain column with an aggregate without GROUP BY: `SELECT name, MAX(salary) FROM employees` is an error in most databases (SQLite allows it but the name is unreliable).
Putting an aggregate in WHERE: `WHERE SUM(amount) > 100` is an error. That is HAVING's job.
dialects: AVG of whole numbers: PostgreSQL and SQLite return a decimal; SQL Server returns a whole number (AVG of 1 and 2 is 1). Use `AVG(x * 1.0)` there.
topics.interviewAnswer: Aggregate functions collapse a set of rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. The detail interviewers probe is NULL handling — COUNT star counts rows, COUNT of a column skips NULLs, and SUM and AVG ignore NULLs, so an average is over the known values only. I also remember that SUM over no rows is NULL, so I COALESCE it to zero when the result feeds a report.

followUps.q: What is the difference between `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(1)` and `COUNT(column)`?
followUps.a: `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(1)` both count rows, at the same speed. `COUNT(column)` counts only rows where that column is not NULL.

followUps.q: What does SUM return when there are no rows?
followUps.a: NULL. COUNT returns 0. Use `COALESCE(SUM(x), 0)` when you need 0.

followUps.q: Can you use an aggregate in WHERE?
followUps.a: No — WHERE runs before rows are grouped. Filter on aggregates with HAVING, or in an outer query.

explain.answer:
AVG skips NULLs. There are 10 orders, but order 106 has no amount, so only 9 amounts are averaged. The 9 known amounts add up to £793, and 793 ÷ 9 = 88.11.

79.3 is 793 ÷ 10: it treats the missing amount as £0. That is a different question ("average per order, counting a missing amount as nothing"). If that is what you want, say so: `SUM(amount) * 1.0 / COUNT(*)`, or `AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0))`.

query.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders,
       COUNT(amount) AS with_amount,
       SUM(amount) AS total,
       ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) AS avg_amount
FROM orders;

write.answer: Four aggregates in one SELECT, with no GROUP BY, give one summary row for the whole table. ROUND keeps the average readable: 125 ÷ 7 = 17.857…

query.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS products,
       MIN(price) AS cheapest,
       MAX(price) AS dearest,
       ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS average_price
FROM products;

predict.answer:
6, 5 and 3.

• `COUNT(*)` counts rows: 6 sign-ups.
• `COUNT(city)` counts values that are not NULL: Zoe has no city, so 5.
• `COUNT(DISTINCT city)` counts different cities: London, Leeds and Bristol, so 3. The NULL is not counted, and the two Londons and two Leeds count once each.

query.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(city), COUNT(DISTINCT city)
FROM customers;

edge.answer:
One row: NULL and 0.

No order is 'refunded', so the aggregates see no rows. COUNT of nothing is 0. But SUM of nothing is NULL, not 0, because there is nothing to add up. (Without GROUP BY, an aggregate query always returns exactly one row, even when no rows match.)

If a report should show 0, write `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)`.

topics.name: GROUP BY: one result row per group
topics.definition: GROUP BY splits the rows into groups that share the same value in the listed columns, and the aggregates then return one row per group.
topics.problem: One total is rarely enough. Managers ask for "revenue per month", "headcount per department", "orders per customer". GROUP BY gives you a total for every group in one query, instead of one query per group.
topics.idea: GROUP BY dept_id puts all rows with the same dept_id into one pile. Each pile becomes one result row, and every aggregate in SELECT is worked out separately for each pile. The golden rule: every column in SELECT must either be in GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate — because a group of 4 employees has 4 names, and the database can't pick one for you. All NULLs fall into one group of their own.
topics.analogy: Sorting a bag of coins into piles by type — all the 10p together, all the £1 together — and then counting each pile. GROUP BY makes the piles; COUNT and SUM count them.
topics.breaks: With coins you can still see each coin in its pile. After GROUP BY, the separate rows are gone from the result: you only see one row per pile, so you can't ask for "the name" of a group unless you aggregate it.
howItWorks: FROM takes all 8 employees.
GROUP BY dept_id makes piles: department 1 (Asha, Ben, Chen, Hana), department 2 (Dara, Eli), department 3 (Fatima), and a NULL pile (Gus).
For each pile, `COUNT(*)` and `AVG(salary)` are worked out: department 1 has 4 people averaging 78750.
SELECT returns one row per pile: dept_id, plus the aggregates.
Department 4 (HR) has no employees, so there is no pile and no row for it. Getting zero rows to show needs a join (Phase 3).

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  E["8 employee rows"] --> G1["dept 1: Asha, Ben, Chen, Hana"]
  E --> G2["dept 2: Dara, Eli"]
  E --> G3["dept 3: Fatima"]
  E --> G0["dept NULL: Gus"]
  G1 --> R1["1 · 4 people · avg 78750"]
  G2 --> R2["2 · 2 people · avg 52500"]
  G3 --> R3["3 · 1 person · avg 52000"]
  G0 --> R0["NULL · 1 person · avg 38000"]
diagram.caption: GROUP BY makes one pile per department, and each pile becomes one result row with its own count and average. NULLs form a pile of their own. HR has nobody, so it gets no pile at all.

examples.title: Headcount and average salary per department
examples.sql:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;
examples.note: Gus forms the NULL group. HR (department 4) is missing because no rows belong to it.

examples.title: Revenue per month
examples.sql:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)
ORDER BY month;
examples.note: You can group by a calculation, not just a column. February has 3 orders but only 2 amounts, because order 106 is NULL.

examples.title: Group by two columns
examples.sql:
SELECT customer_id, status, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id, status
ORDER BY customer_id, status;
examples.note: One row per pair of customer and status that actually appears in the data.

keyPoints: GROUP BY makes one result row per distinct combination of the grouping columns.
Every column in SELECT must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate.
All NULLs in a grouping column form one group.
Groups with no rows don't appear at all. To show zeros (like HR with 0 people), start from the full list and LEFT JOIN (Phase 3).
Grouped results come back in no particular order. Add ORDER BY.
mistakes: Selecting a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated, like `SELECT dept_id, name, COUNT(*) … GROUP BY dept_id`.
Expecting groups with zero rows to appear with a count of 0.
Grouping by too many columns (such as the id), so every group has one row and nothing is summarised.
dialects: SQLite and older MySQL let you select a column that isn't grouped and silently pick a value. PostgreSQL, SQL Server and modern MySQL reject it. Write it the strict way.
GROUP BY an alias (`GROUP BY month`) works in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite, but not in SQL Server — repeat the expression there.
topics.interviewAnswer: GROUP BY partitions the filtered rows into groups by the grouping columns, and aggregates are computed once per group, giving one output row per group. The rule is that every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. Two details I mention: NULLs form a single group, and groups with no rows simply don't appear — so to report zeros I drive the query from the complete dimension table with a LEFT JOIN.

followUps.q: Why must non-aggregated columns be in GROUP BY?
followUps.a: Each group becomes one row. A column that isn't grouped could have many values in the group, and SQL won't guess which one to show.

followUps.q: How do you show departments with zero employees?
followUps.a: `SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_name` — COUNT of a column gives 0 when nothing matched.

explain.answer:
Every column in SELECT must either be in the GROUP BY, or be inside an aggregate.

`SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id` is fine: one dept_id per group, and one count per group.

`SELECT dept_id, name, COUNT(*) … GROUP BY dept_id` breaks the rule. Department 1 has four people (Asha, Ben, Chen and Hana), but the group has room for only one name. Which one? PostgreSQL, SQL Server and (by default) MySQL refuse the query. SQLite runs it and picks one name, which is worse: it looks like an answer but means nothing.

Fix it by grouping by name too, or by aggregating it, for example `MAX(name)` or `GROUP_CONCAT(name)`.

write.answer: Group by category and aggregate the rest. Electronics averages the £40 headphones and the £15 phone case: 27.5.

query.sql:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS products, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;

predict.answer:
4 rows: Bristol, Leeds, London and one group for NULL. Leeds has 2: both of Tom's sign-ups. London also has 2 (Priya and Lena), Bristol 1 (Omar), and the NULL group 1 (Zoe).

GROUP BY puts all the NULLs together in one group. (ORDER BY is added below so the order is fixed.)

query.sql:
SELECT city, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY city;

edge.answer:
SUM skips NULLs, but if every amount in a group is NULL, there is nothing to add and SUM returns NULL. Wrap it: `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)`.

No customer here has only NULL amounts (customer 3 has one NULL and one £60, so their total is 60). To see the COALESCE work, add `WHERE order_id = 106` and customer 3 shows 0.

Note that Omar, who has no orders at all, is not in the result: he has no rows in orders to group. Showing him needs a LEFT JOIN from customers (Phase 3).

query.sql:
SELECT customer_id, COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) AS total_spend
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

topics.name: HAVING: filtering groups, and how it differs from WHERE
topics.definition: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, using aggregates such as `COUNT(*) > 1`, while WHERE filters single rows before any grouping happens.
topics.problem: "Customers with more than one order", "departments whose average salary is over 55000". You can't test those in WHERE, because the counts and averages don't exist until the rows are grouped. HAVING is the filter that runs after grouping.
topics.idea: Think of two sieves. WHERE is the first sieve: it removes rows before they are put into groups. HAVING is the second: it removes whole groups after they are counted. A query can use both: WHERE keeps only delivered orders, GROUP BY makes a group per customer, then HAVING keeps customers whose delivered total is at least £100. If a condition is about one row (status, date), put it in WHERE — it is cheaper, because fewer rows get grouped.
topics.analogy: Picking a football team. WHERE is the trial: players under 16 are sent home before teams are formed. HAVING comes after the teams are formed: any team with fewer than 11 players is dropped from the tournament.
topics.breaks: In football you could also drop a team for one bad player. HAVING can't look at individual rows any more — only at things that describe the whole group, such as counts, sums and the grouping columns.
topics.syntax:
SELECT group_column, COUNT(*)
FROM table_name
WHERE row_condition
GROUP BY group_column
HAVING group_condition;
howItWorks: FROM: all 10 orders.
`WHERE status = 'delivered'`: 7 rows are left.
GROUP BY customer_id: customer 1 has 4 delivered orders (275), customer 2 has 2 (275), customer 3 has 1 (60).
HAVING `SUM(amount) >= 100`: customer 3's group fails and is removed.
SELECT returns customers 1 and 2 with their totals.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["10 orders"] -->|"WHERE status = delivered
filters rows"| B["7 rows"] B -->|"GROUP BY customer_id"| C["3 groups
1: 275 · 2: 275 · 3: 60"] C -->|"HAVING SUM over 100
filters groups"| D["2 groups
customers 1 and 2"]
diagram.caption: Two sieves at two different moments. WHERE removes single rows before grouping; HAVING removes whole groups after their totals are known.

examples.title: Departments with more than one person
examples.sql:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY dept_id;

examples.title: WHERE and HAVING together
examples.sql:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS delivered_total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.note: Priya's shipped order (150) isn't counted: WHERE removed it before the sum. Lena's delivered total is only 60.

keyPoints: WHERE filters rows, before GROUP BY. HAVING filters groups, after GROUP BY.
Aggregates can be used in HAVING but not in WHERE.
A row-level condition belongs in WHERE: it is clearer and faster.
HAVING can test an aggregate that isn't in SELECT, such as `HAVING MAX(salary) > 60000`.
mistakes: Writing `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` — an error, because counts don't exist yet when WHERE runs.
Putting a plain row condition in HAVING (`HAVING status = 'delivered'`): it either fails or does something unexpected.
Using a SELECT alias in HAVING (`HAVING headcount > 1`). Some databases allow it; standard SQL and SQL Server don't. Repeat the aggregate.
topics.interviewAnswer: WHERE and HAVING are both filters but run at different stages. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, so it can't use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, so it can. If a condition doesn't need an aggregate I put it in WHERE, because filtering early means less data to group.

followUps.q: Can you use HAVING without GROUP BY?
followUps.a: Yes. The whole result is treated as one group: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders HAVING COUNT(*) > 5` returns one row or none.

followUps.q: Which is faster for a row condition, WHERE or HAVING?
followUps.a: WHERE, because rows are removed before the work of grouping. Many optimisers move such conditions anyway, but write them in WHERE.

explain.answer:
At a football trial, WHERE is the check at the gate: each player is judged on their own (too young? go home) before any teams exist. HAVING comes after the teams are formed: it judges whole teams (fewer than 11 players? out of the tournament).

With orders: `WHERE status = 'delivered'` throws out single orders that aren't delivered, before grouping. Then GROUP BY customer_id makes one group per customer, and `HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100` drops customers whose delivered total is under £100.

WHERE can't use SUM or COUNT, because the groups don't exist yet. HAVING can, because it runs after GROUP BY.

write.answer: Group the orders per customer, count them, and keep the groups with 2 or more. That is a test on a group, so it goes in HAVING.

query.sql:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY customer_id;

predict.answer:
Only department 1.

The averages are: department 1, (95,000 + 70,000 + 70,000 + 80,000) ÷ 4 = 78,750; department 2, 52,500; department 3, 52,000; and the NULL group (Gus), 38,000. Only 78,750 is over 55,000.

query.sql:
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > 55000;

edge.answer:
`HAVING SUM(amount) > 50`: yes, customer 3 is kept. SUM skips the NULL, so their total is 60, and 60 > 50.

`HAVING COUNT(amount) = COUNT(*)`: no, customer 3 is dropped. `COUNT(amount)` skips the NULL and gives 1, while `COUNT(*)` counts both rows and gives 2. 1 ≠ 2. This is a handy test for "every order in the group has an amount".

The query below shows both tests for every customer, as 1 (true) or 0 (false).

query.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(amount) AS total,
       COUNT(amount) AS with_amount,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(amount) > 50 AS sum_over_50,
       COUNT(amount) = COUNT(*) AS all_known
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

topics.name: Conditional aggregation: counting several things at once
topics.definition: Putting CASE inside an aggregate — `SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` — counts or sums only the rows that match, so one query can produce several different totals, or turn rows into columns (a pivot).
topics.problem: "For each customer, how many orders were delivered and how many weren't?" Running two queries and gluing them together is slow and messy. Interviewers love this pattern because it shows you understand that aggregates work on whatever values you give them.
topics.idea: An aggregate adds up whatever expression you hand it. Hand SUM a CASE that gives 1 for the rows you care about and 0 for the rest, and it counts just those rows. Hand it `CASE WHEN … THEN amount END` and it sums just those amounts. Do this several times in one SELECT, with different conditions, and you get several columns from one pass over the data. Use it with months as the conditions and the rows become columns — that is a pivot. For a percentage, divide one conditional count by `COUNT(*)`, using 100.0 to avoid integer division.
topics.analogy: Counting a class with tally marks on a sheet with several columns: as each pupil walks past, you add a mark under "walked", "cycled" or "came by bus". One walk-past fills in every column at once.
topics.breaks: With tally marks a pupil can only go in one column. Conditional aggregation has no such rule: one row can count towards several columns if several conditions are true, so make your conditions not overlap when they should add up to the total.
topics.syntax:
SELECT group_column,
       SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS how_many,
       SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN value END)    AS how_much
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column;
howItWorks: GROUP BY customer_id makes one group per customer.
For each row, the CASE gives 1 if the order is delivered and 0 if not.
SUM adds those 1s and 0s, which is the number of delivered orders in the group.
A second SUM with the opposite condition counts the rest. `COUNT(*)` gives the total.
For a pivot, each column's CASE picks one month: `CASE WHEN order_date LIKE '2024-01%' THEN amount ELSE 0 END`.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR R["Priya's orders
delivered, delivered,
delivered, shipped, delivered"] --> C["CASE gives
1, 1, 1, 0, 1"] C --> S["SUM = 4 delivered"] R --> T["COUNT(*) = 5 orders"]
diagram.caption: CASE turns each row into a 1 or a 0, and SUM adds them up — a count of just the matching rows, worked out next to the other totals in the same pass.

examples.title: Several counts in one query
examples.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS delivered,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status <> 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS not_delivered
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: A pivot: one column per month
examples.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_date LIKE '2024-01%' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS jan,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_date LIKE '2024-02%' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS feb,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_date LIKE '2024-03%' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS mar
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.note: Rows became columns. Lena's February is 60: order 106's NULL amount is skipped by SUM.

examples.title: A percentage
examples.note: 7 of 10 orders were delivered. 100.0 (not 100) stops integer division. The AVG of 1s and 0s is a neat shortcut for a share.

keyPoints: `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts matching rows; `COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END)` does the same, because COUNT skips the NULLs.
`SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN amount END)` sums only matching amounts.
One pass over the data gives many totals — faster and simpler than several queries.
A pivot is conditional aggregation with one column per value.
For percentages, multiply by 100.0 before dividing.
mistakes: Writing `COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`. COUNT counts the 0s too, because 0 is not NULL. Use SUM, or drop the ELSE.
Computing a percentage with whole numbers: `100 * 7 / 10` is fine but `7 / 10 * 100` is 0.
Conditions that overlap when the columns should add up to the total.
dialects: PostgreSQL and SQLite support a FILTER clause: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered')`. It is the same idea with neater syntax.
SQL Server and Oracle have a PIVOT operator, but CASE works everywhere and interviewers accept it.
topics.interviewAnswer: Conditional aggregation puts a CASE expression inside an aggregate, like SUM of CASE WHEN status is delivered THEN 1 ELSE 0, so I can compute several metrics per group in a single pass — counts by status, revenue by month as columns, or a ratio. For ratios I multiply by 100.0 first to avoid integer division, and I make sure SUM rather than COUNT wraps a CASE that returns zero.

followUps.q: Why is `COUNT(CASE WHEN x THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` wrong?
followUps.a: COUNT counts every non-NULL value, and 0 is not NULL, so it counts all rows. Use SUM, or remove the ELSE so non-matches become NULL.

followUps.q: How do you pivot rows into columns in SQL?
followUps.a: GROUP BY the row label and write one `SUM(CASE WHEN column = value THEN amount END)` per output column.

practice.explain: Explain how `SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts rows.
practice.write: For each department, show the number of employees earning 60000 or more and the number earning less, in one query.
practice.predict: What does `SELECT COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM orders;` return, and why is it not 7?
practice.edge: Write the share of orders that are cancelled, as a percentage with one decimal place, and check it is 10.0.

resources.title: Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL CASE (Using CASE with aggregate functions)

explain.answer:
The CASE runs once for every row and turns it into a number: 1 if the row matches, 0 if it doesn't. SUM then adds up those 1s and 0s. Every match adds 1 and every other row adds nothing, so the total is the number of matching rows.

Because each CASE is its own column, one query can count several different things at once, each with its own condition.

write.answer: Two SUM(CASE …) columns, one per condition, grouped by department. "60000 or more" is `>= 60000`, so Dara (exactly 60,000) counts in the first column.

query.sql:
SELECT dept_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS earn_60k_or_more,
       SUM(CASE WHEN salary < 60000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS earn_less
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;

predict.answer:
10, not 7.

COUNT counts every value that is not NULL. The CASE gives 1 or 0, and 0 is a real value, not NULL, so COUNT counts all 10 rows.

Two fixes: use SUM, which adds the 1s and 0s; or keep COUNT but drop the ELSE, so non-matching rows become NULL and are skipped. Both give 7.

query.sql:
SELECT COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS counted,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 END) AS fixed_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS fixed_sum
FROM orders;

edge.answer: 1 cancelled order out of 10 is 10.0%. Start with 100.0, not 100, so the division is exact. With whole numbers the fraction is cut off: 1 out of 3 would show 33, not 33.3. (SQLite shows 10.0 as 10.)

query.sql:
SELECT ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_cancelled
FROM orders;

topics.name: The order a query really runs in
topics.definition: A query is written SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, but the database works it out in a different order — FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — and that order explains most "why doesn't this work?" errors.
topics.problem: Why can't WHERE use the alias you made in SELECT? Why can ORDER BY use it? Why can't WHERE use COUNT? Without the run order these look like random rules. With it, they are obvious — and interviewers ask about it directly.
topics.idea: Each step works on the output of the step before. FROM (and JOIN) builds the rows. WHERE removes rows. GROUP BY makes groups. HAVING removes groups. SELECT works out the output columns and their aliases (window functions run here too). DISTINCT removes duplicate rows. ORDER BY sorts. LIMIT cuts. So: WHERE runs before SELECT, and can't see its aliases. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so it can. WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so it can't use aggregates — HAVING runs after, so it can.
topics.analogy: Making a sandwich. You write the order as "sandwich: cheese and tomato, on brown bread, cut in half". But you actually get the bread first (FROM), pick the fillings (WHERE), assemble it (GROUP BY and SELECT), and cut it last (ORDER BY, LIMIT). You can't cut what you haven't made yet.
topics.breaks: A cook really does work in that order. A database only has to behave as if it does: the optimiser may reorder the real work — for example, use an index to sort early — as long as the answer is the same.
topics.syntax:
-- written order        -- run order
SELECT    ...           -- 5
FROM      ...           -- 1
WHERE     ...           -- 2
GROUP BY  ...           -- 3
HAVING    ...           -- 4
ORDER BY  ...           -- 6
LIMIT     ...;          -- 7
howItWorks: FROM employees: all 8 rows.
`WHERE salary > 40000`: Gus (38000) is removed, so 7 rows are left.
GROUP BY dept_id: department 1 has 4 rows, department 2 has 2 (Dara, Eli), department 3 has 1 (Fatima).
HAVING `COUNT(*) >= 2`: department 3 is removed.
SELECT works out dept_id and `AVG(salary)` AS avg_salary for the 2 groups left.
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC can use the alias, because SELECT has already run.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR F["1 FROM
and JOIN"] --> W["2 WHERE"] --> G["3 GROUP BY"] --> H["4 HAVING"] --> S["5 SELECT
aliases made here"] --> D["6 DISTINCT"] --> O["7 ORDER BY
can use aliases"] --> L["8 LIMIT"]
diagram.caption: The order the database works in. Anything a step needs must already exist: WHERE can't use SELECT's aliases (made at step 5), but ORDER BY at step 7 can.

examples.title: Every clause in one query
examples.sql:
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 40000
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
examples.note: Follow the steps above: WHERE drops Gus, HAVING drops department 3, and ORDER BY uses the alias made in SELECT.

examples.title: Filtering on an alias: wrap the query
examples.sql:
SELECT name, bonus
FROM (
  SELECT name, salary / 10 AS bonus
  FROM employees
) AS with_bonus
WHERE bonus > 7000
ORDER BY bonus DESC;
examples.note: `WHERE bonus > 7000` fails in a single query in strict databases, because WHERE runs before SELECT makes bonus. The inner query makes it first; Phase 4 covers this properly.

keyPoints: Run order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
WHERE can't use SELECT aliases or aggregates; HAVING can use aggregates; ORDER BY can use aliases.
Window functions are worked out at the SELECT step, so you can't filter on them in WHERE — wrap the query instead.
To filter on a calculated column, repeat the expression in WHERE or wrap the query in a subquery or CTE.
mistakes: Using a SELECT alias in WHERE and getting "no such column".
Expecting LIMIT to run before ORDER BY ("take 3 rows, then sort them").
Filtering on `ROW_NUMBER()` in WHERE — it doesn't exist yet at that step.
dialects: MySQL and SQLite are lenient and let HAVING (and sometimes WHERE) use SELECT aliases. PostgreSQL and SQL Server follow the strict order. Write it the strict way and it runs everywhere.
topics.interviewAnswer: SQL is written SELECT first, but logically processed as FROM and JOINs, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY and finally LIMIT. That explains the common rules: WHERE can't reference SELECT aliases or aggregates because they don't exist yet, HAVING can use aggregates, and ORDER BY can use aliases. To filter on a computed column or a window function, I wrap the query in a CTE and filter outside.

followUps.q: Why can ORDER BY use a column alias but WHERE can't?
followUps.a: ORDER BY runs after SELECT, when the alias exists. WHERE runs before SELECT.

followUps.q: Where do window functions fit in the order?
followUps.a: At the SELECT step, after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING. That is why you filter on them in an outer query.

practice.explain: Recite the run order from memory, and use it to explain why `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` fails.
practice.write: Write a query for categories whose average product price is above £10, sorted by that average from high to low, using an alias in ORDER BY.
practice.predict: In the "every clause" example, what would change if WHERE were `salary > 50000`? Work it out step by step, then run it.
practice.edge: You want employees whose salary is above the company average. Why does `WHERE salary > AVG(salary)` fail, and what would you do instead?

resources.title: SQLBolt — Lesson 12: Order of execution of a Query
resources.source: interactive exercises in the browser, free

resources.title: CS50's Introduction to Databases with SQL — Lecture 0: Querying
PostgreSQL docs — SELECT (how a query is processed)

explain.answer:
FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

WHERE runs second, straight after FROM, while the rows are still single rows. Groups are only made at step 3, so at the time WHERE runs there is no group for COUNT(*) to count. The database refuses: "misuse of aggregate".

A test on a count belongs in HAVING, which runs after GROUP BY.

query.sql:
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
WHERE COUNT(*) > 1
GROUP BY customer_id;

write.answer: HAVING repeats `AVG(price)`, because HAVING runs before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet. (SQLite and MySQL let you use the alias there; PostgreSQL and SQL Server don't.) ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so the alias avg_price works there everywhere.

query.sql:
SELECT category, AVG(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING AVG(price) > 10
ORDER BY avg_price DESC;

predict.answer:
Department 2 disappears, and only department 1 is left, with the same average of 78,750.

1. FROM: all 8 employees.
2. WHERE salary > 50000: Eli (45,000) and Gus (38,000) are removed. 6 left.
3. GROUP BY dept_id: department 1 has Asha, Ben, Chen and Hana; department 2 has only Dara; department 3 has only Fatima.
4. HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2: only department 1 has 2 or more. With the old filter (> 40000), Eli stayed, so department 2 had 2 people and was kept.
5. SELECT: department 1, average (95,000 + 70,000 + 70,000 + 80,000) ÷ 4 = 78,750.

query.sql:
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;

edge.answer:
WHERE runs before any grouping, one row at a time, so it can't use an aggregate. AVG needs all the rows at once, and WHERE only sees one. The database refuses with "misuse of aggregate function AVG()".

Work the average out first, in its own query, and compare with that: a subquery. The company average is 510,000 ÷ 8 = 63,750. Four people are above it.

query.sql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
ORDER BY salary DESC, name;

phases.title: Joins: combining tables
phases.goal: Put rows from two or more tables side by side, keep or drop the rows that have no match on purpose, and spot the joins that quietly double your totals.
phases.bigPicture: Data is split across tables so each fact is stored once. Joins put it back together. Nearly every real query and most interview questions use at least one join — and most wrong answers come from choosing the wrong kind.

topics.name: Joins, and INNER JOIN
topics.definition: A JOIN combines rows from two tables wherever a condition (usually matching keys) is true, and INNER JOIN keeps only the rows that found a match on both sides.
topics.problem: The employees table knows Ben is in department 1, but not that department 1 is called Engineering. That lives in departments. To show "Ben — Engineering" you need columns from both tables in one row. That is a join.
topics.idea: You name two tables and a join condition after ON: `employees e JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id`. The database pairs every employee with every department whose dept_id matches, and each pair becomes one result row holding the columns of both. INNER JOIN (plain JOIN means the same thing) keeps only pairs that matched. So Gus, whose dept_id is NULL, matches nothing and disappears — and HR, which no employee points to, disappears too. The short names e and d are table aliases; they save typing and say which table each column comes from.
topics.analogy: Matching odd socks from two baskets by colour. A red sock from basket A is paired with a red sock from basket B. INNER JOIN only keeps the pairs; any sock without a partner stays in its basket.
topics.breaks: Socks pair one-to-one. Joins don't have to: if one department matches four employees, the department's row is repeated four times — once per partner. That repetition is normal, but it is also where double-counting comes from (see Join traps).
howItWorks: `FROM employees AS e`: take every employee and call the table e.
`JOIN departments AS d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id`: for each employee, find departments with the same dept_id.
Ben (dept_id 1) matches Engineering, so one row: Ben, Engineering.
Gus (dept_id NULL) matches nothing, because NULL never equals anything — so INNER JOIN drops him.
HR (dept_id 4) is never matched by any employee, so it doesn't appear either.
SELECT picks e.name and d.dept_name from each matched pair.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  subgraph E["employees"]
    Ben["Ben · dept 1"]
    Dara["Dara · dept 2"]
    Gus["Gus · dept NULL"]
  end
  subgraph D["departments"]
    D1["1 · Engineering"]
    D2["2 · Sales"]
    D4["4 · HR"]
  end
  Ben -->|"match"| D1
  Dara -->|"match"| D2
  Gus -.->|"no match: dropped"| X["not in result"]
  D4 -.->|"no match: dropped"| X
diagram.caption: INNER JOIN keeps only pairs that match on the key. Gus (NULL department) and HR (no employees) have no partner, so neither appears in the result.

examples.title: Employees with their department name
examples.sql:
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name
FROM employees AS e
INNER JOIN departments AS d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
ORDER BY e.name;
examples.note: 7 rows, not 8: Gus is gone. HR is gone too. INNER JOIN shows only matches.

examples.title: Orders with the customer's name
examples.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date < '2024-02-01'
ORDER BY o.order_id;
examples.note: JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN, and AS is optional for table aliases. Priya's name repeats once per order — that is one-to-many at work.

examples.title: Join, then group: revenue per city
examples.sql:
SELECT c.city, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
examples.note: The join brings the city onto each order; GROUP BY then adds them up. Zoe's order lands in the NULL city group.

keyPoints: A join pairs rows from two tables where the ON condition is true; each pair is one result row.
INNER JOIN (or just JOIN) keeps only matched rows — unmatched rows on either side vanish.
NULL keys never match, so rows with a NULL key always drop out of an INNER JOIN.
Table aliases (e, d) keep queries short. Always prefix columns with them once there is more than one table.
One-to-many joins repeat the "one" side once per match. That is expected.
mistakes: Forgetting the ON condition, which pairs every row with every row (a cross join): 8 × 4 = 32 rows.
Leaving out the prefix on a column both tables have (dept_id), which gives an "ambiguous column" error.
Using INNER JOIN when the question says "all customers" or "every department" — the ones with no match disappear.
dialects: Old-style joins list tables with commas and put the condition in WHERE: `FROM employees e, departments d WHERE d.dept_id = e.dept_id`. It works everywhere, but explicit JOIN … ON is clearer and is what interviewers expect.
topics.interviewAnswer: A join combines rows from two tables based on a condition, normally a foreign key matching a primary key. INNER JOIN returns only rows that match on both sides, so rows with no partner — or a NULL key — are excluded. In a one-to-many join the one side repeats for each match, which is correct but means I have to be careful when summing columns from the one side.

followUps.q: Is JOIN the same as INNER JOIN?
followUps.a: Yes. JOIN on its own is an inner join.

followUps.q: Does a join need a foreign key to exist?
followUps.a: No. Any condition works, even `ON a.x > b.y`. Foreign keys just make the matching column reliable.

followUps.q: Why did my join return fewer rows than the table has?
followUps.a: Rows without a match — or with a NULL key — are dropped by an inner join. Use a LEFT JOIN to keep them.

practice.write: Write a query listing each order_items row with the product name and the quantity, for order 105.
practice.predict: How many rows does `SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;` return?
practice.edge: Which employees vanish from `SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id;`? Why?

explain.answer:
INNER JOIN pairs each employee with the department whose dept_id matches theirs, and keeps only the pairs where `ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id` is true.

Gus: his dept_id is NULL. NULL equals nothing, not even another NULL, so he matches no department and is dropped.

HR: it is department 4, and no employee has dept_id 4. It matches no employee, so it is dropped too.

So INNER JOIN quietly loses rows from both sides that have no partner. You get 7 rows, not 8 employees or 4 departments. If you need the unmatched rows, use a LEFT (or FULL) JOIN.

write.answer: Start from order_items, since that is where the quantity is, and join products to swap product_id for a name. Order 105 has 1 backpack and 3 headphones: 30 + 3 × 40 = £150, its amount.

query.sql:
SELECT oi.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE oi.order_id = 105
ORDER BY p.product_name;

predict.answer:
10 rows, one per order. Every order has exactly one customer: customer_id is NOT NULL and points at a real customer. So each order finds one partner, and none is lost or repeated.

Omar and the second Tom have no orders, so they don't appear, but that doesn't change the count: you start from orders. (It also returns 10 columns, 5 from each table, so the check below just counts.)

edge.answer:
Asha vanishes. 7 rows come back, not 8.

The join looks for the row m whose emp_id equals e's manager_id. Asha's manager_id is NULL, so no row matches her, and an INNER JOIN drops rows with no match. To keep her, with NULL as her manager, use LEFT JOIN.

(The aliases employee and manager are added below, because both columns would otherwise be called name.)

query.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

topics.name: LEFT JOIN: keep every row from one side
topics.definition: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left (first) table, joins matching rows from the right table, and fills the right-hand columns with NULL where there is no match.
topics.problem: "Show every department with its headcount" must include HR with 0. "Every customer and what they spent" must include Omar, who spent nothing. An INNER JOIN silently drops them. LEFT JOIN keeps them.
topics.idea: In `departments d LEFT JOIN employees e`, departments is the left table and every department is kept. Where employees match, you get one row per match, as with INNER JOIN. Where none match — HR — you still get one row, with NULL in every employees column. Count with `COUNT(e.emp_id)`, not `COUNT(*)`, so HR's NULL row counts as 0. RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image (keep every row of the right table); people almost always swap the tables and write a LEFT JOIN instead.
topics.analogy: A class register. Every pupil's name is on it (the left table). Next to each name you write the homework they handed in (the right table). A pupil who handed nothing in stays on the register with a blank next to their name.
topics.breaks: A blank on a register is just empty. In SQL the blank is NULL, and NULL behaves strangely: `COUNT(*)` still counts that row as 1, and a WHERE on a right-hand column can throw the row away again.
howItWorks: Start with every row of the left table, departments: Engineering, Sales, Marketing, HR.
For each, find matching employees. Engineering has 4, so it appears 4 times.
HR has no matching employees, so it appears once, with NULL for the employee columns.
`COUNT(e.emp_id)` counts only non-NULL ids: 4, 2, 1 and 0 for HR.
`COUNT(*)` would wrongly give HR 1, because there is one (NULL-filled) row.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR subgraph L["departments (left): all kept"] D1["Engineering"] D2["Sales"] D4["HR"] end D1 --> R1["Engineering · Asha
Engineering · Ben
…"] D2 --> R2["Sales · Dara
Sales · Eli"] D4 --> R4["HR · NULL
kept, with NULLs"]
diagram.caption: Every row of the left table survives. Matches are filled in as usual; a row with no match (HR) is kept once, with NULL in all the right-hand columns.

examples.title: Every department, with its people
examples.sql:
SELECT d.dept_name, e.name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
ORDER BY d.dept_id, e.name;
examples.note: HR is kept with a NULL name. Gus still isn't here: departments is the side being kept, and he matches no department.

examples.title: Headcount, with zeros
examples.sql:
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS headcount
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
examples.note: `COUNT(e.emp_id)` skips the NULL, so HR shows 0. With `COUNT(*)`, HR would show 1.

examples.title: Every customer and what they spent
examples.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.note: Omar and the second Tom are kept with 0 orders. SUM over their NULL row is NULL, so COALESCE turns it into 0.

keyPoints: LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table; unmatched rows get NULLs on the right.
Put the table you want to keep in full first ("every customer" → customers first).
Count the right side with `COUNT(right.column)`, not `COUNT(*)`, to get 0 for no matches.
Wrap sums of the right side in `COALESCE(…, 0)`.
RIGHT JOIN is LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped; prefer LEFT JOIN for readability.
mistakes: Using `COUNT(*)` after a LEFT JOIN and getting 1 instead of 0 for rows with no match.
Adding `WHERE right_table.column = …`, which throws the NULL rows away and turns the LEFT JOIN back into an INNER JOIN (see Join traps).
Putting the tables the wrong way round, so the side you wanted to keep is on the right.
dialects: LEFT JOIN and LEFT OUTER JOIN are the same thing everywhere. RIGHT JOIN only arrived in SQLite in version 3.39 (2022); it has always worked in the other databases.
topics.interviewAnswer: A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table and the matching rows from the right; where there is no match, the right-hand columns are NULL. I use it whenever the question says "all" or "every" — every customer, including those with no orders. After a LEFT JOIN I count a right-hand column rather than COUNT star, so unmatched rows give zero, and I COALESCE sums to zero.

followUps.q: LEFT JOIN or INNER JOIN — how do you choose?
followUps.a: Ask whether rows without a match should appear. "Every customer" means LEFT JOIN; "customers who ordered" means INNER JOIN.

followUps.q: Can a LEFT JOIN return more rows than the left table has?
followUps.a: Yes. A left row that matches three right rows appears three times. It returns at least as many rows as the left table.

resources.title: Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL LEFT JOIN

explain.answer:
A LEFT JOIN promises to keep every row of the left table, here departments, whether or not it finds a match. HR has no employees, so it gets one row with NULL in every employee column.

An INNER JOIN keeps only pairs that match. HR has nobody to pair with, so it is dropped.

That is why "show every department, even empty ones" needs LEFT JOIN, with departments on the left.

write.answer: Products on the left, so every product stays. SUM of no rows is NULL, so wrap it in COALESCE to show 0 for the phone case.

query.sql:
SELECT p.product_name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0) AS total_sold
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
ORDER BY p.product_id;

predict.answer:
12 rows. Each customer appears once per order: Priya 5, Tom (id 2) 2, Lena 2, Zoe 1. That is 10. Customers with no orders still get one row each, with NULLs: Omar and the second Tom (id 6). 10 + 2 = 12.

The query below shows just three columns so it fits on screen.

query.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;

edge.answer:
HR changes from 0 to 1. The other departments stay the same.

The LEFT JOIN gives HR one row, with NULLs in the employee columns. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, so it counts that row: 1. `COUNT(e.emp_id)` counts only values that are not NULL, and HR's emp_id is NULL: 0.

After a LEFT JOIN, count a column from the right-hand table (ideally its key), not `*`.

query.sql:
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS count_emp_id, COUNT(*) AS count_star
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
ORDER BY d.dept_id;

topics.name: Finding what is missing: anti-joins
topics.definition: An anti-join returns rows from one table that have no match in another — written as `LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL`, or as `WHERE NOT EXISTS (…)`.
topics.problem: "Customers who never ordered", "products that never sold", "employees with no manager on file" — finding what is absent is one of the most common interview questions and real tasks. You can't find it with WHERE alone, because the missing rows aren't there to filter.
topics.idea: Do a LEFT JOIN, so every left row is kept and unmatched ones get NULL on the right. Then keep only the unmatched ones: `WHERE o.order_id IS NULL`. Test a column that can never be NULL in a real match — the right table's primary key is perfect. NOT EXISTS says the same thing more directly: "keep the customer if no order exists for them". Its opposite, the semi-join, keeps rows that do have a match, each only once: `WHERE EXISTS (…)` or `WHERE id IN (…)`.
topics.analogy: Checking a guest list against the sign-in sheet. Hold the list (left table) next to the sheet (right table); the names with an empty space next to them on the sheet are the people who didn't come.
topics.breaks: With a list you just look for blanks. In SQL you must test the right column for the blank: test a column that might legitimately be NULL (like amount) and you will wrongly report customers whose real order just has no amount.
topics.syntax:
SELECT a.*
FROM table_a a
LEFT JOIN table_b b ON b.key = a.key
WHERE b.key IS NULL;
howItWorks: customers LEFT JOIN orders keeps all 6 customers; Omar and the second Tom get NULLs for every order column.
`WHERE o.order_id IS NULL` keeps only those NULL rows: the customers with no orders.
order_id is the orders primary key, so it is NULL only when there was no match — never in a real order.
NOT EXISTS version: for each customer, look for any order with their id; keep the customer if there is none.
Avoid NOT IN for this when the inner list can hold a NULL — it returns nothing (Phase 4 shows why).

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["all 6 customers"] -->|"LEFT JOIN orders"| J["4 with orders: matched
Omar, Tom 6: NULL orders"] J -->|"WHERE order_id IS NULL"| R["Omar, Tom 6
never ordered"]
diagram.caption: Keep everyone with a LEFT JOIN, then keep only the rows where the join found nothing. What is left is exactly the missing set.

examples.title: Customers who never ordered: LEFT JOIN … IS NULL
examples.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: Products never sold: NOT EXISTS
examples.sql:
SELECT p.product_name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM order_items oi
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id
)
ORDER BY p.product_name;
examples.note: For each product, the inner query looks for any order line with that product. NOT EXISTS keeps the product when it finds none. Phase 4 explains EXISTS fully.

examples.title: The opposite, a semi-join: rows that do have a match
examples.sql:
SELECT dept_name
FROM departments
WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees)
ORDER BY dept_name;
examples.note: Each department appears once, however many employees it has. A JOIN would repeat Engineering four times.

keyPoints: Anti-join = rows with no match: `LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.pk IS NULL`, or `NOT EXISTS`.
Semi-join = rows with at least one match, each once: `EXISTS` or `IN`.
In the IS NULL test, use a column that is never NULL in a real match — the right table's primary key or join key.
NOT EXISTS is the safest anti-join: it handles NULLs correctly, and optimisers run it efficiently.
Don't use `NOT IN (subquery)` if the subquery can return NULL.
mistakes: Testing a nullable column (`WHERE o.amount IS NULL`), which also returns Lena because order 106 has no amount.
Using INNER JOIN and wondering why the missing rows never appear.
Using `NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees)`: Gus's NULL dept_id makes it return no rows at all.
dialects: Every database supports both forms. Some (SQL Server, Oracle) also have EXCEPT / MINUS for "ids in A but not in B".
topics.interviewAnswer: To find rows with no match I use an anti-join: either a LEFT JOIN with WHERE the right table's key IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery. I prefer NOT EXISTS because it states the intent directly and is NULL-safe, and I avoid NOT IN against a subquery, since a single NULL in that list makes the whole condition unknown and returns nothing.

followUps.q: Why not use NOT IN to find customers without orders?
followUps.a: If the subquery returns any NULL, `x NOT IN (…)` is never true, so you get no rows. NOT EXISTS has no such problem.

followUps.q: Which column should you test for IS NULL after the LEFT JOIN?
followUps.a: One that is never NULL in a real matched row — the right table's primary key or the join column.

resources.title: Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL Joins with Comparison Operators

explain.answer:
1. LEFT JOIN, then keep the rows with no match: `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL`. Unmatched rows get NULLs in every right-hand column, so you keep just those.
2. NOT EXISTS: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)`. Keep the row if the subquery finds nothing.

The IS NULL column matters because NULL can mean two things: "no match" or "matched, but this value is empty". Test a column that is never NULL in a real match: the right table's primary key, or the column you joined on. If you test amount instead, Lena's order 106 (which has no amount) looks like "no order", and Lena wrongly appears.

write.answer: Departments on the left. A department with no employees gets NULL in e.emp_id, and emp_id is the primary key, so it is never NULL for a real employee. Only HR is left.

query.sql:
SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
WHERE e.emp_id IS NULL
ORDER BY d.dept_id;

predict.answer:
Lena, Omar and the second Tom (id 6), instead of just Omar and Tom.

Omar and Tom have no orders, so their order columns are NULL, amount included. Lena does have orders, but one of them, 106, has a NULL amount, so that row passes the test too. A NULL amount can mean "no order" or "an order with no amount", and this test can't tell them apart. That is why you test the key.

query.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.amount IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

edge.answer:
It returns no rows at all, even though HR has no employees.

The subquery returns every employee's dept_id, and Gus's is NULL. So for HR the test is `4 NOT IN (1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, NULL, 1)`, which means "4 <> 1 AND … AND 4 <> NULL". `4 <> NULL` is unknown, and anything AND unknown can't be true, so HR is not kept. One NULL in the list makes NOT IN fail for every row.

Fix it with NOT EXISTS, which doesn't have this trap, or keep NOT IN but add `WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.

topics.name: Self joins: a table joined to itself
topics.definition: A self join joins a table to itself under two different aliases, so a row can be compared with another row of the same table — such as an employee with their manager.
topics.problem: manager_id points into the same employees table. To show "Hana reports to Ben", you need Hana's row and Ben's row side by side. There is only one table, so you use it twice.
topics.idea: Give the table two aliases and treat them as two copies: e for the employee, m for the manager. Join on `m.emp_id = e.manager_id`, meaning "the manager copy's id equals the employee copy's manager_id". Now each result row has the employee's columns and their manager's columns. Use a LEFT JOIN if you want to keep Asha, who has no manager. Self joins also compare rows with each other — pairs in the same department, or rows on consecutive days.
topics.analogy: Two photocopies of the staff list on your desk. On the left copy you find Hana and read "manager: 2". On the right copy you find person 2 — Ben — and write his name next to hers.
topics.breaks: The photocopies are real copies. SQL doesn't copy anything: the aliases are just two names for the same table, which is why you must prefix every column (e.name, m.name) — otherwise "name" is ambiguous.
howItWorks: e and m are both the employees table.
For Hana (manager_id 2), find the m row with emp_id 2: Ben.
The result row holds e.name = Hana and m.name = Ben.
Asha's manager_id is NULL, so she has no match; LEFT JOIN keeps her with a NULL manager.
To compare rows, add a condition: `a.emp_id < b.emp_id` makes each pair appear once and stops a row pairing with itself.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  subgraph E["employees as e"]
    H["Hana · manager_id 2"]
    B1["Ben · manager_id 1"]
  end
  subgraph M["employees as m"]
    B2["2 · Ben"]
    A["1 · Asha"]
  end
  H -->|"m.emp_id = e.manager_id"| B2
  B1 --> A
diagram.caption: The same table plays two parts. Each employee row (e) is matched with the row of its manager (m) by comparing m.emp_id with e.manager_id.

examples.title: Each employee and their manager
examples.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

examples.title: Pairs of colleagues in the same department
examples.sql:
SELECT a.name AS first, b.name AS second, a.dept_id
FROM employees a
JOIN employees b ON b.dept_id = a.dept_id AND a.emp_id < b.emp_id
ORDER BY a.dept_id, a.name, b.name;
examples.note: `a.emp_id < b.emp_id` keeps each pair once (Asha–Ben, never also Ben–Asha) and never pairs someone with themselves.

examples.title: How many people report to each manager
examples.sql:
SELECT m.name AS manager, COUNT(*) AS direct_reports
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.name
ORDER BY direct_reports DESC, manager;

keyPoints: A self join uses the same table twice with two aliases.
Read the ON condition carefully: `m.emp_id = e.manager_id` means "m is e's manager".
Use LEFT JOIN to keep rows whose pointer is NULL (the top of the tree).
`a.id < b.id` gives each pair once; `a.id <> b.id` gives each pair twice.
A self join reaches one level. For a whole chain of managers, use a recursive CTE (Phase 4).
mistakes: Swapping the condition (`e.emp_id = m.manager_id`), which lists each person's reports instead of their manager.
Forgetting prefixes, so `name` is ambiguous.
Using INNER JOIN and losing the CEO.
topics.interviewAnswer: A self join joins a table to itself with two aliases so I can compare rows within it — the classic case is employees and managers through a self-referencing manager_id. I join the manager alias's primary key to the employee alias's manager_id, use a LEFT JOIN if the top of the hierarchy must appear, and for pair comparisons I add id less-than id to avoid self-pairs and mirrored duplicates.

followUps.q: How would you find employees who earn more than their manager?
followUps.a: Self join e to m on `m.emp_id = e.manager_id`, then `WHERE e.salary > m.salary`. Here it returns Hana.

followUps.q: How do you get the whole chain of managers, not just one level?
followUps.a: A recursive CTE that starts from the employee and repeatedly joins to the manager until manager_id is NULL.

explain.answer:
Read the employees table twice, as two copies: e for the employee, m for the manager. `m.emp_id = e.manager_id` says: "for this employee e, find the row in m whose id is the number written in e's manager_id".

For Hana, manager_id is 2, so the match is the row with emp_id 2: Ben. So m.name is her manager's name.

write.answer: Join once to get the manager (m), then join again from the manager to their manager (mm). Use LEFT JOINs so people at the top still show, with NULLs: Asha has no manager, and the people under Asha have no manager's manager.

query.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager, mm.name AS managers_manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m  ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
LEFT JOIN employees mm ON mm.emp_id = m.manager_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

predict.answer: 7 rows instead of 8. Asha is missing: her manager_id is NULL, so she has no matching manager row, and an INNER JOIN drops her.

query.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

edge.answer:
Join each employee to their manager, then compare the two hire dates: `WHERE e.hire_date < m.hire_date`.

In this data the answer is nobody: no rows. Every manager joined before the people under them. (Asha joined in 2019, Dara and Ben in 2020, and everyone they manage later.) An empty result is a real answer; don't "fix" the query until it returns something.

Asha has no manager. The INNER JOIN drops her before the WHERE runs. With a LEFT JOIN she would reach the WHERE, but `e.hire_date < NULL` is unknown, so she would be dropped anyway. Either way, she is never counted as "hired before her manager", which is right.

query.sql:
SELECT e.name, e.hire_date, m.name AS manager, m.hire_date AS manager_hired
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.hire_date < m.hire_date
ORDER BY e.name;

topics.name: Joining three or more tables
topics.definition: You join more than two tables by adding one JOIN … ON per table, walking along the keys — orders to customers, orders to order_items, order_items to products — so each row can hold columns from all of them.
topics.problem: "What did each customer buy?" needs the customer's name (customers), the order (orders), the line items (order_items) and the product names (products). That is four tables. Many-to-many relationships always need at least three.
topics.idea: Each JOIN adds one table to the rows you have so far, so a chain of joins follows the arrows in the database diagram. Start from the table whose grain you want in the result — here, one row per item bought, so order_items — or from the table you must keep in full. Each new JOIN needs its own ON condition linking it to a table already in the query. GROUP BY afterwards sums across all of them, for example revenue per category = `SUM(quantity × price)`.
topics.analogy: Following a paper trail. A receipt line says "product 6, quantity 3, order 101". You look up order 101 to find the customer, then customer 1 to find the name, then product 6 to find "Headphones". Each lookup is one join.
topics.breaks: On paper you choose which lookups to do. SQL does every join for every row, and an INNER JOIN anywhere in the chain drops rows that fail to match at that step — like order 106, which has no items.
topics.syntax:
SELECT ...
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id
JOIN products p     ON p.product_id  = oi.product_id;
howItWorks: FROM orders o: one row per order.
JOIN customers c: each order gains its customer's columns. Still one row per order.
JOIN order_items oi: an order with 2 items becomes 2 rows. The grain is now one row per item.
JOIN products p: each item row gains the product name and price.
Order 106 has no items, so the INNER JOIN to order_items drops it. Use LEFT JOINs if it must stay.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  C["customers"] ---|"customer_id"| O["orders"]
  O ---|"order_id"| OI["order_items"]
  OI ---|"product_id"| P["products"]
diagram.caption: Each JOIN walks one step along a key. To get from a customer to a product name you must pass through orders and order_items, the link table.

examples.title: What each order contained
examples.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, c.name AS customer, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_date < '2024-01-22'
ORDER BY o.order_id, p.product_name;
examples.note: Orders 102 and 103 each appear twice — one row per item. The grain changed when order_items joined in.

examples.title: Revenue per category
examples.sql:
SELECT p.category, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
examples.note: quantity × price is worked out per item row, then summed per category. The five add up to 793, the same as all order amounts.

examples.title: Customers who bought headphones
examples.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE p.product_name = 'Headphones'
ORDER BY c.name;
examples.note: Priya bought headphones in two orders, so without DISTINCT her name would appear twice.

keyPoints: One JOIN … ON per extra table; each ON links the new table to one already joined.
Follow the keys in the diagram. Many-to-many goes through the link table.
Know the grain after every join: joining a "many" table multiplies rows.
One INNER JOIN in a chain can drop rows; switch to LEFT JOIN where rows must survive.
Use clear aliases (c, o, oi, p) and line the ON conditions up so the chain is easy to read.
mistakes: Joining two tables on the wrong pair of columns (`oi.product_id = o.order_id`) — it runs but returns nonsense.
Mixing LEFT and INNER joins so that a later INNER JOIN removes the rows the LEFT JOIN kept.
Summing an order-level column (o.amount) after joining item rows, which counts it once per item (see Join traps).
topics.interviewAnswer: For multi-table queries I follow the foreign keys one hop at a time, adding a JOIN with its own ON condition per table, and I keep track of the grain after each join — joining a child table like order_items turns one row per order into one row per item. For many-to-many I go through the junction table, and I use LEFT JOINs wherever rows without a match must survive.

followUps.q: Does the order of INNER JOINs matter?
followUps.a: Not for the result — inner joins can be reordered freely, and the optimiser picks its own order. With LEFT JOINs, order does matter.

followUps.q: How do you get from customers to products?
followUps.a: customers → orders (customer_id) → order_items (order_id) → products (product_id).
