resources.title: CS50's Introduction to Databases with SQL — Lecture 1: Relating

explain.answer:
Count the rows after each step:

1. orders: 10 rows.
2. JOIN customers: still 10. Each order has exactly one customer, so nothing is added or lost.
3. JOIN order_items: 14. Each order is repeated once per item line (order 102 has two lines, so it now appears twice), and order 106, which has no items, is dropped.
4. JOIN products: still 14. Each item line has exactly one product.
5. WHERE order_date < '2024-01-22': 6 rows, the item lines of orders 101 to 104.

The rule: joining to the "one" side keeps the count; joining to the "many" side multiplies it; an INNER JOIN with no match removes rows.

query.sql:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) AS orders_only,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o
          JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id) AS with_items,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o
          JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
          WHERE o.order_date < '2024-01-22') AS after_where;

write.answer: Walk the keys from customers to orders to order_items to products, keep Priya, then group by product and add up the quantities. Mug, Notebook and Pen tie on 5, so the name breaks the tie.

query.sql:
SELECT p.product_name, SUM(oi.quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE c.name = 'Priya'
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
ORDER BY total_quantity DESC, p.product_name;

predict.answer: 14 rows: one per item line, not one per order. They cover 9 of the 10 orders. Order 106 is missing, because it has no items, so the INNER JOIN finds nothing to pair it with.

edge.answer:
Make the join to order_items a LEFT JOIN, and the join after it (products) a LEFT JOIN too. If products stayed an INNER JOIN, order 106's NULL product_id would match no product, and the row would be dropped again. Once a chain goes LEFT, every join after it must stay LEFT.

The full query returns 15 rows (14 item lines plus 106). The WHERE below only keeps the result short enough to read; delete it to see all 15.

query.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, c.name AS customer, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c         ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-02-01'
ORDER BY o.order_id, p.product_name;

topics.name: FULL OUTER JOIN and CROSS JOIN
topics.definition: A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps every row from both tables, with NULLs wherever either side has no match; a CROSS JOIN pairs every row of one table with every row of the other.
topics.problem: Comparing two lists — "which employees have no department, and which departments have no employees?" — needs the unmatched rows from both sides at once. Building a report grid — every customer × every month, zeros included — needs every combination. These two joins do those jobs.
topics.idea: FULL OUTER JOIN = a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN together: matches as usual, plus the unmatched left rows (right columns NULL) and the unmatched right rows (left columns NULL). It is mainly for reconciling two sources. CROSS JOIN has no ON at all: 6 customers × 3 months = 18 rows. On its own that is rarely what you want, but it is the standard way to build a complete grid, which you then LEFT JOIN the real data onto so gaps show as zero.
topics.analogy: FULL OUTER JOIN is comparing two class registers after a merger: you list everyone who is on both, plus the names that are only on one register. CROSS JOIN is a timetable grid: every class against every period, whether or not anything is scheduled there.
topics.breaks: A timetable grid is small. A cross join of two big tables is enormous — a million rows × a million rows is a trillion — so it is only safe when at least one side is tiny.
howItWorks: FULL OUTER JOIN employees and departments: the 7 matched pairs, plus Gus (no department), plus HR (no employees).
Gus's row has NULL department columns; HR's row has NULL employee columns.
CROSS JOIN customers and months: each customer row is paired with each month row, with no condition.
LEFT JOIN the orders onto that grid on customer and month: cells with no orders get NULL.
`COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)` turns those NULLs into zeros, so the report has no gaps.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD
  subgraph F["FULL OUTER JOIN"]
    F1["matched pairs"]
    F2["left rows with no match"]
    F3["right rows with no match"]
  end
  subgraph X["CROSS JOIN: 2 customers × 3 months"]
    X1["Tom · Jan"] --- X2["Tom · Feb"] --- X3["Tom · Mar"]
    X4["Lena · Jan"] --- X5["Lena · Feb"] --- X6["Lena · Mar"]
  end
diagram.caption: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps matches plus the leftovers from both sides. CROSS JOIN makes every combination — 2 customers × 3 months is 6 rows — ready to have real data joined onto it.

examples.title: FULL OUTER JOIN: the unmatched from both sides
examples.sql:
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name
FROM employees e
FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
ORDER BY d.dept_id, e.name;
examples.note: Gus (no department) and HR (no employees) both appear. Neither an INNER nor a LEFT JOIN shows both.

examples.title: CROSS JOIN: every combination
examples.sql:
SELECT p.product_name, d.dept_name
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN departments d
WHERE p.category = 'Stationery'
ORDER BY p.product_name, d.dept_id;
examples.note: A supply sheet: every stationery item for every department. 2 products × 4 departments = 8 rows.

examples.title: A complete grid with zeros: CROSS JOIN, then LEFT JOIN
examples.sql:
SELECT c.name, m.month, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS spent
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month FROM orders) AS m
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
 AND strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) = m.month
WHERE c.customer_id IN (2, 3)
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name, m.month
ORDER BY c.customer_id, m.month;
examples.note: Without the grid, Tom's February and Lena's January would be missing rows instead of zeros — which breaks charts and month-on-month maths.

keyPoints: FULL OUTER JOIN = matches + unmatched left rows + unmatched right rows.
CROSS JOIN has no ON and returns rows(a) × rows(b).
Grid pattern: CROSS JOIN the dimensions, LEFT JOIN the facts, COALESCE to 0.
A join with a missing or always-true ON condition is an accidental cross join.
mistakes: Running a CROSS JOIN between two large tables.
Forgetting an ON condition and getting a cross join by accident — the row count explodes.
Using WHERE on one side after a FULL OUTER JOIN, which removes the other side's unmatched rows.
dialects: MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN: write a LEFT JOIN, then UNION it with the unmatched rows of a RIGHT JOIN. SQLite added FULL OUTER JOIN in 3.39.
PostgreSQL can build date grids directly with `generate_series('2024-01-01', '2024-03-01', interval '1 month')`.
topics.interviewAnswer: A FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched rows plus the unmatched rows from both sides, with NULLs filling the gaps — useful for reconciling two sources. A CROSS JOIN is the Cartesian product, every row paired with every row; I mostly use it to build a complete grid such as every customer by every month, then LEFT JOIN the facts onto it so missing combinations show as zero instead of disappearing.

followUps.q: How many rows does a CROSS JOIN of 6 and 4 rows return?
followUps.a: 24 — every row of one with every row of the other.

followUps.q: How do you do a FULL OUTER JOIN in MySQL?
followUps.a: LEFT JOIN UNION the RIGHT JOIN rows where the left side is NULL (UNION ALL with that filter avoids duplicates).

practice.explain: Explain when you would use FULL OUTER JOIN instead of LEFT JOIN.
practice.write: Build a grid of every product category × every order status, with the number of items sold in each cell (0 where none).
practice.predict: How many rows does `SELECT * FROM customers CROSS JOIN departments;` return?
practice.edge: In the FULL OUTER JOIN example, add `WHERE e.salary > 40000`. Which rows disappear, and why does HR go too?

explain.answer:
Use LEFT JOIN when one table is the main list and you only care about its unmatched rows: "every department, even empty ones".

Use FULL OUTER JOIN when unmatched rows on both sides matter: "everything in either list, and show me what doesn't line up". With employees and departments it shows Gus (no department) and HR (no employees) in the same result. In real work it is for comparing two sources, such as payments against invoices, or yesterday's file against today's: missing on the left, missing on the right, and matched.

(MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN; you write a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN and UNION them.)

write.answer:
Make the grid first: every category CROSS JOIN every status. Then LEFT JOIN the real numbers onto it, worked out in a subquery (items sold per category and status), and COALESCE the gaps to 0.

The full grid is 5 categories × 4 statuses = 20 cells. The WHERE below keeps two categories so the result fits on screen; delete it to see all 20. Every 'cancelled' cell is 0, because the only cancelled order, 106, has no items.

query.sql:
SELECT cat.category, st.status, COALESCE(s.items, 0) AS items_sold
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) AS cat
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT status FROM orders) AS st
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT p.category, o.status, SUM(oi.quantity) AS items
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  JOIN orders o   ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  GROUP BY p.category, o.status
) AS s ON s.category = cat.category AND s.status = st.status
WHERE cat.category IN ('Electronics', 'Home')
ORDER BY cat.category, st.status;

predict.answer: 24 rows: every one of the 6 customers paired with every one of the 4 departments, 6 × 4. A CROSS JOIN has no ON, so nothing is matched and nothing is dropped. (It also has 8 columns, so the check below just counts.)

edge.answer:
Gus disappears, because he earns 38,000. HR disappears too, even though the filter is about salaries.

HR's row has no employee, so e.salary is NULL there. `NULL > 40000` is unknown, and WHERE drops anything that isn't true. The same happens to every row a FULL or LEFT JOIN filled with NULLs: a WHERE on the other table's columns removes them, and the outer join quietly becomes an inner join.

To keep HR, filter the employees before the join (in a subquery, or in the ON), or allow the empty side: `WHERE e.salary > 40000 OR e.emp_id IS NULL`.

query.sql:
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name
FROM employees e
FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary > 40000
ORDER BY d.dept_id, e.name;

topics.name: Join traps: double counting, and ON versus WHERE
topics.definition: The two classic join bugs are fan-out — joining a "many" table repeats the "one" side, so its numbers get summed several times — and putting a right-table filter in WHERE, which silently turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
topics.problem: Both bugs return a result with no error, and the numbers look believable. The total revenue comes out as 1131 instead of 793; customers with no delivered orders quietly vanish from an "all customers" report. Interviewers test for exactly these.
topics.idea: Fan-out: after orders JOIN order_items, an order with 2 items appears on 2 rows, each carrying the full order amount. `SUM(o.amount)` now counts it twice. The fix is to sum at the right grain: aggregate the many side first (in a subquery or CTE), then join one row per order. ON versus WHERE with a LEFT JOIN: a condition in ON decides which right rows match, and left rows are kept regardless. A condition in WHERE runs after the join, on the finished rows — and for unmatched rows the right columns are NULL, so `WHERE o.status = 'delivered'` is unknown and the row is thrown away.
topics.analogy: Fan-out is like counting a family's income once for each child in the family: join families to children and sum family income, and a family with three children is counted three times. ON versus WHERE is the difference between "invite every pupil, and note which ones brought a permission slip" and "invite only the pupils who brought one".
topics.breaks: With a family you would notice the triple count. SQL can't: it has no idea which column belongs to which grain. Checking the row count after each join is the habit that catches it.
topics.syntax:
-- keep all left rows, filter which right rows match:
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered'

-- aggregate the many side first, then join:
JOIN (SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS items FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) i
  ON i.order_id = o.order_id
howItWorks: orders has 10 rows. Joined to order_items it has 14 rows, because 5 orders have 2 items each (and order 106 has none).
Each of those rows carries its order's full amount, so summing amount adds 102, 103, 105, 109 and 110 twice: 1131.
Fix: sum o.amount on orders alone, or pre-aggregate order_items to one row per order before joining.
LEFT JOIN with `AND o.status = 'delivered'` in ON: all 6 customers are kept; only delivered orders are attached.
The same condition in WHERE: customers with no delivered order have NULL status, so they are removed — 3 customers vanish.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR O["order 102
amount 80"] --> I1["item: Desk lamp
amount 80"] O --> I2["item: Backpack
amount 80"] I1 --> S["SUM(amount) = 160
counted twice"] I2 --> S
diagram.caption: Fan-out: joining one order to its two items copies the order's amount onto both rows. Summing after the join counts it twice. Sum at the order level, or aggregate the items first.

examples.title: Fan-out: the total that is too big
examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(o.amount) AS total_after_join,
       (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders) AS true_total
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id;
examples.note: Orders with two items are counted twice. Nothing errors — the number is just wrong.

examples.title: The fix: aggregate the many side first
examples.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, o.amount, i.item_lines
FROM orders o
JOIN (
  SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS item_lines
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY order_id
) AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.customer_id = 1
ORDER BY o.order_id;
examples.note: The subquery shrinks order_items to one row per order before the join, so each order — and its amount — appears once.

examples.title: WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN
examples.sql:
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;
examples.note: Omar, Zoe and the second Tom have vanished, even though this is a LEFT JOIN.

examples.title: Move the condition into ON to keep everyone
examples.sql:
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered'
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;
examples.note: Now every customer is kept, and only delivered orders are attached. Zoe's pending order isn't shown, but Zoe is.

keyPoints: After every join, ask: what does one row mean now? Did the row count grow?
Never sum a "one"-side column after joining a "many" table. Sum first, or pre-aggregate the many side.
Using DISTINCT to hide fan-out hides the bug, not fixes it — sums can still be wrong.
With a LEFT JOIN, conditions on the right table go in ON; conditions on the left table go in WHERE.
With an INNER JOIN, ON and WHERE give the same result.
mistakes: `SUM(order.amount)` after joining order_items.
`COUNT(*)` after a fan-out join, counting items instead of orders. Use `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)`.
`LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.col = x` in an "all customers" report.
topics.interviewAnswer: The two join bugs I always check for are fan-out and misplaced filters. Fan-out happens when a one-to-many join repeats the parent row, so summing a parent column double-counts — I fix it by aggregating the child table to the parent's grain before joining. And with a LEFT JOIN, a filter on the right table belongs in the ON clause; in WHERE it discards the NULL-extended rows and silently becomes an inner join.

followUps.q: How do you detect fan-out?
followUps.a: Compare `COUNT(*)` with `COUNT(DISTINCT parent_id)` after the join, or check the total against the parent table alone.

followUps.q: Is there any difference between ON and WHERE for an INNER JOIN?
followUps.a: No difference in the result. It only matters for outer joins.

followUps.q: Can I fix fan-out with DISTINCT?
followUps.a: It may fix a list of names, but `SUM(DISTINCT amount)` is wrong too — two different orders of £80 would be counted once. Fix the grain instead.

explain.answer:
Order 102 is worth £80 and has two item lines (the lamp and the backpack). Join orders to order_items and order 102 becomes two rows, both carrying amount 80. `SUM(o.amount)` then adds £80 twice: £160 for one £80 order. That repeating is fan-out: the "one" side is copied once per row on the "many" side.

Two ways to avoid it:
1. Aggregate the many side first, down to one row per order (`GROUP BY order_id` in a subquery), and then join. Now it is one-to-one again.
2. Don't join a table you don't need for that number. Sum the amounts from orders alone. Or use the right level: the item lines' own `quantity * price`. For counts, `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)` also works; for sums it doesn't.

query.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, o.amount, oi.product_id
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_id = 102
ORDER BY oi.product_id;

write.answer:
After joining items, each order appears once per item line, so `COUNT(o.order_id)` would count item lines. `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)` counts each order once. `COUNT(oi.order_id)` counts item lines, and skips the NULLs from orders with none (106) and customers with none.

LEFT JOINs keep Omar and the second Tom with 0 and 0. Lena has 2 orders but only 1 item line, because 106 is empty.

query.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders,
       COUNT(oi.order_id) AS item_lines
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

predict.answer: 14 and 9. The join makes one row per item line (14). Those rows cover 9 different orders: every order except 106, which has no items. The gap between the two numbers is exactly the fan-out.

edge.answer:
The salary condition must go in the ON, not the WHERE.

In the ON, it decides which employees count as a match. Departments with no high earners still keep their row (with NULLs), and `COUNT(e.emp_id)` gives them 0.

In the WHERE, it runs after the join, and the NULL rows fail `e.salary > 60000`. Sales, Marketing and HR vanish, and you get only Engineering. (Dara earns exactly 60,000, so Sales really is 0.)

query.sql:
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS over_60k
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id AND e.salary > 60000
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
ORDER BY d.dept_id;

phases.title: Subqueries, CTEs and set operations
phases.goal: Use the result of one query inside another, break hard questions into named steps with WITH, walk trees with recursion, and stack results with UNION.
phases.bigPicture: A query's result is a table, so it can feed another query. That one idea turns hard questions ("customers who spend more than the average customer") into a chain of easy ones — and CTEs let you write that chain top to bottom, the way you would explain it.

topics.name: Subqueries: a query inside a query
topics.definition: A subquery is a SELECT inside another query, in brackets: it can return one value (to compare with), a list (for IN), or a whole table (to select FROM).
topics.problem: "Who earns more than the average?" needs the average first, then a comparison. "What is the average customer's total spend?" needs a total per customer first, then an average of those. Each needs two steps, and a subquery puts both steps into one query.
topics.idea: The database runs the inner query and uses its result in the outer one. There are three shapes. A scalar subquery returns one value — `(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)` — and goes anywhere a single value can. A list subquery returns one column of many rows and goes after IN. A table subquery (a derived table) goes in FROM, needs an alias, and is used like any other table — which is how you aggregate an aggregate.
topics.analogy: Asking a friend to look something up while you wait. "What is the average salary?" — they come back with 63750 — "OK, then show me everyone above that." The inner question is answered first and its answer is slotted into the outer one.
topics.breaks: Your friend answers once. A correlated subquery (next lesson) is different: it is asked again for every outer row, with that row's values plugged in.
topics.syntax:
WHERE column > (SELECT one_value FROM ...)
WHERE column IN (SELECT one_column FROM ...)
FROM (SELECT ... ) AS alias
howItWorks: The inner query `SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees` runs first and returns 63750.
The outer query becomes, in effect, `WHERE salary > 63750`.
Asha, Hana, Ben and Chen pass; the rest don't.
For IN, the inner query returns a list of customer ids (2, 1, 5), and the outer query keeps customers whose id is in the list.
For a derived table, the inner query makes a small table (one total per customer) that the outer query averages.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR I["inner query
SELECT AVG(salary)"] -->|"63750"| O["outer query
WHERE salary over 63750"] O --> R["Asha, Hana, Ben, Chen"]
diagram.caption: The inner query runs first and hands its answer to the outer one. Here it hands over a single number; it can also hand over a list (for IN) or a whole table (for FROM).

examples.title: One value: above the average salary
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
ORDER BY salary DESC, name;

examples.title: A list: customers who ordered in March
examples.sql:
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= '2024-03-01'
)
ORDER BY name;
examples.note: Only the first Tom (customer 2) ordered in March. Each customer appears once, even with several March orders.

examples.title: A table: the average of totals
examples.note: You can't write `AVG(SUM(amount))`. Make the totals first (425, 275, 60, 33), then average them.

keyPoints: A subquery is a query in brackets, run to feed the outer query.
Scalar subquery: exactly one value. If it returns more than one row, the query fails.
IN subquery: one column, any number of rows.
Derived table in FROM: give it an alias. Use it to aggregate an aggregate or to filter on a calculated column.
Most subqueries can also be written as a join or a CTE; pick whichever reads most clearly.
mistakes: A scalar subquery that returns several rows ("more than one row returned by a subquery").
Forgetting the alias on a derived table (required in PostgreSQL before version 16, MySQL and SQL Server).
Nesting subqueries three deep. Rewrite it with CTEs so it reads top to bottom.
topics.interviewAnswer: A subquery is a nested SELECT whose result the outer query uses: as a single value for comparison, as a list for IN, or as a derived table in FROM. I use derived tables when I need to aggregate in two stages — like averaging per-customer totals — and once nesting gets deeper than one level I switch to CTEs so the logic reads top to bottom.

followUps.q: Subquery or join — which is faster?
followUps.a: Usually the same: modern optimisers rewrite IN and EXISTS subqueries as joins. Choose for clarity, then check the plan if it is slow.

followUps.q: What happens if a scalar subquery returns no rows?
followUps.a: It returns NULL, so a comparison with it is unknown and filters everything out.
