explain.answer:
1. One value (a scalar subquery): one row, one column, such as `(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)`. It goes anywhere a single value can: in a WHERE comparison (`salary > (…)`), or as a column in SELECT.
2. A list: one column, many rows, such as `(SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`. It goes after IN or NOT IN in a WHERE (or inside EXISTS).
3. A table: many rows and columns. It goes in FROM (or a JOIN), like a table, and needs a name: `FROM (…) AS per_customer`.

The question to ask: how many rows and columns does my subquery return? That decides where it can go.

write.answer: A scalar subquery works out the average (125 ÷ 7 = 17.86), and the outer query compares every price with it.

query.sql:
SELECT product_name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)
ORDER BY price DESC;

predict.answer:
Priya and Zoe. Tom drops out.

The March orders are 108 (Tom, 1 March), 109 (Priya, 10 March) and 110 (Zoe, 16 March). From 5 March only 109 and 110 are left, so the list becomes customers 1 and 5.

query.sql:
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= '2024-03-05'
)
ORDER BY name;

edge.answer:
This uses `=`, which expects one value, but the subquery returns a customer_id for every delivered order (7 of them):

`SELECT name FROM customers WHERE customer_id = (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered');`

PostgreSQL and SQL Server stop with an error ("more than one row returned by a subquery"). SQLite doesn't: it quietly uses the first row and ignores the rest, which is worse, because the result looks fine.

Fix 1: you meant "any of them", so use IN. That gives Priya, Tom and Lena (below).
Fix 2: you meant one particular value, so make the subquery return exactly one row: aggregate it, or sort and take one. `WHERE customer_id = (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1)` gives Tom, who placed the biggest delivered order (£200).

topics.name: Correlated subqueries, EXISTS, and the NOT IN trap
topics.definition: A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer row, so it is worked out once per outer row; EXISTS asks "does the subquery return any row at all?", which makes it the safe way to test for a match.
topics.problem: "Each customer's latest order", "employees paid above their own department's average", "customers with at least one delivered order" — the comparison changes for every row. And the obvious way to find "no match", NOT IN, has a trap that returns nothing at all when NULLs are around.
topics.idea: In `WHERE o.order_date = (SELECT MAX(o2.order_date) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id)`, the inner query uses o.customer_id from the outer row, so it is re-run (in effect) for each order. EXISTS (subquery) is true if the subquery finds at least one row; what it selects doesn't matter, so people write `SELECT 1`. NOT EXISTS is true when it finds none. The NOT IN trap: `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` means `x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL`, and the last part is always unknown — so the whole test is never true.
topics.analogy: A correlated subquery is a teacher checking each pupil's mark against that pupil's own previous best, not one class-wide number. EXISTS is calling out "is anyone here from Leeds?" — one hand up is enough, and nobody has to say their name.
topics.breaks: A teacher really does check each pupil one at a time. A database usually doesn't: the optimiser rewrites most correlated subqueries into a join that does all the rows at once. Think of it as row by row; don't assume it is slow.
topics.syntax:
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM other o
  WHERE o.key = outer_table.key
)
howItWorks: Outer row: order 101 of customer 1. Inner query: the latest order_date for customer 1 is 2024-03-10. 101's date is 2024-01-06, so it fails.
Order 109 of customer 1 has date 2024-03-10, which equals the latest, so it is kept.
This repeats for every order, so each customer's latest order is kept.
EXISTS: for customer Omar, the inner query finds no delivered orders, so EXISTS is false and Omar is dropped.
NOT IN with a list containing NULL is never true, so `dept_id NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees)` returns no rows — because Gus's dept_id is NULL.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD A["outer row: customer Priya"] --> B["inner query uses Priya's id:
any delivered order?"] B -->|"found one"| K["EXISTS is true: keep Priya"] C["outer row: customer Omar"] --> D["inner query uses Omar's id:
any delivered order?"] D -->|"none"| X["EXISTS is false: drop Omar"]
diagram.caption: A correlated subquery is asked again for each outer row, using that row's values. EXISTS only needs to know whether at least one row comes back.

examples.title: Each customer's latest order (correlated)
examples.sql:
SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_id, o.order_date
FROM orders o
WHERE o.order_date = (
  SELECT MAX(o2.order_date)
  FROM orders o2
  WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id
)
ORDER BY o.customer_id;
examples.note: `o2.customer_id = o.customer_id` is the link to the outer row. If a customer had two orders on their latest day, both would appear.

examples.title: EXISTS: customers with a delivered order
examples.sql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered'
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: The NOT IN trap
examples.note: HR has no employees, yet nothing comes back. The list contains Gus's NULL, so "not in the list" is never true.

examples.title: NOT EXISTS gets it right
examples.sql:
SELECT d.dept_name
FROM departments d
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM employees e
  WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id
);

keyPoints: A correlated subquery uses outer-row columns; logically it runs once per outer row.
EXISTS is true when the subquery returns at least one row; `SELECT 1` inside is a convention.
NOT EXISTS is the NULL-safe "no match" test. Prefer it to NOT IN.
`x NOT IN (… NULL …)` is never true. `x IN (… NULL …)` still works for the values that match.
Correlated subqueries are clear for "compare with my own group"; window functions (Phase 5) often do the same faster.
mistakes: Using NOT IN against a column that can be NULL.
Forgetting the correlation (`WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id`), which compares every row with the overall maximum instead.
Thinking EXISTS cares what the subquery selects. It only checks whether a row exists.
dialects: All major databases support EXISTS, NOT EXISTS and correlated subqueries the same way. If you must use NOT IN, add `WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.
topics.interviewAnswer: A correlated subquery references the outer query's row, so logically it is evaluated per row — useful for comparisons against a row's own group, like each customer's latest order. EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns any row, and NOT EXISTS is my default anti-join, because NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery yields a single NULL: x not in a list containing NULL can never be true.

followUps.q: Why is NOT IN dangerous?
followUps.a: `x NOT IN (a, NULL)` means `x <> a AND x <> NULL`. The second part is unknown, so the whole condition is never true and no rows return.

followUps.q: EXISTS or IN — which is better?
followUps.a: For "has a match" they are equivalent and usually optimised the same. For "has no match", use NOT EXISTS because of NULLs.

followUps.q: Are correlated subqueries slow?
followUps.a: Not necessarily: optimisers often turn them into joins. On big data, a window function or a pre-aggregated join is usually faster and clearer.

practice.explain: Explain, with the HR example, why NOT IN returned nothing.
practice.write: Using EXISTS, write a query for products that appear in at least one order of Priya's.
practice.predict: What does `SELECT name FROM employees e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees r WHERE r.manager_id = e.emp_id) ORDER BY name;` return?
practice.edge: Make the NOT IN version of the HR query return HR, by changing only the subquery.

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs — Subquery Expressions (EXISTS, IN, NOT IN)
W3Schools — SQL EXISTS Operator
resources.source: short page with a try-it editor, free

explain.answer:
The subquery returns every employee's dept_id, and Gus's is NULL. So for HR (dept 4) the test is `4 NOT IN (1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, NULL, 1)`.

NOT IN means "not equal to each one": 4 <> 1 AND 4 <> 2 AND … AND 4 <> NULL. The last part is unknown, because nobody can say whether 4 equals an unknown value. TRUE AND unknown is unknown, and WHERE only keeps true. So HR is dropped, and so is every other department. One NULL in the list empties the whole result.

NOT EXISTS asks a different question: "is there any employee row with this dept_id?". For HR the answer is plainly no, so it works.

write.answer: For each product, EXISTS asks: "is there at least one item line for this product, in an order placed by Priya?". It stops at the first one it finds. Only the phone case fails.

query.sql:
SELECT p.product_name
FROM products p
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o    ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id AND c.name = 'Priya'
)
ORDER BY p.product_name;

predict.answer:
Chen, Eli, Fatima, Gus and Hana: everyone who manages nobody.

For each employee e, the subquery looks for anyone whose manager_id is e. Asha (1), Ben (2) and Dara (4) appear as someone's manager, so for them a row exists and they are dropped. Nobody reports to the other five.

edge.answer:
Take the NULL out of the list. With Gus's NULL gone, the list is just 1, 2 and 3, and `4 NOT IN (1, 2, 3)` is true.

Use this whenever the column in a NOT IN subquery can be NULL. Or just use NOT EXISTS.

topics.name: CTEs: naming each step with WITH
topics.definition: A CTE (common table expression) is a named, temporary result written at the top of a query with WITH name AS (…), which later parts of the query can use like a table.
topics.problem: Subqueries inside subqueries read inside-out and quickly become unreadable. In an interview, the person watching needs to follow your thinking. CTEs let you write a hard query as a list of small, named steps, in the order you would explain them.
topics.idea: `WITH per_customer AS (SELECT …)` defines a step and gives it a name. The main query after it can use per_customer like a table — even more than once. You can chain several CTEs, separated by commas, and each one can use the ones above it. A CTE exists only for that one query. It is mostly about readability: the database runs it much like the equivalent subquery.
topics.analogy: A recipe that says "first make the sauce; set it aside" before the main steps. Later steps just say "add the sauce". You name the sub-result once and refer to it by name.
topics.breaks: Sauce made once is used everywhere it is needed. A database may compute a CTE once or re-run it each time it is used — that is up to the optimiser — so don't use CTEs as a speed trick.
howItWorks: per_customer: one row per customer with their total spend (425, 275, 60, 33).
The main query joins per_customer to customers to get names.
The WHERE uses per_customer a second time to work out the average total (198.25).
Customers above that average are kept: Priya and Tom.
Each step can be tested alone: select from it while you build the query.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR O["orders"] --> A["CTE per_customer
total per customer"] A --> M["main query:
join names,
keep totals above average"] A -->|"used again"| AV["average of the totals"] AV --> M C["customers"] --> M
diagram.caption: Each CTE is a named step. The main query reads them like tables — and can use one step twice, here both for the rows and for their average.

examples.title: Customers who spend more than the average customer
examples.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, p.total
FROM per_customer p
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id
WHERE p.total > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM per_customer)
ORDER BY p.total DESC;

examples.title: Several steps, read top to bottom
examples.sql:
WITH delivered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, amount
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'delivered'
),
totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders, SUM(amount) AS delivered_total
  FROM delivered
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, t.delivered_orders, t.delivered_total,
       CASE WHEN t.delivered_total >= 200 THEN 'gold' ELSE 'standard' END AS tier
FROM totals t
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
ORDER BY t.delivered_total DESC, c.name;
examples.note: Filter, then total, then label: three small steps instead of one tangle.

keyPoints: WITH name AS (query) defines a CTE; separate several with commas, and use WITH only once.
A CTE can use the CTEs defined above it, and the main query can use any of them, more than once.
A CTE lasts for one statement only.
Use CTEs to make the steps of a hard query readable — interviewers love seeing this.
Build and test one CTE at a time.
mistakes: Writing WITH before every CTE. It is `WITH a AS (…), b AS (…)`.
A comma after the last CTE, before the main SELECT.
Expecting a CTE to exist in the next query. It is gone after the statement ends.
dialects: PostgreSQL before version 12 always computed a CTE separately (an "optimisation fence"); since 12 it can fold it into the main query, and you can force either with MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED.
MySQL supports CTEs from version 8.0.
topics.interviewAnswer: A CTE is a named subquery defined with WITH at the top of a statement, which the rest of the query can reference like a table, even multiple times. I use CTEs to break a hard problem into steps — filter, aggregate, rank, then select — which makes the query easy to read and to debug one step at a time. Performance is usually the same as the equivalent subquery.

followUps.q: CTE or subquery — what is the difference?
followUps.a: Mostly readability: a CTE is named, defined once, can be reused within the query, and reads top to bottom. CTEs can also be recursive.

followUps.q: CTE or temporary table?
followUps.a: A CTE lasts one statement and isn't stored. A temporary table lasts the session, can be indexed, and suits large intermediate results reused by several queries.

practice.explain: Explain why a CTE makes a query easier to read than nested subqueries.
practice.write: Using two CTEs, find the product category with the highest revenue.
practice.predict: In the first example, what changes if `>` becomes `<`?
practice.edge: Customer 3 has an order with a NULL amount. Does it affect per_customer's total for Lena, or the average? Explain.

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs — WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions)
CS50's Introduction to Databases with SQL — Lecture 3: Writing
Mode SQL Tutorial — Writing Subqueries in SQL

explain.answer:
Nested subqueries read inside out: you have to find the innermost bracket first and work outwards, and a step needed twice has to be written twice.

A CTE reads top to bottom, like a recipe. Each step gets a name that says what it is (per_customer, delivered, totals), and later steps use it like a table. In the first example, per_customer is used twice, once to join and once for the average, but written only once. Each step can also be run and checked on its own while you build the query.

(It is about readability. In most databases a CTE is not faster than the same subquery.)

write.answer:
Step 1 (line_revenue): the revenue of each item line, with its category. Step 2 (category_revenue): add those up per category. Then keep the category whose revenue equals the maximum. Electronics wins with £440: 11 headphones at £40.

Using `= MAX(…)` instead of `ORDER BY … LIMIT 1` keeps both categories if two ever tie.

query.sql:
WITH line_revenue AS (
  SELECT p.category, oi.quantity * p.price AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
),
category_revenue AS (
  SELECT category, SUM(revenue) AS revenue
  FROM line_revenue
  GROUP BY category
)
SELECT category, revenue
FROM category_revenue
WHERE revenue = (SELECT MAX(revenue) FROM category_revenue);

predict.answer:
You get the customers who spend less than average, instead of more: Lena (£60) and Zoe (£33), instead of Priya (£425) and Tom (£275).

The per-customer totals are 425, 275, 60 and 33, and their average is 793 ÷ 4 = 198.25. Omar and the second Tom are not in per_customer at all (they have no orders), so they are not below the average either.

query.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, p.total
FROM per_customer p
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id
WHERE p.total < (SELECT AVG(total) FROM per_customer)
ORDER BY p.total DESC;

edge.answer:
Not here.

SUM skips NULLs, so Lena's total is just her £60 order. The NULL is ignored: her total is not NULL and not lower. The average is then taken over the 4 totals (425, 275, 60, 33), so it is 198.25 either way.

It would matter if all of a customer's amounts were NULL. Their total would be NULL, and AVG would skip that customer entirely: the average would be over 3 customers, not 4. If that customer should count as £0, use `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)`.

query.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total,
         COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS with_amount
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, total, orders, with_amount,
       (SELECT AVG(total) FROM per_customer) AS avg_total
FROM per_customer
ORDER BY customer_id;

topics.name: Recursive CTEs: walking trees and filling in dates
topics.definition: A recursive CTE refers to itself: an anchor query gives the starting rows, and a recursive part, joined with UNION ALL, keeps adding rows from the previous round until no new rows appear.
topics.problem: An org chart can be any number of levels deep, so a fixed number of self joins can't walk it. The same goes for folder trees, category trees and "every day in this range, including days with no orders". Recursion handles any depth.
topics.idea: The anchor runs once: for the org chart, "the person with no manager" (Asha, level 0). Then the recursive part runs on the rows found in the previous round: "employees whose manager is in the previous round" (Ben, Chen, Dara, Fatima, level 1), then their reports (Eli, Gus, Hana, level 2), and so on. When a round finds nothing, it stops. Always give it a way to stop — a WHERE that eventually fails — or it runs forever.
topics.analogy: Passing a message down a phone tree. The boss calls her direct reports, each of them calls theirs, and the calling stops when someone has nobody left to call.
topics.breaks: A phone tree stops on its own. Data can loop — if A manages B and B manages A — and a recursive CTE would go round forever. Put a limit on the depth when the data might not be a clean tree.
howItWorks: Anchor: `WHERE manager_id IS NULL` finds Asha, level 0.
Round 1: employees whose manager_id is Asha's id get level 0 + 1 = 1.
Round 2: employees managed by anyone found in round 1 get level 2: Eli and Gus (Dara), Hana (Ben).
Round 3 finds nobody managed by Eli, Gus or Hana, so the recursion stops.
For a date range, the anchor is the first day and each round adds one day until the last day.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD A["anchor · level 0
Asha"] --> B["round 1 · level 1
Ben, Chen, Dara, Fatima"] B --> C["round 2 · level 2
Hana (under Ben)
Eli, Gus (under Dara)"] C --> D["round 3: nobody new
stop"]
diagram.caption: Each round finds the people who report to someone found in the round before. When a round finds nobody new, the recursion stops.

examples.title: The simplest: count to 5
examples.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 5
)
SELECT n
FROM numbers
ORDER BY n;
examples.note: Start at 1; each round adds 1; `WHERE n < 5` is the stop rule.

examples.title: The whole org chart, with levels
examples.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE chart AS (
  SELECT emp_id, name, 0 AS level
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, chart.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chart ON e.manager_id = chart.emp_id
)
SELECT name, level
FROM chart
ORDER BY level, name;

examples.title: Every day in a range, even days with no orders
examples.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT '2024-01-05'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE day < '2024-01-09'
)
SELECT d.day, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM days d
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date = d.day
GROUP BY d.day
ORDER BY d.day;
examples.note: The CTE makes the calendar; the LEFT JOIN brings in orders, so the empty days show 0.

keyPoints: Shape: WITH RECURSIVE name AS (anchor UNION ALL recursive part).
The recursive part joins the table to the CTE itself, using only the rows found in the previous round.
There must be a stop rule — a WHERE that eventually returns no new rows.
Carry extra columns (level, a path string) to know how deep each row is.
Common uses: org charts, category or folder trees, bill of materials, and generating number or date series.
mistakes: No stop rule, so it runs until the database gives up.
Using UNION instead of UNION ALL by habit. UNION ALL is the normal choice; UNION removes duplicates and can stop cycles, but costs more.
Joining the wrong way round (`chart.manager_id = e.emp_id`), which walks up the tree instead of down.
dialects: PostgreSQL, MySQL 8+ and SQLite need the word RECURSIVE. SQL Server and Oracle use plain WITH.
PostgreSQL makes date series easier with `generate_series`. SQL Server limits recursion to 100 rounds unless you add `OPTION (MAXRECURSION n)`.
topics.interviewAnswer: A recursive CTE has an anchor member that produces the starting rows and a recursive member, unioned with UNION ALL, that joins back to the CTE to produce the next level, repeating until no new rows appear. I use it for hierarchies of unknown depth, like an org chart with a level column, and for generating date series to fill gaps — always with a clear termination condition, and a depth limit if the data might contain cycles.

followUps.q: How does a recursive CTE know when to stop?
followUps.a: When the recursive part returns no new rows. A WHERE condition (like n < 5, or reaching people with no reports) makes that happen.

followUps.q: How do you protect against cycles in the data?
followUps.a: Carry a level or a path column and stop at a maximum depth, or stop when the next id is already in the path.

practice.explain: Explain what the anchor and the recursive part each do, using the org chart.
practice.write: Write a recursive CTE that shows Hana's chain of managers as one string: 'Hana → Ben → Asha'.
practice.predict: In the org-chart example, what level does each person get if the anchor is `WHERE name = 'Dara'`?
practice.edge: What would happen if Asha's manager_id were set to 8 (Hana), making a loop? How would you stop the query running forever?

write.answer: Walk up instead of down. The anchor is Hana's row; each round joins to the row of the current person's manager and adds " → name" to the path. The top of the chain is the row whose manager_id is NULL, so keep only that one.

query.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE chain(emp_id, manager_id, path) AS (
  SELECT emp_id, manager_id, name
  FROM employees
  WHERE name = 'Hana'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT m.emp_id, m.manager_id, chain.path || ' → ' || m.name
  FROM chain
  JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = chain.manager_id
)
SELECT path
FROM chain
WHERE manager_id IS NULL;

predict.answer:
Dara is level 0, and Eli and Gus are level 1. That is all: nobody reports to Eli or Gus.

The anchor decides where the walk starts. Starting from Dara, you only see Dara's part of the tree; Asha, Ben and the rest are never reached.

query.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE chart AS (
  SELECT emp_id, name, 0 AS level
  FROM employees
  WHERE name = 'Dara'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, chart.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chart ON e.manager_id = chart.emp_id
)
SELECT name, level FROM chart ORDER BY level, name;

edge.answer:
Two things go wrong.

The org-chart query as written starts from `manager_id IS NULL`. With the loop nobody has a NULL manager, so the anchor finds nothing, and the result is empty.

Start from Asha by name instead, and it never ends: Asha → Ben → Hana → Asha → … Each round finds "new" rows (the same people, one level deeper), so the recursion never runs out. SQLite runs until it is stopped; SQL Server stops after 100 rounds with an error.

Ways to stop it:
• a depth limit: `WHERE chart.level < 10` in the recursive part;
• a visited list: carry the ids seen so far and refuse to visit one again (below);
• PostgreSQL 14+ has a CYCLE clause that does this for you.

Below, the UPDATE makes the loop, and the visited list stops the walk when it gets back to Asha.

query.sql:
UPDATE employees SET manager_id = 8 WHERE name = 'Asha';

WITH RECURSIVE chart AS (
  SELECT emp_id, name, 0 AS level, ',' || emp_id || ',' AS visited
  FROM employees
  WHERE name = 'Asha'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.name, chart.level + 1, chart.visited || e.emp_id || ','
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chart ON e.manager_id = chart.emp_id
  WHERE chart.visited NOT LIKE '%,' || e.emp_id || ',%'
)
SELECT name, level FROM chart ORDER BY level, name;

topics.name: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT and EXCEPT
topics.definition: Set operators stack the results of two queries: UNION ALL keeps every row, UNION removes duplicates, INTERSECT keeps rows found in both, and EXCEPT keeps rows in the first but not the second.
topics.problem: Sometimes the rows you need come from two places: every city mentioned by departments or customers; cities that have both a department and a customer. Joins put tables side by side; set operators put results on top of each other.
topics.idea: Write two SELECTs with the same number of columns, of matching types, and put a set operator between them. The column names come from the first SELECT. UNION ALL simply stacks the rows — fast, and keeps duplicates. UNION stacks them and removes duplicate rows — which costs a sort or hash. INTERSECT keeps rows in both results; EXCEPT keeps rows of the first that are not in the second. A single ORDER BY at the very end sorts the combined result.
topics.analogy: Two class lists. UNION ALL staples them together. UNION staples them and crosses out anyone listed twice. INTERSECT is pupils on both lists. EXCEPT is pupils on the first list but not on the second.
topics.breaks: Pupils are matched by name. Set operators match whole rows, column by column — so adding a column that differs (like a source label) stops rows from counting as duplicates.
topics.syntax:
SELECT col_a, col_b FROM table_one
UNION ALL
SELECT col_x, col_y FROM table_two
ORDER BY col_a;
howItWorks: Both SELECTs return one column: department locations and customer cities.
UNION stacks them (10 rows) and removes duplicate rows, leaving 5 different cities, including NULL.
UNION ALL keeps all of them; a source column shows where each row came from.
INTERSECT keeps only cities in both lists: Leeds and London.
EXCEPT keeps department cities with no customer: Manchester.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR
  A["query 1 rows"] --> U["UNION ALL: all rows"]
  B["query 2 rows"] --> U
  A --> UD["UNION: all rows, duplicates removed"]
  B --> UD
  A --> I["INTERSECT: rows in both"]
  B --> I
  A --> E["EXCEPT: rows in query 1 only"]
diagram.caption: Set operators combine two results vertically. Both queries must return the same number of columns, with matching types; the names come from the first query.

examples.title: UNION: every city, once
examples.sql:
SELECT location AS city FROM departments
UNION
SELECT city FROM customers
ORDER BY city;
examples.note: Duplicates are removed, and the NULLs collapse into one row too.

examples.title: UNION ALL: keep everything, with a label
examples.sql:
SELECT 'department' AS source, location AS city FROM departments
UNION ALL
SELECT 'customer', city FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY city, source;

examples.title: INTERSECT: in both
examples.sql:
SELECT city FROM customers
INTERSECT
SELECT location FROM departments
ORDER BY city;

examples.title: EXCEPT: in the first, not the second
examples.sql:
SELECT location FROM departments
EXCEPT
SELECT city FROM customers
ORDER BY location;

keyPoints: Both queries need the same number of columns, in the same order, with compatible types.
UNION ALL keeps duplicates and is faster; UNION removes them.
Use UNION ALL unless you really need duplicates removed.
INTERSECT and EXCEPT also remove duplicates from their result.
One ORDER BY, at the end, sorts the combined result; column names come from the first query.
mistakes: Using UNION when the two sets can't overlap — paying for duplicate removal you don't need.
Putting ORDER BY on the first query instead of at the end.
Lining columns up in a different order in the second query: they are matched by position, not by name.
dialects: Oracle calls EXCEPT `MINUS`. MySQL only added INTERSECT and EXCEPT in version 8.0.31.
topics.interviewAnswer: Set operators combine two result sets vertically, matching columns by position. UNION ALL appends everything; UNION also removes duplicate rows, which costs a sort or hash, so I default to UNION ALL unless duplicates must go. INTERSECT returns rows present in both results and EXCEPT returns rows in the first but not the second — a neat alternative to an anti-join when comparing id lists.

followUps.q: UNION vs UNION ALL?
followUps.a: UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps them all and is faster because it skips that step.

followUps.q: JOIN vs UNION?
followUps.a: A join adds columns by matching rows side by side; a union adds rows by stacking results on top of each other.

practice.explain: Explain the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, and when each is right.
practice.write: Write one query that lists every person's name from both employees and customers, with a column saying which table they came from.
practice.predict: How many rows does `SELECT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT location FROM departments;` return?
practice.edge: Does UNION treat two NULL cities as duplicates? Check with the first example, and explain how that differs from `=`.

resources.title: W3Schools — SQL UNION Operator
resources.source: short page with a try-it editor, free

explain.answer:
Both stack two results on top of each other. UNION then removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps every row.

Use UNION when you want a list of different values, such as "every city we have a customer or an office in, once each".

Use UNION ALL when every row counts, such as stacking January's and February's orders before adding them up, or when duplicates can't happen anyway (each half has a different label). It is also faster: UNION has to sort or hash everything to find duplicates.

A useful habit: write UNION ALL by default, and use UNION only when you really mean "remove duplicates".

write.answer:
Both halves need the same number of columns, in the same order. The label column is a fixed text value in each half. Column names come from the first half, so the second can skip AS.

Tom appears twice because he signed up twice. UNION would merge those two identical rows; whether you want that depends on whether you are listing people or sign-ups.

query.sql:
SELECT name, 'employee' AS source FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT name, 'customer' FROM customers
ORDER BY source, name;

predict.answer: 10 rows: 6 customer cities plus 4 department locations. UNION ALL removes nothing, so the duplicate Londons and Leeds, and Zoe's NULL, all stay.

edge.answer:
Yes. UNION (like DISTINCT and GROUP BY) treats two NULLs as duplicates and keeps one. In the first example only Zoe's city is NULL, so add a second NULL to check: below, two NULLs go in and one comes out.

That differs from `=`, where `NULL = NULL` is unknown, not true. The rule: for comparisons, NULL equals nothing; for removing duplicates and grouping, all NULLs count as the same.

query.sql:
SELECT city FROM customers
UNION
SELECT NULL
ORDER BY city;

phases.title: Window functions: ranking, running totals and comparing rows
phases.goal: Calculate across related rows — rank them, compare each with the one before, keep running totals — without losing the individual rows the way GROUP BY does.
phases.bigPicture: Window functions are the single most tested "advanced" SQL topic. Top N per group, month-on-month growth, running totals, streaks — all of them become short once you think in windows: for each row, look at a set of related rows, and work something out.

topics.name: What a window function is: OVER and PARTITION BY
topics.definition: A window function calculates a value for each row from a set of related rows (its "window"), defined by OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …), and — unlike GROUP BY — keeps every row in the result.
topics.problem: "Show each employee with their department's average salary next to them." GROUP BY gives you the averages but throws away the employees; joining the averages back is clumsy. A window function puts the group's number on every row in one step.
topics.idea: Add OVER (…) after a function and it becomes a window function. OVER () with nothing inside means "the window is every row". PARTITION BY dept_id splits the rows into windows, one per department, like GROUP BY — but the rows stay separate, and each row gets its own window's answer. ORDER BY inside OVER sets an order within each window, which ranking and running totals need. Any aggregate (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX) can be used this way, plus special window-only functions such as ROW_NUMBER and LAG.
topics.analogy: A class photo where each pupil holds a card. GROUP BY would replace each form group with one person holding the group's average. A window function keeps every pupil in the photo, and each one's card shows their own form group's average.
topics.breaks: In the photo the card is written once. A window function is worked out in the SELECT step, after WHERE and GROUP BY — so WHERE can't filter on it. To filter on a window result, wrap the query in a CTE.
howItWorks: FROM and WHERE produce the rows: 7 employees with a department.
PARTITION BY dept_id makes three windows: department 1 (4 people), 2 (2 people), 3 (1 person).
`AVG(salary)` is worked out over each window: 78750, 52500, 52000.
Each row gets the answer for its own window, and no rows are removed.
OVER () with no partition makes one window of all rows: `COUNT(*) OVER ()` is 8 on every row.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR subgraph W1["window: dept 1 · avg 78750"] A["Asha 95000"] B["Ben 70000"] C["Chen 70000"] H["Hana 80000"] end subgraph W2["window: dept 2 · avg 52500"] D["Dara 60000"] E["Eli 45000"] end W1 --> R["every row kept,
each with its own window's average"] W2 --> R
diagram.caption: PARTITION BY draws a box around related rows. The function is worked out inside each box, and the answer is written onto every row in it — no row disappears.

examples.title: Each employee next to their department average
examples.sql:
SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY dept_id, name;
examples.note: GROUP BY dept_id would give 3 rows. The window keeps all 7.

examples.title: Group sizes and the grand total on every row
examples.sql:
SELECT name, dept_id,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_size,
       COUNT(*) OVER () AS company_size
FROM employees
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.note: OVER () is one window holding every row. Gus forms his own NULL partition.

examples.title: How far each salary is from the department average
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary,
       salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS diff_from_avg
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 1
ORDER BY salary DESC, name;

keyPoints: A window function keeps every row; GROUP BY collapses rows.
PARTITION BY = which rows share a window. No PARTITION BY = one window of all rows.
ORDER BY inside OVER = the order within each window (needed for ranks, LAG and running totals).
Window functions run in the SELECT step: you can't use them in WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING. Wrap in a CTE to filter.
Any aggregate becomes a window function when you add OVER.
mistakes: Writing `WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…) = 1` — not allowed. Filter in an outer query.
Adding GROUP BY when you wanted every row kept.
Confusing the ORDER BY inside OVER (order within the window) with the query's ORDER BY (order of the output).
dialects: Window functions work in PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL 8+ and SQLite 3.25+. Older MySQL (5.7) has none.
topics.interviewAnswer: A window function computes a value over a set of rows related to the current row, defined by the OVER clause — PARTITION BY says which rows share the window and ORDER BY orders them — but unlike GROUP BY it doesn't collapse rows, so each row keeps its detail and gains the computed value. Because they are evaluated in the SELECT phase, I filter on them from an outer query or CTE.

followUps.q: GROUP BY or a window function — how do you choose?
followUps.a: If you want one row per group, GROUP BY. If you want every row plus a group value next to it (an average, a rank, a running total), a window function.

followUps.q: Why can't you use a window function in WHERE?
followUps.a: WHERE runs before the SELECT step where window functions are computed. Put the window function in a CTE and filter outside.

practice.explain: Explain the difference between `AVG(salary) … GROUP BY dept_id` and `AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)`.
practice.write: For every order, show the order_id, amount, and the customer's total spend across all their orders.
practice.predict: What does `SELECT name, MAX(salary) OVER () FROM employees;` return? How many rows?
practice.edge: Gus has a NULL dept_id. What dept_avg does he get in the first example if you remove the WHERE?

resources.title: Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL Window Functions

explain.answer:
`AVG(salary) … GROUP BY dept_id` squashes each department into one row: 8 employees in, 4 rows out (one per department, Gus's NULL included). The names are gone.

`AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)` works out the same averages but keeps all 8 rows. Each employee gets their department's average written next to them, so you can compare: "Ben earns 70,000; his department averages 78,750".

Use GROUP BY when you want one row per group, and a window function when you want every row plus a group figure.

query.sql:
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS dept_avg
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;

write.answer: PARTITION BY customer_id makes one window per customer, and SUM adds up that customer's amounts. Every order keeps its own row. Order 106's NULL is skipped, so Lena's total is 60.

query.sql:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_id;

predict.answer:
8 rows, one per employee, each with 95,000 next to the name.

`OVER ()` is an empty window: no PARTITION BY, so the window is the whole table, and the highest salary in the whole table is Asha's 95,000. A window function never removes rows. (The query has no ORDER BY, so add one if you want the names in a fixed order.)

edge.answer:
38,000: his own salary.

PARTITION BY, like GROUP BY, puts all NULLs into one group. Gus is the only employee with a NULL dept_id, so he is alone in his window and the average of one salary is that salary.

That is technically right but can mislead: "no department" is not a real department. That is why the example filtered him out with `WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL`.

query.sql:
SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept_id, name;

topics.name: Ranking: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK
topics.definition: ROW_NUMBER numbers rows 1, 2, 3, 4 with no ties; RANK gives ties the same number and then skips (1, 2, 2, 4); DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without skipping (1, 2, 2, 3).
topics.problem: "Top 3 per department", "the second-highest salary", "each customer's first order" — ranking questions are the most common window-function questions in interviews. The only hard part is ties, and the three functions differ exactly there.
topics.idea: All three need ORDER BY inside OVER, which decides who comes first. ROW_NUMBER always gives different numbers, so if two rows tie, which one gets 3 and which gets 4 is arbitrary unless you add a tiebreaker column. RANK is like a sports ranking: two people sharing 3rd place means nobody is 4th. DENSE_RANK doesn't leave gaps, so "the 2nd highest salary" is simply DENSE_RANK = 2. Add PARTITION BY to restart the numbering in each group.
topics.analogy: A race with two runners crossing the line together in third. ROW_NUMBER is the finish-line camera that must put one of them first. RANK is the medal table: both get third, and the next runner is fifth. DENSE_RANK is "positions": both third, the next runner fourth.
topics.breaks: A photo finish has a real answer. ROW_NUMBER's choice between tied rows doesn't — it can differ between runs — so always add a tiebreaker (like name or id) when you use ROW_NUMBER.
topics.syntax:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x DESC, tiebreaker)
RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x DESC)
DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x DESC)
howItWorks: Sort by salary, highest first: Asha 95000, Hana 80000, then Ben and Chen on 70000, then Dara 60000.
ROW_NUMBER: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — Ben and Chen get different numbers; the tiebreaker (name) puts Ben first.
RANK: 1, 2, 3, 3, 5 — they share 3, and 4 is skipped.
DENSE_RANK: 1, 2, 3, 3, 4 — they share 3, and Dara is 4.
To keep only the top rows, compute the rank in a CTE and filter with WHERE outside it.

diagram.caption: Same sorted rows, three ways to number them. The only difference is what happens at the tie on 70000: unique numbers, shared with a gap after, or shared with no gap.

examples.title: The three side by side
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank_num,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_num
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, name;
examples.note: Look at Ben and Chen, then at Dara: 5 by RANK, 4 by DENSE_RANK.

examples.title: Ranking within each department
examples.sql:
SELECT dept_id, name, salary,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank_in_dept
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY dept_id, rank_in_dept, name;
examples.note: PARTITION BY restarts the count at 1 for every department.

examples.title: Filter on a rank: each customer's second order
examples.sql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS nth_order
  FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date
FROM numbered
WHERE nth_order = 2
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.note: The number is made in the CTE, then filtered outside. Zoe has only one order, so she has no second.

keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER: unique 1, 2, 3, 4. Add a tiebreaker so it is the same every run.
RANK: ties share a number, then a gap (1, 2, 2, 4).
DENSE_RANK: ties share a number, no gap (1, 2, 2, 3). Use it for "Nth highest value".
PARTITION BY restarts the numbering per group.
Pattern for top N per group: rank in a CTE, then `WHERE rank <= N` outside.
mistakes: Using ROW_NUMBER for "top 3 salaries" when ties should all be included — use RANK or DENSE_RANK.
Using RANK for "the 2nd highest salary" — after a tie at 1st, there is no rank 2.
Forgetting the tiebreaker in ROW_NUMBER, so results change from run to run.
dialects: Naming a column `rank` fails in MySQL 8, where RANK is a reserved word. Use rank_num or rnk.
topics.interviewAnswer: All three number rows in the order given by the OVER clause's ORDER BY, optionally restarting per PARTITION BY. ROW_NUMBER gives unique sequential numbers, so I add a deterministic tiebreaker; RANK gives tied rows the same rank and leaves gaps; DENSE_RANK gives the same rank without gaps. For "Nth highest distinct value" I use DENSE_RANK, and for "exactly one row per group" I use ROW_NUMBER — always filtering in an outer query.

followUps.q: Which would you use for "the second highest salary"?
followUps.a: DENSE_RANK = 2, so a tie for first doesn't leave you with no second.

followUps.q: How do you keep exactly one row per customer — their latest order?
followUps.a: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC)`, then keep row number 1.

followUps.q: What happens to ROW_NUMBER with ties if there is no tiebreaker?
followUps.a: Tied rows get different numbers in an arbitrary order, which can change between runs.

practice.explain: Explain the difference between RANK and DENSE_RANK using Ben, Chen and Dara.
practice.write: Write a query for the most expensive product in each category, using ROW_NUMBER.
practice.predict: With `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)`, which employees have rank 3? Who has rank 4?
practice.edge: Rewrite "each customer's latest order" so that, if two orders shared the latest date, only one comes back — and say which one.

resources.title: Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL Window Functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK

explain.answer:
Sorted by salary, highest first: Asha 95,000 (1st), Hana 80,000 (2nd), then Ben and Chen tie on 70,000, then Dara on 60,000.

Both functions give Ben and Chen the same number, 3. The difference is what comes next:
• RANK skips: two people took places 3 and 4, so Dara is 5. Like a race: two runners share third, and the next one finishes fifth.
• DENSE_RANK doesn't skip: Dara is 4, the next different salary.

So "the third-highest salary" is DENSE_RANK = 3, while "the person in fourth place" may not exist with RANK.

write.answer:
Number the products inside each category from most to least expensive, then keep number 1. The CTE is needed because WHERE runs before window functions, so you can't filter on rn in the same query.

ROW_NUMBER always picks exactly one product, even if two tie on price. product_name is added to the ORDER BY so that pick is fixed, not random. To keep every tied product, use RANK instead.

query.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category, product_name, price,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC, product_name) AS rn
  FROM products
)
SELECT category, product_name, price
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY category;

predict.answer:
Rank 3: Ben and Chen, who tie on 70,000.

Rank 4: nobody. The tie used up places 3 and 4, so RANK jumps straight to 5 for Dara.

edge.answer:
Use ROW_NUMBER, which never gives two rows the same number, and add a tie-breaker to its ORDER BY so you decide which one wins: `ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC`. Here, if two orders shared the latest date, the one with the higher order_id (the one created later) comes back.

Without the tie-breaker, ROW_NUMBER still returns one row, but which one could change from run to run. RANK or DENSE_RANK would return both.

(No customer here has two orders on the same day, so the tie-breaker changes nothing yet; it is there for when one does.)

query.sql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date
FROM numbered
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

topics.name: LAG and LEAD: comparing with the previous or next row
topics.definition: `LAG(column)` returns the value from the previous row and `LEAD(column)` the value from the next row, in the order set by OVER (… ORDER BY …), so a row can be compared with its neighbour.
topics.problem: "How much did revenue change since last month?", "how many days between a customer's orders?", "did the price go up?" — each compares a row with the one before it. Without LAG, that means a tricky self join on "the previous date". With LAG it is one line.
topics.idea: `LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)` looks one row back in month order. The first row has no previous row, so it gets NULL (or a default you give as the third argument: `LAG(revenue, 1, 0)`). LEAD looks forward instead. The second argument says how far: `LAG(revenue, 12)` is the same month last year in monthly data. Add PARTITION BY customer_id and the looking-back stops at each customer's boundary, so one customer's first order never looks back into another customer's orders.
topics.analogy: Reading a bank statement line by line with your finger on the line above. LAG is that line above; the difference between them is the change.
topics.breaks: On a statement the line above is always the day before. LAG gives the previous row, not the previous day: if a month has no orders, it has no row, and LAG silently compares March with January. Fill the gaps first when it matters.
topics.syntax:
LAG(column, offset, default)  OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY d)
LEAD(column, offset, default) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY d)
howItWorks: A CTE makes one row per month: January 445, February 210, March 138.
`LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)`: January has no previous row, so NULL; February gets 445; March gets 210.
revenue − `LAG(revenue)` gives the change: NULL, −235, −72.
With PARTITION BY customer_id, each customer's first order gets NULL from LAG.
LEAD works the same way, looking forward: the last row gets NULL.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR J["2024-01
445"] -->|"LAG for Feb"| F["2024-02
210
previous: 445"] F -->|"LAG for Mar"| M["2024-03
138
previous: 210"]
diagram.caption: In month order, LAG hands each row the value from the row before it. The first row has nothing before it, so it gets NULL.

examples.title: Change from the previous month
examples.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

examples.title: Days between a customer's orders
examples.sql:
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
       LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS previous_order,
       julianday(order_date)
         - julianday(LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)) AS days_since
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (1, 2)
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
examples.note: PARTITION BY customer_id stops Tom's first order looking back at Priya's last one.

examples.title: LEAD: who was hired next
examples.sql:
SELECT name, hire_date,
       LEAD(name) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date) AS next_hire
FROM employees
ORDER BY hire_date;

keyPoints: LAG = previous row's value; LEAD = next row's value, in the window's ORDER BY.
The first row (LAG) or last row (LEAD) of each partition gets NULL, or the default you pass.
`LAG(x, n)` looks n rows back — 12 for "same month last year" in monthly data.
PARTITION BY keeps each group's comparisons inside the group.
LAG looks at the previous row, not the previous date: fill missing dates first if gaps matter.
mistakes: Forgetting PARTITION BY, so one customer's first order is compared with another customer's last.
Assuming the previous row is the previous day or month when there are gaps.
Dividing by LAG without guarding against NULL or zero.
dialects: Date differences: PostgreSQL `order_date - LAG(order_date) OVER (…)` gives days directly for DATE columns; MySQL uses DATEDIFF; SQL Server uses `DATEDIFF(day, …)`.
topics.interviewAnswer: LAG and LEAD return a value from a preceding or following row within the window, in the order given by the OVER clause's ORDER BY. I use them for period-over-period changes — revenue minus LAG of revenue — and gaps between events per user with PARTITION BY user. I watch out for the first row returning NULL and for missing periods, since LAG goes to the previous row, which isn't necessarily the previous calendar month.

followUps.q: How would you compute month-over-month growth as a percentage?
followUps.a: `ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER w) / LAG(revenue) OVER w, 1)`, guarding with NULLIF in case last month was 0.

followUps.q: How do you get a value from two rows back?
followUps.a: Pass an offset: `LAG(column, 2) OVER (…)`.

practice.explain: Explain what LAG returns for the first row of each partition, and why.
practice.write: For each of Priya's orders, show the amount and the difference from her previous order's amount.
practice.predict: In the first example, what would `LEAD(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)` give for each month?
practice.edge: If February had no orders at all, what would LAG return for March in the first example, and how would you fix it?

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs — Window Functions (LAG and LEAD)
Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL Window Functions: LAG and LEAD

explain.answer:
NULL. LAG looks one row back inside the same partition, in the order given by OVER (… ORDER BY …). The first row of a partition has no row before it, so there is nothing to return. LAG never reaches into another partition: the first order of customer 2 doesn't see customer 1's last order.

If you want something else there, give a default as the third argument: `LAG(amount, 1, 0)` returns 0 for the first row.

write.answer:
Keep Priya's orders, then take each amount minus LAG(amount) in date order. Her first order has nothing to compare with, so its change is NULL.

The WHERE runs before the window function, so LAG only ever sees Priya's orders. That is exactly what you want here.

query.sql:
SELECT order_id, order_date, amount,
       amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS change_from_previous
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1
ORDER BY order_date;

predict.answer: Each month gets the next month's revenue: January 210 (February's), February 138 (March's), and March NULL, because there is no month after it. LEAD is LAG looking forward.

query.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       LEAD(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS next_revenue
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

edge.answer:
January's revenue, 445. With no February orders, the monthly CTE has no February row at all. LAG just takes the row before, which is now January, so March is compared with January but labelled "previous month". No error, just a wrong comparison.

Fix it by making the list of months complete before using LAG. Generate every month (a recursive CTE, or a calendar table), LEFT JOIN the orders onto it, and COALESCE empty months to 0. Then February exists with 0, and March is compared with it.

Below, the two DELETEs remove February (its item lines first, because of the foreign key), and the fixed query still shows February.

query.sql:
DELETE FROM order_items WHERE order_id IN (105, 107);
DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_date LIKE '2024-02%';

WITH RECURSIVE months(month) AS (
  SELECT '2024-01'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', date(month || '-01', '+1 month'))
  FROM months
  WHERE month < '2024-03'
),
monthly AS (
  SELECT m.month, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS revenue
  FROM months m
  LEFT JOIN orders o ON strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) = m.month
  GROUP BY m.month
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

topics.name: Running totals and moving averages: window frames
topics.definition: With ORDER BY inside OVER, SUM and AVG become running totals; a frame such as `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` limits the window to nearby rows, giving a moving average.
topics.problem: "Cumulative revenue by day", "7-day moving average of sign-ups" — growth charts are built on these. They also hide a classic trap: the default frame treats tied rows as one, which surprises almost everyone.
topics.idea: `SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)` adds up everything from the first row to the current row: a running total. The frame says which rows count: `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` means this row and the two before it — so AVG over it is a 3-row moving average. The trap: when you write ORDER BY without a frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and RANGE includes every row tied with the current one. So two orders on the same day both show the total after both. Write ROWS explicitly when you want one row at a time.
topics.analogy: A running total is a savings jar you never empty: each week you add the new amount and read the total. A moving average is a "last three weeks" window you slide along: the oldest week drops out as a new one comes in.
topics.breaks: Weeks never tie. Rows can: with the default RANGE frame, two rows with the same ORDER BY value are treated as arriving at the same moment, so both see the total including each other.
topics.syntax:
SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)                                   -- running total
AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)          -- running total, row by row
howItWorks: Order the rows by date. For each row, the frame is "from the first row up to me".
SUM over that frame grows: 120, 200, 245, 445, 595…
Order 106's NULL amount adds nothing, so the total stays at 595 on that row.
With `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, the frame is at most 3 rows, so AVG gives a 3-order moving average.
Ties: ordering salaries with the default frame, Ben and Chen (both 70000) both show 315000. With ROWS they show 245000 and 315000.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR R1["row 1
120"] --> R2["row 2
80"] --> R3["row 3
45"] --> R4["row 4
200"] R4 --> F["frame for row 4:
ROWS 2 PRECEDING = rows 2, 3, 4
moving average 108.3"] R4 --> T["frame for row 4:
UNBOUNDED PRECEDING = rows 1 to 4
running total 445"]
diagram.caption: The frame is the part of the window a row can see. "Unbounded preceding" sees everything so far (a running total); "2 preceding" sees only the last three rows (a moving average).

examples.title: Running total of revenue
examples.sql:
SELECT order_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date;
examples.note: The last row is 793, the grand total. The NULL row adds nothing.

examples.title: A running total per customer
examples.sql:
SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS customer_running_total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (1, 3)
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
examples.note: Lena's running total starts as NULL: the SUM of nothing but a NULL is NULL. `COALESCE(…, 0)` would show 0.

examples.title: A 3-order moving average
examples.sql:
SELECT order_date, amount,
       ROUND(AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS moving_avg_3
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date;
examples.note: The first two rows average fewer than 3 values. AVG skips the NULL, so 2024-02-12 is the average of 200 and 150.

examples.title: The trap: RANGE (the default) versus ROWS
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary,
       SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS default_range,
       SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS rows_frame
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, name;
examples.note: Ben and Chen tie on 70000. The default RANGE frame counts both of them on both rows (315000). ROWS goes one row at a time.

keyPoints: Aggregate + OVER (ORDER BY …) = a running total (or running count, max…).
The default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — tied rows are included together.
Write ROWS explicitly for row-by-row running totals and for moving averages.
`ROWS BETWEEN n PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` = the last n + 1 rows.
Without ORDER BY in OVER, the frame is the whole partition, so you get the total, not a running total.
mistakes: Getting the same running total on tied rows and not knowing why (the RANGE default).
A "7-day" moving average with ROWS 6 PRECEDING when some days are missing — that is 7 rows, not 7 days.
Forgetting PARTITION BY, so one customer's running total continues into the next customer's.
dialects: PostgreSQL, SQLite and Oracle also allow RANGE with an offset for real time windows: `RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` (PostgreSQL).
SQL Server supports ROWS and RANGE frames, but RANGE only with UNBOUNDED or CURRENT ROW.
topics.interviewAnswer: Adding ORDER BY to an aggregate's OVER clause makes it cumulative, which gives running totals; a frame clause like ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW narrows it to a sliding window for moving averages. The subtle point is the default frame, RANGE up to the current row, which lumps tied ORDER BY values together — so I specify ROWS explicitly, with a unique tiebreaker, whenever ties are possible.

followUps.q: What is the default window frame?
followUps.a: With ORDER BY: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Without ORDER BY: the whole partition.

followUps.q: ROWS or RANGE — what is the difference?
followUps.a: ROWS counts physical rows. RANGE works on values, so all rows with the same ORDER BY value are in or out together.

followUps.q: Why might a LAST_VALUE return the current row instead of the last one?
followUps.a: Because the default frame ends at the current row. Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL Window Functions: running totals

explain.answer:
When OVER has an ORDER BY but no frame, the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE works on values, not rows: it means "every row whose ORDER BY value is up to and including mine", and that includes rows that tie with me (my peers).

Ben and Chen both earn 70,000, so they are peers. For Ben, the frame already contains Chen, and for Chen it contains Ben. Both get the same total, 315,000 (95 + 80 + 70 + 70 thousand), instead of 245,000 then 315,000.

To count strictly one row at a time, say ROWS (`ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING`) and add a tie-breaker to the ORDER BY, so the order of the tied rows is fixed.

write.answer: `COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date)` counts the rows from the start up to this one. No two people were hired on the same day, so the RANGE default is fine here. If two could share a date, use ROW_NUMBER (or ROWS with a tie-breaker), or both would get the same count.

query.sql:
SELECT name, hire_date,
       COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY hire_date) AS hires_so_far
FROM employees
ORDER BY hire_date;

predict.answer:
81.7. The frame is the row before, this row and the row after: 120 (6 Jan), 80 (7 Jan) and 45 (8 Jan). (120 + 80 + 45) ÷ 3 = 81.67, rounded to 81.7. This is a centred average rather than a trailing one.

Note 2024-02-12, order 106: its amount is NULL, and AVG skips it, so that row averages only its two neighbours: (150 + 60) ÷ 2 = 105.

edge.answer:
Lena's first order (106) has a NULL amount, and a SUM over nothing but a NULL is NULL. The COALESCE goes around the whole window function, outside the OVER: `COALESCE(SUM(amount) OVER (…), 0)`. It only steps in when the running total itself is NULL.

`SUM(COALESCE(amount, 0)) OVER (…)` also works here. It turns each missing amount into 0 before adding. The difference shows only in meaning: the first says "no total yet, show 0"; the second says "a missing amount counts as £0".

Putting a COALESCE inside the OVER brackets wouldn't help: what is in there only decides which rows are in each window and in what order, not the values that are added up.

query.sql:
SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount,
       COALESCE(SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date), 0) AS customer_running_total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (1, 3)
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;

topics.name: Share of total, NTILE and FIRST_VALUE
topics.definition: `x / SUM(x) OVER ()` gives each row's share of the total; `NTILE(n)` splits ordered rows into n roughly equal buckets; FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE pull a value from the first or last row of the window.
topics.problem: "What percentage of revenue does each category bring?", "put customers into spending quartiles", "show the top earner's name next to everyone in their department" — all common analytics asks that window functions answer in one line.
topics.idea: `SUM(revenue) OVER ()` is the grand total, written on every row, so `100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER ()` is the percentage of the total. With PARTITION BY you get the share within each group instead. `NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)` deals the sorted rows into 4 buckets, like dealing cards: 1 is the top quarter. `FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC)` is the name on the first row of each department's window — the top earner.
topics.analogy: A pie chart, a league split into divisions, and a team captain. Share of total is each slice of the pie; NTILE puts teams into divisions by points; FIRST_VALUE is the captain's name printed on every player's shirt.
topics.breaks: Divisions in a league can be unequal by design. NTILE always makes buckets as equal as possible, so tied values can land in different buckets — fine for "roughly top 25%", wrong if ties must stay together.
topics.syntax:
100.0 * x / SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g)
NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY x DESC)
FIRST_VALUE(col) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x DESC)
howItWorks: A CTE adds up revenue per category: Electronics 440, Home 150, Bags 120, Kitchen 48, Stationery 35.
`SUM(revenue) OVER ()` is 793 on every row.
100.0 × 440 ÷ 793 = 55.5% for Electronics, and so on.
`NTILE(4)` over 8 employees sorted by salary gives buckets of 2: 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4.
`FIRST_VALUE(name)`, ordered by salary DESC within each department, is that department's top earner.

diagram.code:
pie title Share of revenue by category
  "Electronics" : 440
  "Home" : 150
  "Bags" : 120
  "Kitchen" : 48
  "Stationery" : 35
diagram.caption: Each slice is one row's revenue divided by SUM(revenue) OVER () — the grand total of 793 that the window puts on every row.

examples.title: Each category's share of revenue
examples.sql:
WITH by_category AS (
  SELECT p.category, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT category, revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total
FROM by_category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

examples.title: NTILE: salary quartiles
examples.sql:
SELECT name, salary,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name) AS quartile
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, name;

examples.title: FIRST_VALUE: the top earner on every row
examples.sql:
SELECT dept_id, name, salary,
       FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS top_earner
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC, name;

keyPoints: `SUM(x) OVER ()` = grand total on every row; `SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g)` = group total.
Share of total: `100.0 * x / SUM(x) OVER (…)` — the 100.0 avoids integer division.
`NTILE(n)` makes n buckets as equal in size as possible, in the window's order.
FIRST_VALUE is safe with the default frame; LAST_VALUE needs `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.
You can use a window function over an aggregate (`SUM(SUM(x)) OVER ()`) in a GROUP BY query, but a CTE is easier to read.
mistakes: Integer division in a share: `revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER ()` gives 0 for every row.
Using LAST_VALUE with the default frame and getting the current row's value.
Expecting NTILE to keep tied values in the same bucket.
topics.interviewAnswer: For share-of-total I divide each row by SUM over an empty or partitioned window, multiplying by 100.0 to avoid integer division. NTILE buckets ordered rows into n near-equal groups for quartiles or deciles, and FIRST_VALUE picks the first row's value in each window — for LAST_VALUE I widen the frame to unbounded following, because the default frame stops at the current row.

followUps.q: How would you show each product's share of revenue within its category?
followUps.a: Use `SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category)` as the divisor.

followUps.q: `NTILE(4)` on 10 rows — how big are the buckets?
followUps.a: 3, 3, 2, 2. The leftover rows go to the first buckets.

explain.answer:
`OVER ()` is an empty window. There is no PARTITION BY, so every row is in one big window: the whole result. There is no ORDER BY, so there is no running frame: the window is always all of it. SUM of the same rows is the same number, so every row gets the grand total.

That is exactly what share of total needs: each row divided by the same grand total.

write.answer:
First add up each customer (the CTE), then divide each total by the sum of all totals. Multiply by 100.0, not 100, so the division keeps its decimals.

The rounded shares add up to 100.1, not 100. That is normal when you round each part.

query.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, p.total,
       ROUND(100.0 * p.total / SUM(p.total) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_all
FROM per_customer p
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id
ORDER BY p.total DESC;

predict.answer:
8 rows into 3 buckets don't divide evenly, so the first buckets get the extra rows: sizes 3, 3 and 2.

• Bucket 1: Asha, Hana, Ben.
• Bucket 2: Chen, Dara, Fatima.
• Bucket 3: Eli, Gus.

Notice Ben and Chen earn the same but land in different buckets. NTILE cuts by position, not by value; the name in the ORDER BY decides which side of the cut each one lands on.

edge.answer:
Sort each department from highest to lowest salary, so the lowest earner is the last row. Then set the frame to the whole partition: `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`.

Without that frame, the default ends at the current row, so on each row "the last row of the window" is the current row: every person is named as their own lowest earner.

In department 1, Ben and Chen tie for lowest. The name in the ORDER BY makes Chen the last row, so the tie is broken the same way every time.

query.sql:
SELECT dept_id, name, salary,
       LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (
         PARTITION BY dept_id
         ORDER BY salary DESC, name
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
       ) AS lowest_earner
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC, name;

phases.title: Building tables and changing data
phases.goal: Create tables with the right rules, add, change and remove rows safely, group changes into transactions, and design tables that don't contradict themselves.
phases.bigPicture: So far you have only read data. Real systems also write it — and writing is where data gets damaged. Constraints stop bad rows getting in, transactions stop half-finished changes, and normalisation stops the same fact being stored twice and drifting apart.

topics.name: CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE
topics.definition: CREATE TABLE defines a new table — its name, its columns, their types and rules — and ALTER TABLE changes an existing table, for example by adding a column.
topics.problem: Before data can be stored, the database needs to know its shape. Choosing the columns, types and keys well at the start saves painful fixes later, when the table holds millions of rows.
topics.idea: CREATE TABLE lists each column with its type and any rules (constraints): `name TEXT NOT NULL`. One column, or a group of columns, is the PRIMARY KEY. DEFAULT gives a value to use when an INSERT doesn't mention the column. ALTER TABLE changes the table afterwards: ADD COLUMN, RENAME COLUMN, DROP COLUMN. These commands change the structure (the schema), not the rows, and they belong to the part of SQL called DDL.
topics.analogy: Designing a paper form before printing it: you decide the boxes (columns), what may be written in each (types), which ones must be filled in (NOT NULL), and which are pre-filled (DEFAULT). ALTER TABLE is printing a new version of the form with an extra box.
topics.breaks: A reprinted form doesn't change the forms already filled in. ALTER TABLE does: adding a column adds it to every existing row (with its default or NULL), and on a huge table that can take a long time or lock it.
howItWorks: CREATE TABLE suppliers makes an empty table with three columns.
supplier_id is the primary key: unique and never NULL.
country has DEFAULT 'UK', so an INSERT that leaves it out gets 'UK'.
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN in_stock … DEFAULT 1 adds the column to all 7 existing rows, each with 1.
Neither command returns rows; a SELECT afterwards shows the effect.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["CREATE TABLE
new, empty table
with columns and rules"] --> I["INSERT rows"] I --> A["ALTER TABLE
add a column:
every row gets the default"]
diagram.caption: CREATE TABLE sets up the shape, INSERT fills it, and ALTER TABLE reshapes it later — the new column is added to every row that already exists.

examples.title: Create a table and use its default
examples.note: The first INSERT names only two columns, so country takes its default.

examples.title: Add a column to an existing table
examples.note: Every existing product gets in_stock = 1. A NOT NULL column added to a table with rows needs a DEFAULT.

keyPoints: CREATE TABLE: name, then each column with its type and rules, separated by commas.
Give every table a primary key.
DEFAULT fills a column when an INSERT leaves it out.
ALTER TABLE ADD / RENAME / DROP COLUMN changes the structure of an existing table.
CREATE, ALTER and DROP are DDL: they change the schema, not the data.
mistakes: No primary key, so duplicate rows can't be told apart or removed cleanly.
Adding a NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT to a table that already has rows — most databases refuse.
Storing several values in one column ('Pen, Mug'). Each column should hold one value — see normalisation.
dialects: Auto-numbered ids: PostgreSQL `id INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` (or SERIAL); MySQL `AUTO_INCREMENT`; SQL Server `IDENTITY(1,1)`; SQLite `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` does it automatically.
SQLite's ALTER TABLE is limited (add, rename and drop column only). PostgreSQL can also change a column's type with `ALTER COLUMN … TYPE`.
topics.interviewAnswer: CREATE TABLE defines a table's columns, data types and constraints — a primary key, NOT NULL, defaults, foreign keys — and ALTER TABLE evolves it later, such as adding a column. I always give tables a primary key, choose types deliberately — DECIMAL for money, proper DATE types for dates — and treat schema changes on big tables carefully, because adding or changing columns can rewrite or lock the table.

followUps.q: What is a schema?
followUps.a: The structure of the database: its tables, columns, types and constraints. Also, in PostgreSQL, a named group of tables inside a database.

followUps.q: How do you add a NOT NULL column to a table that already has data?
followUps.a: Give it a DEFAULT, or add it as nullable, fill in the values with UPDATE, then add the NOT NULL rule.
