explain.answer:
`CREATE TABLE suppliers ( … )` makes a new, empty table called suppliers, with the columns listed in the brackets.

• `supplier_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`: a whole-number column that identifies each row. Primary key means it must be unique and can't be NULL. (In SQLite, an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is also numbered automatically if you leave it out.)
• `name TEXT NOT NULL`: a text column that must always have a value. An INSERT without a name is refused.
• `country TEXT DEFAULT 'UK'`: a text column that may be left out; if an INSERT doesn't mention it, it gets 'UK'.

The statement changes the structure (the schema) and returns no rows. It is DDL.

write.answer:
Each rule from the question becomes a constraint: REFERENCES makes product_id point at a real product, CHECK keeps the rating between 1 and 5, and DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE fills in today's date if an insert leaves it out (here both inserts give a date, so the result is fixed).

Try inserting a rating of 9: the database refuses it with "CHECK constraint failed: rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5".

predict.answer: 'UK'. The INSERT names only supplier_id and name, so country takes its DEFAULT. (Every run starts from the original database, so the query below creates the suppliers table first.)

edge.answer:
The database refuses the row: "NOT NULL constraint failed: suppliers.name". name has no DEFAULT, so leaving it out would make it NULL, and NOT NULL forbids that. The whole INSERT fails and nothing is stored.

That is the point of the rule: a supplier without a name is bad data, and the database stops it at the door, whatever program sent it.

topics.name: Constraints: the rules that keep bad data out
topics.definition: Constraints are rules the database enforces on every write — PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT — so that rows which break them are refused instead of stored.
topics.problem: Application code has bugs, and data arrives from many places. Tom could sign up twice because nothing said emails must be unique. A rule in the database is checked on every insert and update, from every program, every time.
topics.idea: NOT NULL: a value is required. UNIQUE: no two rows may share the value. PRIMARY KEY: unique and not NULL — the row's identity. FOREIGN KEY (REFERENCES): the value must exist in another table's key, and you choose what happens when that row is deleted (refuse, ON DELETE CASCADE, or ON DELETE SET NULL). CHECK: any condition, such as `price > 0` or `plan IN ('free', 'pro')`. If a write breaks a rule, the whole statement fails with an error and nothing is changed.
topics.analogy: The rules at a passport desk. No photo, no passport (NOT NULL). One passport number per person (UNIQUE). The country you list must be a real country (FOREIGN KEY). Your age can't be negative (CHECK). The officer refuses the form; they don't "fix it later".
topics.breaks: An officer might let a small mistake through. A constraint never does — which is the point, but it also means a bulk load can fail on row 9,999,999. Clean or check the data before loading, or load into a staging table first.
topics.syntax:
email   TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
price   INTEGER CHECK (price > 0),
dept_id INTEGER REFERENCES departments(dept_id) ON DELETE SET NULL
howItWorks: Every INSERT and UPDATE is checked against every constraint on the table.
subscribers.email is the primary key, so a second row with the same email is a conflict.
`ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING` tells the database to skip that row quietly instead of failing.
Inserting an order for customer 99, who doesn't exist, breaks the foreign key: refused.
Inserting a department with an existing dept_id breaks the primary key: refused.

diagram.caption: Each write passes every rule on the table. If any rule fails, the statement is refused and the table is left exactly as it was.

examples.title: UNIQUE and CHECK, and skipping duplicates on purpose
examples.note: Tom's second sign-up is skipped. Try it yourself with plan 'gold' and watch the CHECK refuse it.

examples.title: A foreign key refuses an order for a customer who doesn't exist
examples.sql:
INSERT INTO orders (order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount, status)
VALUES (111, 99, '2024-03-20', 10, 'pending');
examples.note: There is no customer 99, so the row is never stored.

examples.title: A primary key refuses a duplicate id
examples.sql: INSERT INTO departments VALUES (1, 'Legal', 'York');
examples.note: Department 1 already exists. A primary key is a UNIQUE rule plus NOT NULL.

keyPoints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK and DEFAULT are the six to know.
PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL, one per table.
Foreign key delete options: refuse (default), ON DELETE CASCADE, ON DELETE SET NULL.
A failed constraint fails the whole statement; nothing is half-written.
Put rules in the database, not only in the app — the database sees every write.
mistakes: Relying on the app alone to prevent duplicates (that is how Tom signed up twice).
Using ON DELETE CASCADE without thinking: deleting one customer silently deletes all their orders.
Expecting UNIQUE to stop two NULLs. In most databases it doesn't — NULL isn't equal to NULL.
dialects: SQLite checks foreign keys only after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;`. MySQL ignored CHECK constraints before version 8.0.16.
Upsert syntax: PostgreSQL and SQLite `ON CONFLICT … DO NOTHING / DO UPDATE`; MySQL `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`; SQL Server `MERGE`.
topics.interviewAnswer: Constraints let the database enforce integrity on every write: NOT NULL for required values, UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY for identity, FOREIGN KEY for valid references with a chosen delete behaviour, and CHECK for any rule on a row. I put these rules in the schema rather than only in application code, because the database sees every writer, and a violation fails the statement atomically instead of leaving bad data behind.

followUps.q: Can a UNIQUE column hold NULLs?
followUps.a: Yes, in most databases, and usually more than one NULL, because NULLs aren't equal to each other. (SQL Server allows only one by default.)

followUps.q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
followUps.a: Deleting the parent row also deletes the child rows that reference it — handy for order_items when an order is deleted, dangerous elsewhere.

followUps.q: Why not just validate in the application?
followUps.a: Several apps, scripts and people write to the same database, and app checks can race. Constraints are checked by the database itself, atomically.

explain.answer:
• NOT NULL, a value is required: employees.name. Every employee must have a name.
• UNIQUE, no two rows may share the value: customers.email should have had it. It doesn't, which is exactly how Tom signed up twice.
• PRIMARY KEY, the row's identity (unique and not NULL): employees.emp_id, and in order_items the pair (order_id, product_id).
• FOREIGN KEY, the value must exist in another table: orders.customer_id must be a real customer_id in customers.
• CHECK, any rule about the row: none here yet, but `price > 0` on products or `status IN ('delivered', 'shipped', 'cancelled', 'pending')` on orders would be natural.
• DEFAULT, the value used when an INSERT leaves the column out: for example `status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'` on orders.

write.answer:
The table and the valid row are below. Each of these is refused, and the table stays unchanged:

• A second row with the same email: `INSERT INTO listings VALUES (2, 'shop@mail.com', 35);` gives "UNIQUE constraint failed: listings.email".
• A price that isn't positive: `INSERT INTO listings VALUES (3, 'other@mail.com', 0);` gives "CHECK constraint failed: price > 0".

Add either line after the INSERT and run it to see the error.

predict.answer:
No. employees.dept_id is a foreign key to departments, and there is no department 9, so the update is refused: "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed". Gus keeps his NULL dept_id.

(NULL itself is allowed in a foreign key column, meaning "no department"; a value that points at nothing is not.)

query.sql: UPDATE employees SET dept_id = 9 WHERE emp_id = 7;

edge.answer:
Yes, both go in. UNIQUE means "no two equal values", and NULL is not equal to anything, not even another NULL, so two NULLs don't clash. PostgreSQL and MySQL behave the same way.

SQL Server is the exception: it allows only one NULL in a UNIQUE column. And PostgreSQL 15+ lets you ask for that with `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. If an email is really required, the fix is `NOT NULL` as well as UNIQUE.

topics.name: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
topics.definition: INSERT adds new rows, UPDATE changes values in existing rows, and DELETE removes rows — and both UPDATE and DELETE act on every row their WHERE matches, or on every row of the table if there is no WHERE.
topics.problem: A database is only useful if it can be kept up to date: new customers, price changes, cancelled orders. These three statements do all of that — and one missing WHERE can change or wipe every row, so they deserve care.
topics.idea: `INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (…)` adds a row; list the columns so the order is clear. `INSERT … SELECT` copies rows from a query. `UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition` changes matching rows, and the new value can use the old one (`salary = salary + 5000`). `DELETE FROM table WHERE condition` removes matching rows. An upsert — `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` — inserts a row, or updates it if the key already exists.
topics.analogy: Editing a spreadsheet. INSERT adds a new line at the bottom. UPDATE is find-and-replace — and WHERE is the "only in this selection" box. DELETE removes lines. Forgetting WHERE is "replace all" across the whole sheet.
topics.breaks: A spreadsheet has Undo. The database doesn't: once a change is committed, it is permanent. That is why you run the WHERE as a SELECT first, and use transactions (next lesson) so you can roll back.
howItWorks: INSERT adds Ravi as customer 7. The constraints are checked first.
`UPDATE employees SET salary = salary + 5000 WHERE dept_id = 2`: Dara and Eli get the raise, nobody else.
`DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 6` removes Tom's duplicate sign-up (he has no orders, so the foreign key allows it).
Upsert: inserting product 7 again hits the primary key, so DO UPDATE changes its price instead.
Safe habit: write `SELECT * FROM t WHERE …` first, check the rows, then turn it into the UPDATE or DELETE.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR T["a table"] --> I["INSERT
adds rows"] T --> U["UPDATE … WHERE
changes matching rows"] T --> D["DELETE … WHERE
removes matching rows"] U -.->|"no WHERE"| ALL["every row changed"] D -.->|"no WHERE"| ALL2["every row removed"]
diagram.caption: UPDATE and DELETE act on whatever their WHERE matches. Leave the WHERE out and they act on every row in the table.

examples.title: INSERT a new customer
UPDATE using the old value
examples.sql:
UPDATE employees
SET salary = salary + 5000
WHERE dept_id = 2;
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 2
ORDER BY name;

examples.title: DELETE one row
examples.note: Every run on this page starts from the original data, so this delete doesn't affect other examples.

examples.title: Upsert: insert, or update if it already exists
examples.sql:
INSERT INTO products (product_id, product_name, category, price)
VALUES (7, 'Phone case', 'Electronics', 12)
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE SET price = excluded.price;
SELECT product_id, product_name, price
FROM products
WHERE category = 'Electronics'
ORDER BY product_id;
examples.note: `excluded` means "the row you tried to insert". The phone case already existed, so its price was updated from 15 to 12.

keyPoints: Always list the columns in INSERT; don't rely on the table's column order.
UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE change every row.
Run the WHERE as a SELECT first, and check how many rows it hits.
`INSERT INTO t (…) SELECT …` copies rows from a query.
An upsert inserts or updates in one atomic statement.
mistakes: Forgetting WHERE on an UPDATE or DELETE.
Deleting parent rows that child rows still reference — the foreign key refuses, or cascades if set to.
Updating with a value computed from another table without checking the join returns one row per target row.
dialects: PostgreSQL and SQLite support `RETURNING` to see the rows you changed: `DELETE FROM t WHERE … RETURNING *`. SQL Server uses `OUTPUT`.
UPDATE with a join: PostgreSQL `UPDATE t SET … FROM other WHERE …`; MySQL `UPDATE t JOIN other ON … SET …`; SQL Server `UPDATE t SET … FROM t JOIN other …`.
topics.interviewAnswer: INSERT adds rows, ideally with an explicit column list; UPDATE changes columns in rows matched by WHERE, and DELETE removes matched rows. My safety habits are to run the WHERE as a SELECT first, wrap risky changes in a transaction so I can roll back, and use an upsert — insert on conflict do update — when a row may or may not exist, so it is a single atomic statement rather than a check-then-write race.

followUps.q: How would you safely delete a lot of rows?
followUps.a: Check the count with SELECT first, do it inside a transaction, and on very large tables delete in batches to avoid long locks.

followUps.q: Why is "check if it exists, then insert" a problem?
followUps.a: Two requests can both check, both see nothing, and both insert. An upsert or a UNIQUE constraint makes it atomic.

explain.answer:
UPDATE and DELETE act on every row their WHERE matches, and there is no undo once it is committed. A WHERE that is slightly wrong (a typo, `OR` where you meant `AND`, a NULL you forgot) can change far more rows than you meant, or none at all.

Running the same WHERE as a SELECT first shows you exactly which rows will be hit and how many. If you expected 2 rows and see 2,000, you have just avoided a disaster. Then turn the SELECT into the UPDATE or DELETE, ideally inside a transaction, and check that the number of rows changed matches.

write.answer: Multiply by 110 and divide by 100. With whole numbers, the division drops any pence, which is what "whole pounds" asks for. The department is found by its name, so the query doesn't depend on remembering that Engineering is 1.

query.sql:
UPDATE employees
SET salary = salary * 110 / 100
WHERE dept_id = (SELECT dept_id FROM departments WHERE dept_name = 'Engineering');
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept_id = 1
ORDER BY name;

predict.answer:
7 rows: the item lines with a quantity of 3 or more. They are (101, headphones, 3), (103, mug, 5), (104, headphones, 5), (105, headphones, 3), (108, desk lamp, 3), (109, pen, 5) and (109, notebook, 4). 7 of the 14 remain.

In SQLite, `changes()` reports how many rows the last statement changed.

query.sql:
DELETE FROM order_items WHERE quantity >= 3;
SELECT changes() AS rows_removed, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items) AS rows_left;

edge.answer:
It fails: "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed". Priya (customer 1) has five orders, and each one's customer_id points at her. Deleting her would leave those orders pointing at nobody, so the database refuses, and nothing is deleted.

With `ON DELETE CASCADE` on orders.customer_id, deleting Priya would also delete her five orders automatically. Those orders have 9 item lines in order_items, so that foreign key would need CASCADE too; otherwise it would still block the delete. One innocent-looking DELETE would remove 15 rows across three tables, which is why CASCADE should be a deliberate choice.

query.sql: DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1;

topics.name: Transactions and ACID
topics.definition: A transaction groups several statements into one all-or-nothing unit — BEGIN, then the changes, then COMMIT to keep them or ROLLBACK to undo them — and ACID names the four guarantees it gives: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.
topics.problem: Moving money means taking £100 from one account and adding it to another. If the system crashes between the two, £100 vanishes. Transactions make sure either both changes happen or neither does — and that two people working at once don't corrupt each other's changes.
topics.idea: BEGIN starts a transaction. Changes made inside are visible to you but not yet permanent. COMMIT makes them all permanent at once; ROLLBACK throws them all away. ACID: Atomic — all or nothing. Consistent — the data moves from one valid state to another, never breaking a constraint. Isolated — transactions running at the same time don't see each other's half-finished work (how strictly depends on the isolation level). Durable — once committed, it survives a crash.
topics.analogy: A bank transfer slip that only counts when it is stamped. You can fill in both lines — take from here, add to there — but nothing happens until the stamp (COMMIT). Tear up the slip (ROLLBACK) and it is as if you never started.
topics.breaks: A torn-up slip leaves no trace. Inside a database, a long open transaction holds locks that can make other people wait. Keep transactions short: never wait for user input inside one.
howItWorks: BEGIN opens the transaction.
Two UPDATEs move Gus into HR and give him a raise. Only this transaction can see the changes so far.
COMMIT makes both changes permanent together. A crash before COMMIT would undo both.
In the second example, DELETE removes every item — then ROLLBACK undoes it, and all 14 rows are back.
If any statement fails, you roll back, and the data is exactly as it was before BEGIN.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR B["BEGIN"] --> S1["change 1"] --> S2["change 2"] S2 --> C["COMMIT
both kept, permanently"] S2 --> R["ROLLBACK or a crash
both undone"]
diagram.caption: Everything between BEGIN and COMMIT is one unit. It is either kept completely or thrown away completely — never half done.

examples.title: Two changes, committed together
ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN
examples.note: All 14 rows were deleted inside the transaction, then restored. Try adding a SELECT `COUNT(*)` before ROLLBACK to see 0.

keyPoints: BEGIN … COMMIT makes several statements one all-or-nothing unit; ROLLBACK cancels it.
Atomic: all or nothing. Consistent: constraints always hold. Isolated: concurrent transactions don't interfere. Durable: committed means saved.
Isolation levels trade safety for speed: READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE.
Anomalies the levels prevent: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads.
Keep transactions short; long ones hold locks and block others.
Locks, write skew and transactions that span several services (sagas) are in the System Design tab, Phases 3 and 4.
mistakes: Running related changes without a transaction, so a failure halfway leaves the data inconsistent.
Leaving a transaction open (forgetting COMMIT), which holds locks.
Assuming the default isolation level prevents every race. Two transactions can still both read a balance and both write it.
dialects: Default isolation: PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle use READ COMMITTED; MySQL InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ; SQLite is effectively SERIALIZABLE.
Most databases run each statement in its own transaction automatically (autocommit) unless you BEGIN one.
topics.interviewAnswer: A transaction groups statements into an atomic unit — BEGIN, changes, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK. ACID means atomicity, all or nothing; consistency, constraints hold before and after; isolation, concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted work; and durability, committed changes survive crashes. Isolation is tunable — read committed, repeatable read, serializable — trading anomalies like non-repeatable or phantom reads against concurrency, so for something like a balance update I lock the row with SELECT FOR UPDATE or use serializable.

followUps.q: What is a dirty read?
followUps.a: Reading another transaction's changes before it commits. If it then rolls back, you read data that never existed. READ COMMITTED prevents it.

followUps.q: What is a phantom read?
followUps.a: Running the same query twice in one transaction and getting new rows the second time because someone inserted them. SERIALIZABLE prevents it.

followUps.q: How do you stop two transfers overdrawing an account at the same time?
followUps.a: Lock the row while you check and update it (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`), use SERIALIZABLE, or update with a condition: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 100`.

practice.explain: Explain each letter of ACID with the bank-transfer example.
practice.write: In one transaction, move Eli to Marketing and give him a £3000 raise, then show his row.
practice.predict: What does the second example return if you remove the ROLLBACK line?
practice.edge: Two people run "read the stock, subtract 1, write it back" at the same moment on a product with 1 left. What can go wrong, and how do you prevent it?

explain.answer:
Moving £100 from account A to account B is two UPDATEs: subtract from A, add to B.

• Atomic: they happen together or not at all. If the server crashes after the first UPDATE, the transaction is rolled back, so £100 can't disappear.
• Consistent: every rule still holds afterwards. If a CHECK says balances can't go below zero, a transfer that would overdraw A fails, and nothing changes.
• Isolated: someone reading the balances while the transfer runs never sees the halfway point (A already £100 down, B not yet £100 up).
• Durable: once COMMIT returns, the transfer is saved on disk and survives a crash or power cut a second later.

write.answer:
Both changes sit between BEGIN and COMMIT, so they are saved together. Marketing is department 3. Eli's salary goes from 45,000 to 48,000.

Notice his manager_id is still 4 (Dara, in Sales). A real move would probably change that too, in the same transaction.

predict.answer:
0. Inside the open transaction, the DELETE has already removed all 14 item lines, and the transaction sees its own changes.

The bigger problem is that the transaction is never finished. Nothing is permanent yet, and it holds locks that block other writers until someone commits, rolls back, or disconnects (which rolls it back). Forgetting to end a transaction is a classic way to freeze an application.

edge.answer:
Both read stock = 1, both compute 1 − 1 = 0, and both write 0. Both sales go through, so one item has been sold twice: a lost update. The second writer overwrote the first one's change without knowing it existed.

Prevent it by making "check and subtract" one atomic step:
• A conditional update: `UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE product_id = 7 AND stock >= 1`, then check how many rows changed. 0 means sold out.
• Or lock the row while you read it: `SELECT stock … FOR UPDATE`, then update. The second buyer waits, then reads 0.
• Plus a `CHECK (stock >= 0)` as a final safety net.

Below, a stock column is added with 1 left, and two buyers run the conditional update. The second one changes 0 rows, so it knows it must refuse the sale.

topics.name: Normalisation: designing tables that don't contradict themselves
topics.definition: Normalisation is designing tables so each fact is stored in exactly one place — usually to third normal form (3NF): one value per cell, and every column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
topics.problem: If every order row stored the customer's email, changing Priya's email means updating five rows — miss one and the database says two different things. That is an update anomaly. Normalisation designs it out, and it is a favourite interview question.
topics.idea: First normal form (1NF): one value per cell, no lists like 'Pen, Mug', and no repeating columns like item1, item2. Second (2NF): in a table with a composite key, every column must depend on the whole key — the product name depends only on product_id, so it belongs in products, not in order_items. Third (3NF): no column depends on another non-key column — a customer's city name shouldn't carry the city's country too; that belongs in a cities table. The practice database is already normalised: customers, orders, order_items and products each hold one kind of fact. Denormalisation is copying data back on purpose, for read speed, accepting the risk.
topics.analogy: A school keeping each pupil's address in one office file, instead of writing it on every exercise book. When a family moves, one change updates everything — and no book can show an old address.
topics.breaks: In a school, looking up the office file is quick. In a database, every split costs a join at read time. That is why analytics warehouses often denormalise on purpose: reads there matter more than updates.
howItWorks: Start with one wide "flat" table: order, customer name, email, product, price, quantity.
Priya's email appears on every line she bought — 9 times. Changing it means 9 updates.
1NF: one product per row, not 'Headphones, Backpack' in one cell.
2NF: product_name and price depend only on product_id, so they move to products; customer details move to customers.
3NF: nothing depends on a non-key column. What is left is the practice database: each fact once, joined back when needed.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR F["one flat table
order, customer name, email,
product, price, quantity"] -->|"normalise"| C["customers
id, name, email"] F --> O["orders
id, customer_id, date"] F --> OI["order_items
order_id, product_id, quantity"] F --> P["products
id, name, price"]
diagram.caption: Normalising splits a wide table so each fact lives in one place. Joins put the flat view back together when you need it — the next example does exactly that.

examples.title: What one flat table would look like (built with joins)
examples.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, c.email, p.product_name, p.price, oi.quantity
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o    ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p  ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.customer_id = 1
ORDER BY o.order_id, p.product_name;
examples.note: Priya's email is repeated 9 times and each price several times. Stored like this, one missed update would make them disagree. Normalised, each is stored once.

keyPoints: 1NF: one value per cell; no lists, no repeating column groups.
2NF: 1NF, and no column depends on just part of a composite key.
3NF: 2NF, and no column depends on another non-key column.
Normalised data avoids update, insert and delete anomalies; the cost is more joins.
Denormalise on purpose (reporting tables, caches) when reads matter more than keeping one copy.
mistakes: Storing comma-separated lists in a column.
Copying a value (like a price) into another table without deciding whether it should change when the source changes.
Normalising so far that simple questions need eight joins. 3NF is usually the right stop.
dialects: Real order systems often store unit_price in order_items on purpose: the price paid at the time must not change when the product's price changes later. That isn't a 2NF violation — it is a different fact.
topics.interviewAnswer: Normalisation organises tables so each fact is stored once, which prevents update, insert and delete anomalies. First normal form means atomic values with no repeating groups; second, no partial dependency on part of a composite key; third, no transitive dependency through a non-key column — every column depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key. I normalise transactional systems to about 3NF and denormalise deliberately for analytics or read-heavy paths.

followUps.q: What is an update anomaly?
followUps.a: When the same fact is stored in several rows and an update changes some but not all of them, so the data contradicts itself.

followUps.q: When would you denormalise?
followUps.a: For read-heavy reporting or performance — for example a star schema in a data warehouse — accepting extra storage and the work of keeping copies in sync.

followUps.q: What is BCNF?
followUps.a: Boyce–Codd normal form, a slightly stricter 3NF: every determinant must be a candidate key. It rarely comes up beyond the definition.

practice.explain: Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF in one sentence each, using the shop tables.
practice.write: Write the query that rebuilds the flat view for Tom (customer 2), and count how many times his email appears.
practice.predict: If products also stored the category's manager name, which normal form would that break, and why?
practice.edge: Should order_items store the price at the time of the order? Argue both sides.

resources.title: CS50's Introduction to Databases with SQL — Lecture 2: Designing
W3Schools — SQL FOREIGN KEY (linking normalised tables)
resources.source: short page with a try-it editor, free

explain.answer:
• 1NF, one value per cell: an order can't store 'Headphones, Backpack' in one column; each product gets its own row in order_items.
• 2NF, every column depends on the whole key: in order_items the key is (order_id, product_id), and quantity depends on both, but a product_name would depend on product_id alone, so names live in products.
• 3NF, no column depends on another non-key column: orders shouldn't hold the customer's email, because the email depends on customer_id, not on the order; it lives once, in customers.

write.answer: The same four-table join as the lesson, for customer 2. Tom has two orders with one item each, so his email appears 2 times. (His second sign-up, customer 6, repeats the same email in customers, but has no orders.)

query.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, c.email, p.product_name, p.price, oi.quantity
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o    ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products p  ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.customer_id = 2
ORDER BY o.order_id, p.product_name;

predict.answer:
Third normal form. The manager's name depends on the category, not on the product: product_id → category → manager. That is a transitive dependency, through a column that isn't the key.

The symptom: the Stationery manager's name would be stored on the pen row and the notebook row. Change the manager and miss one row, and the table says two different things. The fix is a categories table (category, manager_name), with products keeping only the category.

edge.answer:
For storing it:
• The price paid is a different fact from today's price. When the headphones go from £40 to £45, last month's order must still say £40, for invoices, refunds and revenue reports.
• Without it, every old order would silently change value whenever a price changes.
• So it is not a 2NF violation: unit_price in order_items depends on the whole key (this product, in this order), not on product_id alone.

Against:
• If prices truly never change, it is a redundant copy taking space.
• Two columns called "price" invite mistakes: which one does a report use?
• An alternative is a price-history table with "valid from" dates, joined on the order date. It is fully normalised, but every read becomes more complex.

In practice, almost every real order system stores the price at the time of the order.

topics.name: Views: saved queries you can use like tables
topics.definition: A view is a named, saved SELECT that you query like a table; it stores no data of its own, so it always shows the current data, while a materialised view stores the result and must be refreshed.
topics.problem: The same "customer totals" query gets copied into ten reports, and when the rule changes, nine get fixed. A view keeps one definition in the database that everyone uses. Views can also hide columns people shouldn't see.
topics.idea: `CREATE VIEW customer_totals AS SELECT …` saves the query under a name. `SELECT * FROM customer_totals` runs it. Because the view is only a query, a new order shows up the next time you read it. A materialised view (PostgreSQL, Oracle) is different: it saves the rows, so reading is fast, but the data is only as fresh as the last REFRESH.
topics.analogy: A saved search in your email: "unread from my manager". It doesn't copy any emails; it runs the search every time you open it. A materialised view is a printed list of those emails — fast to read, but out of date as soon as a new one arrives.
topics.breaks: A saved search is free to run. A view over a big, complex query costs the full query every time you read it — a view makes queries shorter to write, not faster to run.
howItWorks: CREATE VIEW stores the query text under the name customer_totals.
Selecting from the view runs that query and then applies your WHERE and ORDER BY.
Insert a new order for Omar, read the view again, and his total is already there.
A materialised view would still show his old total until it is refreshed.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR T["orders + customers
(real tables)"] -->|"view runs its query
every time"| V["customer_totals
(view: no data stored)"] V --> Q["your SELECT"] T -.->|"copied at refresh"| M["materialised view
(stored rows)"]
diagram.caption: A view is a window onto the tables: it runs its query each time, so it is always current. A materialised view is a stored copy — fast, but only as fresh as its last refresh.

examples.title: Create a view and query it like a table
examples.sql:
CREATE VIEW customer_totals AS
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;

SELECT name, total_spent
FROM customer_totals
WHERE total_spent > 50
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

examples.title: A view is always up to date
examples.note: Omar had spent 0. The new order appears straight away, because the view re-runs its query.

keyPoints: A view is a saved query, used like a table. It stores no rows.
Views give one shared definition of a metric, and can hide sensitive columns.
A view is as fast as its underlying query — it doesn't speed things up.
A materialised view stores the result: fast reads, stale until refreshed.
mistakes: Expecting a normal view to make a slow query fast.
Stacking views on views until no one can tell what a query really does.
Forgetting to refresh a materialised view and reporting old numbers.
dialects: Materialised views: PostgreSQL `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` + `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`; Oracle has them; SQL Server uses "indexed views"; MySQL and SQLite have none.
topics.interviewAnswer: A view is a stored query that behaves like a virtual table: it holds no data, so it is always current, and it is useful for sharing one definition of a metric or for restricting which columns people see. It doesn't make queries faster. When the query is expensive and slight staleness is fine, I use a materialised view, which stores the result and is refreshed on a schedule.

followUps.q: View or materialised view?
followUps.a: A view runs its query on every read and is always fresh. A materialised view stores the result: fast to read, stale until refreshed.

followUps.q: Can you INSERT into a view?
followUps.a: Into simple views over one table, often yes. Views with joins or aggregates generally can't be written to without extra rules or triggers.

practice.explain: Explain the difference between a view and a materialised view.
practice.write: Create a view product_sales with each product and the total quantity sold (0 if none), then select the top 3 from it.
practice.predict: If you UPDATE an order amount, does SELECT from customer_totals show the new total? Would a materialised view?
practice.edge: Your view uses `SELECT *` from a table, and someone adds a column to that table. What might happen? Why is it safer to list columns?

resources.title: W3Schools — SQL Views
resources.source: short page with a try-it editor, free

explain.answer:
A view is a saved query with a name. It stores no rows: every time you select from it, it runs its query against the current tables, so it is always up to date, and only as fast as that query.

A materialised view runs the query once and stores the result rows. Reading it is fast (it is like reading a table), but it is a snapshot: new orders don't appear until you REFRESH it. Use a view for one shared definition of a query; use a materialised view when the query is expensive and slightly old numbers are fine (such as a dashboard refreshed every hour).

write.answer:
The LEFT JOIN keeps every product, and COALESCE turns the phone case's NULL total into 0. The view is then queried like a table.

The desk lamp and the mug tie on 6 for second place; the name in the ORDER BY decides which comes first, and both make the top 3 here.

query.sql:
CREATE VIEW product_sales AS
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0) AS total_sold
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name;

SELECT product_name, total_sold
FROM product_sales
ORDER BY total_sold DESC, product_name
LIMIT 3;

predict.answer:
Yes. The view stores only its query, so the next SELECT re-runs it against the updated orders table. Below, order 109 goes from £30 to £50, and Priya's total goes from 425 to 445 straight away.

A materialised view would not: it would keep showing 425 until someone ran REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.

edge.answer:
It depends on the database, and every option is bad.

• SQLite expands the * every time the view is read, so the new column appears in the view by itself. If that column is sensitive, it leaks. Below, a view meant to be safe to share suddenly shows a password_hash.
• PostgreSQL expands the * once, when the view is created, so the new column never appears, and the view quietly stops matching its table. Dropping a column the view uses, or changing its type, is refused.
• In SQL Server, the view's stored column list can go out of step with the table until it is refreshed, and columns can come back shifted.

Listing the columns makes the view's shape fixed and visible: nothing new appears by accident, nothing sensitive leaks, and anything that depends on the view keeps getting the same columns.

topics.name: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL — and DELETE versus TRUNCATE versus DROP
topics.definition: SQL commands fall into four families — DDL changes structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML changes data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DCL controls access (GRANT, REVOKE) and TCL controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK) — and DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP remove rows, all rows, or the whole table.
topics.problem: "What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?" is one of the most asked SQL theory questions. Knowing the four families answers it neatly, because the three belong to different families.
topics.idea: DDL (Data Definition Language) defines the shape: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE. DML (Data Manipulation Language) works on rows: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. DCL (Data Control Language) gives and takes permissions: GRANT, REVOKE. TCL (Transaction Control Language): BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT. DELETE is DML: it removes rows one by one, can have a WHERE, fires triggers, and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE is DDL-like: it empties the whole table at once, very fast, with no WHERE. DROP removes the table itself — rows, structure, indexes and all.
topics.analogy: A filing cabinet. DELETE takes out chosen files one at a time. TRUNCATE tips the whole drawer into the bin. DROP throws away the cabinet.
topics.breaks: Bins can be searched afterwards. Whether TRUNCATE can be undone depends on the database: PostgreSQL and SQL Server can roll it back inside a transaction; MySQL and Oracle commit it immediately.
topics.syntax:
DELETE FROM t WHERE condition;   -- DML: chosen rows
TRUNCATE TABLE t;                -- DDL: all rows, fast
DROP TABLE t;                    -- DDL: the table itself
howItWorks: `DELETE FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 110` removes 2 of the 14 rows; 12 remain.
TRUNCATE would remove all 14 rows instantly and keep the empty table (SQLite has no TRUNCATE; DELETE without WHERE does the same job).
DROP TABLE order_items removes the table completely: querying it afterwards is an error.
The catalog (the database's list of its own tables) shows the table is gone.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR D["DELETE … WHERE
DML · chosen rows
can roll back"] --> T["TRUNCATE
all rows, fast
table stays"] --> X["DROP
table, rows,
indexes: all gone"]
diagram.caption: From least to most destructive: DELETE removes the rows you choose, TRUNCATE empties the table but keeps it, and DROP removes the table itself.

examples.title: DELETE with a WHERE removes only some rows
examples.sql:
DELETE FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 110;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS items_left FROM order_items;

examples.title: DROP removes the table itself
examples.note: sqlite_master is SQLite's list of its own tables; PostgreSQL and MySQL use information_schema.tables.

keyPoints: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE. DML: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. DCL: GRANT, REVOKE. TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.
DELETE: chosen rows, WHERE allowed, row by row, fires triggers, can be rolled back.
TRUNCATE: every row, no WHERE, very fast, usually resets auto-numbering.
DROP: the table and everything about it.
TRUNCATE and DROP are refused if other tables' foreign keys point at the table (unless you CASCADE).
mistakes: Using TRUNCATE when you meant to keep some rows — it has no WHERE.
Assuming TRUNCATE can always be rolled back — not in MySQL or Oracle.
Dropping a table that views or foreign keys still depend on.
dialects: SQLite has no TRUNCATE; `DELETE FROM t;` without WHERE is optimised to do the same thing.
PostgreSQL: `TRUNCATE … RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE` resets numbering and empties referencing tables too.
topics.interviewAnswer: SQL commands split into DDL for structure, DML for data, DCL for permissions and TCL for transactions. DELETE is DML: it removes rows matching a WHERE, logs each row, fires triggers and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE removes all rows at once — much faster, no WHERE, often resets identity counters, and in some databases can't be rolled back. DROP removes the table definition along with its data, indexes and permissions.

followUps.q: Which is faster for emptying a big table, DELETE or TRUNCATE?
followUps.a: TRUNCATE: it deallocates the data in one step instead of deleting and logging each row.

followUps.q: Is SELECT DML or something else?
followUps.a: Usually counted as DML; some books call it DQL (Data Query Language).

practice.explain: Explain DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP with the filing-cabinet analogy, then technically.
practice.write: Delete all cancelled orders and their items (items first, because of the foreign key), then count what is left in both tables.
practice.predict: After `DELETE FROM products;`, how many rows are in products — and does the statement succeed? (Think about order_items.)
practice.edge: Which family does each belong to: GRANT, SAVEPOINT, ALTER, SELECT, TRUNCATE?

resources.source: short page with a try-it editor, free

resources.title: SQLBolt — Lesson 18: Dropping tables
resources.source: interactive exercises in the browser, free

explain.answer:
With a filing cabinet: DELETE takes out the files you choose, one at a time. TRUNCATE tips the whole drawer into the bin but keeps the drawer. DROP throws away the cabinet itself.

Technically:
• DELETE is DML. It removes the rows matching a WHERE (or all rows without one), row by row, logging each one and firing triggers. It can be rolled back.
• TRUNCATE is DDL. It empties the whole table in one fast step, with no WHERE, and usually resets the auto-numbering. Whether it can be rolled back depends on the database (yes in PostgreSQL and SQL Server, no in MySQL and Oracle).
• DROP is DDL. It removes the table completely: rows, columns, indexes, constraints and permissions. Querying it afterwards is an error.

write.answer:
Delete the children first, then the parents: the foreign key from order_items to orders would refuse it the other way round. Wrapping both in one transaction means you never end up with half the clean-up done.

The only cancelled order is 106, and it has no items, so 9 orders and all 14 item lines remain.

predict.answer: It fails, and products still has all 7 rows. order_items points at products 1 to 6, so deleting those products would leave item lines pointing at nothing: "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed". A statement either succeeds completely or not at all, so not even the phone case (which no item uses) is deleted.

query.sql: DELETE FROM products;

edge.answer:
• GRANT: DCL (Data Control Language): it gives a permission.
• SAVEPOINT: TCL (Transaction Control Language): it marks a point inside a transaction you can roll back to.
• ALTER: DDL (Data Definition Language): it changes a table's structure.
• SELECT: DML (Data Manipulation Language). Some books give it its own family, DQL (Data Query Language).
• TRUNCATE: DDL. It removes rows, but it works on the table as a whole, not row by row, which is why it is DDL and not DML.

phases.title: Performance: indexes and query plans
phases.goal: Know why a query is slow, read the plan the database chose, and write queries and indexes that let it find rows without reading the whole table.
phases.bigPicture: On six small tables everything is instant. On a hundred million rows, the difference between reading every row and jumping straight to the right ones is seconds versus milliseconds. Interviewers for backend and data roles always ask how you would make a slow query fast.

topics.name: Indexes: how a B-tree makes lookups fast
topics.definition: An index is a separate, sorted copy of one or more columns — usually a B-tree — with pointers back to the rows, so the database can jump to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table.
topics.problem: Without an index, `WHERE order_date = '2024-02-12'` must read every row and check it: a full table scan. On 100 million rows that is slow, and it gets slower as the table grows. An index turns it into a few quick steps.
topics.idea: A B-tree index keeps the column's values in sorted order, in a shallow tree: a root page points to branch pages, which point to leaf pages holding each value and the row it belongs to. To find a value, the database walks from the root down — about 3 or 4 steps even for millions of rows — instead of reading everything. The primary key is indexed automatically. Indexes speed up WHERE, JOIN … ON, ORDER BY and MIN/MAX on the indexed column. The cost: every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also update every index, and indexes take space.
topics.analogy: The index at the back of a textbook. To find "photosynthesis" you don't read every page; you look it up alphabetically and jump to page 214. A full table scan is reading the book cover to cover.
topics.breaks: A book index never changes once printed. A database index must be updated on every write — so a table with ten indexes is slow to write to. Index what you search by, not everything.
howItWorks: Without an index on order_date, the plan says SCAN orders: every row is read.
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date ON orders(order_date) builds a sorted list of dates, each pointing to its row.
Now the plan says SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_date (order_date=?): the database jumps to the date.
A lookup by the primary key uses the table's own key: SEARCH … USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY.
For 10 rows the difference is invisible; for 100 million it is the difference between a full read and a handful of page reads.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD R["root page
dates before 2024-02-01 · from 2024-02-01"] --> B1["branch
Jan dates"] R --> B2["branch
Feb and Mar dates"] B2 --> L1["leaf: 2024-02-02 → order 105"] B2 --> L2["leaf: 2024-02-12 → order 106"] B2 --> L3["leaf: 2024-02-20 → order 107"]
diagram.caption: A B-tree index: sorted values in a shallow tree. Finding 2024-02-12 takes one step per level — root, branch, leaf — then one jump to the row, instead of reading every row.

examples.title: No index: the database scans every row
examples.sql:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date = '2024-02-12';
examples.note: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows the plan instead of running the query. Read the detail column: SCAN means every row.

examples.title: With an index: the database searches
examples.note: SEARCH … USING INDEX means it jumps straight to the matching date.

examples.title: The primary key is already indexed
examples.sql:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = 105;

rows: SEARCH orders USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)

keyPoints: An index is a sorted structure (usually a B-tree) pointing back to the rows.
It helps WHERE, JOIN … ON, ORDER BY and GROUP BY on the indexed columns.
Primary keys and UNIQUE constraints get an index automatically; foreign keys usually don't — index them yourself.
Every index slows down writes and uses space. Index the columns you filter and join on.
An index helps most when it narrows the search to a small share of the rows (high selectivity).
B-trees versus LSM trees, and indexing at scale, are in the System Design tab, Phase 3.
mistakes: Indexing every column "just in case", which slows every write.
Forgetting to index foreign keys, so joins and deletes on the parent table are slow.
Indexing a column with only a few values (like status) and expecting it to help a query that matches half the table.
dialects: PostgreSQL also has hash, GIN (for arrays, JSON and full-text) and BRIN (for huge, naturally ordered tables) indexes. MySQL InnoDB stores the table itself in primary-key order (a clustered index).
topics.interviewAnswer: An index is a separate sorted structure, typically a B-tree, mapping column values to row locations, so the database can find matching rows in logarithmic time instead of scanning the table. I index columns used in selective WHERE filters, join keys — especially foreign keys — and ORDER BY, and I keep in mind the trade-off: every index adds work to inserts, updates and deletes, and uses storage.

followUps.q: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
followUps.a: A clustered index stores the table's rows themselves in index order (one per table, often the primary key, as in SQL Server and MySQL InnoDB). A non-clustered index is a separate structure that points to the rows.

followUps.q: Why not index every column?
followUps.a: Each index must be updated on every write and takes space, and the optimiser can only use a few per query anyway.

followUps.q: Why might the database ignore your index?
followUps.a: If the query matches a large share of the rows, a full scan is cheaper than thousands of index jumps. Or the query wraps the column in a function, so the index can't be used.

practice.explain: Explain an index using the textbook analogy, and say what it costs.
practice.write: Create an index that would help `SELECT * FROM employees WHERE dept_id = 1;`, and check the plan before and after.
practice.predict: Will `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 3` use an index without you creating one? Why?
practice.edge: A status column has only four values and 50% of rows are 'delivered'. Would an index on status help `WHERE status = 'delivered'`? What about `WHERE status = 'pending'`?

W3Schools — SQL CREATE INDEX
resources.source: short page with a try-it editor, free

explain.answer:
An index is like the index at the back of a textbook. To find "photosynthesis" you don't read every page; you look the word up in the sorted list and jump to page 214. Without an index, the database has to read the whole table (a full scan), like reading the book cover to cover. With one, it searches a sorted copy of the column (a B-tree) and follows a pointer straight to the matching rows.

What it costs:
• Slower writes: every INSERT, DELETE, and UPDATE of the indexed column must also update the index. A book's index is printed once; a database's is kept up to date all the time.
• Space: the index is a second copy of the column, on disk and in memory.
So you index the columns your important queries filter, join or sort on, not every column.

write.answer:
Before, the plan is `SCAN employees`: every row is read. Create an index on the filtered column, run the same EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, and it becomes a SEARCH using the new index.

(With 8 rows a scan is just as fast; the plan matters when the table has millions.)

query.sql:
CREATE INDEX idx_employees_dept ON employees(dept_id);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM employees WHERE dept_id = 1;

predict.answer: Yes. customer_id is the primary key, and a primary key is always indexed: the database needs that to check uniqueness on every insert. In SQLite an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the row's own id (the rowid), so the plan searches straight to it.

query.sql: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 3;

rows: SEARCH customers USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)

edge.answer:
`WHERE status = 'delivered'`: probably not. Half the table matches, so the index would find half a million row pointers (in a million-row table), and fetching each row one by one, jumping around the disk, is slower than simply reading the whole table in order. A good optimiser, with statistics, ignores the index and scans.

`WHERE status = 'pending'`: yes, if pending orders are rare (say 1%). The index jumps straight to the few matching rows. This is the case where an index on a column with few values can pay off.

The usual answer for "a rare value of a common column" is a partial index, which only holds the rows you search for: `CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending ON orders(order_date) WHERE status = 'pending';`. It is tiny and cheap to maintain.

(SQLite only knows how values are spread after you run ANALYZE. Without it, it will happily use an index on status for 'delivered' too.)

topics.name: Reading a query plan with EXPLAIN
topics.definition: EXPLAIN shows the plan the database chose for a query — which tables it scans, which indexes it searches, how it joins and sorts — without (or, with ANALYZE, while) running it.
topics.problem: "This query is slow — what do you do?" The first answer is always: look at the plan. Guessing wastes time; the plan tells you whether the database is scanning a huge table, missing an index, or sorting millions of rows.
topics.idea: Put EXPLAIN in front of a query (in SQLite, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN). Read each line as one step. The words to look for: SCAN (reading a whole table — fine if small, a red flag if big), SEARCH … USING INDEX (jumping to rows — good), and TEMP B-TREE or Sort (building a sort or grouping — costly on big data). For a join, each line is one table, in the order the database reads them: it scans one and searches the other for each row. PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and shows real times and row counts — compare estimated rows with actual rows to spot bad estimates.
topics.analogy: A satnav showing the route before you drive. You can see it plans to go through the city centre (a full scan) instead of the bypass (an index), and fix it before you set off.
topics.breaks: A satnav's route is the same every time. A query plan can change as the data grows or statistics update — a plan that is fine on 10 rows may be terrible on 10 million. Always check plans on realistic data.
topics.syntax:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT ...;   -- SQLite
EXPLAIN SELECT ...;              -- PostgreSQL, MySQL: the plan
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...;      -- PostgreSQL: run it, real timings
howItWorks: Before an index on orders.customer_id: SCAN o (read every order), and for each one SEARCH c by primary key.
Add the index: now the plan is SCAN c (only 6 customers), and SEARCH o USING INDEX for each customer.
The order of the lines is the order the tables are read in: the outer table first.
For GROUP BY without a helpful index, you see USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY: a temporary sort.
Fixes usually mean: add or change an index, filter earlier, or rewrite a condition so the index can be used.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR Q["slow query"] --> E["EXPLAIN it"] E --> S{"SCAN on a big table?"} S -->|"yes"| I["add an index on the
filter or join column"] S -->|"no"| T{"big sort or
TEMP B-TREE?"} T -->|"yes"| O["index the ORDER BY
or GROUP BY columns"] I --> E O --> E
diagram.caption: Tuning is a loop: read the plan, find the expensive step (a big scan or a big sort), change the index or the query, and read the plan again.

examples.title: A join plan before indexing the foreign key
examples.sql:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT c.name, o.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.city = 'Leeds';

rows: SEARCH c USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)

examples.note: Every order is read, and for each one the customer is looked up by its primary key.

examples.title: After indexing orders.customer_id
examples.note: The plan flipped: read the few customers in Leeds, then jump to each one's orders through the new index.

examples.title: A grouping that needs a temporary sort
examples.sql:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount)
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

rows: USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY

examples.note: With an index on customer_id the rows would already be in order, and the temporary B-tree would disappear.

keyPoints: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL) runs it and shows real times and rows.
SCAN = read everything; SEARCH / Index Scan = jump via an index.
Sorts and temp B-trees for ORDER BY, GROUP BY or DISTINCT are expensive on big data.
In a join plan, the first table is the outer loop; the inner table should be searched by index.
Big gaps between estimated and actual row counts point to stale statistics (run ANALYZE).
mistakes: Tuning by guesswork instead of reading the plan.
Judging a plan on a tiny test table — the optimiser may choose differently on real data.
Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a DELETE or UPDATE in production. It really runs the statement.
dialects: PostgreSQL plan words: Seq Scan (full scan), Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Bitmap Heap Scan, Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join, Sort.
MySQL: `EXPLAIN` gives a table with a `type` column — ALL is a full scan, ref/range/const use an index. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` exists from 8.0.18.
topics.interviewAnswer: My first step with a slow query is EXPLAIN, or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL to see real timings and row counts. I look for sequential scans on large tables, expensive sorts, nested loops over big inputs, and estimates that are far from actual counts. Typical fixes are an index on the filter or join columns, rewriting a non-sargable condition, filtering earlier, or refreshing statistics — then I re-check the plan.

followUps.q: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
followUps.a: EXPLAIN shows the plan and estimated costs without running the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and adds the actual time and row counts for each step.

followUps.q: What does it mean if estimated rows are 10 but actual rows are 1,000,000?
followUps.a: The optimiser's statistics are wrong or stale, so it may pick a bad plan. Run ANALYZE to refresh them.

practice.explain: Explain what SCAN and SEARCH mean in a plan, and which one you want on a big table.
practice.write: Write EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for "employees in department 2", then add an index and show the plan changes.
practice.predict: What plan do you expect for `SELECT * FROM products WHERE product_id = 3`? Check it.
practice.edge: Add an index on orders(customer_id) and re-run the GROUP BY plan. Does the temporary B-tree disappear? Why might it still be there?

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — a guide to database performance for developers

explain.answer:
SCAN means the database reads every row of the table (or of an index) from start to finish. SEARCH means it uses an index to jump straight to the matching rows, like using a book's index instead of reading every page.

On a big table you want SEARCH for selective filters and joins. A SCAN of a million-row table on every request is usually the reason a query is slow. A SCAN is fine when the table is tiny, or when you really need most of its rows (then reading in order beats jumping around).

write.answer:
Before: `SCAN employees`. The index below holds dept_id and name together, so the plan becomes a SEARCH with a COVERING INDEX: the query needs only name, which is already in the index, so the database never reads the table itself.

An index on dept_id alone would also turn the SCAN into a SEARCH, but each match would then need a second lookup into the table to fetch the name.

query.sql:
CREATE INDEX idx_employees_dept_name ON employees(dept_id, name);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM employees WHERE dept_id = 2;

rows: SEARCH employees USING COVERING INDEX idx_employees_dept_name (dept_id=?)

predict.answer: A SEARCH by the primary key: product_id is an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, which in SQLite is the rowid, so it goes straight to the one row. No index needs to be created.

query.sql: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM products WHERE product_id = 3;

rows: SEARCH products USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)

edge.answer:
Here it disappears. Before the index, the plan is `SCAN orders` plus `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY`: the rows come out in any order, so SQLite builds a temporary sorted structure to group them. With the index, it reads orders through idx_orders_customer, which already returns rows sorted by customer_id, so the groups arrive in order and no sort is needed.

Why it might still be there:
• The index doesn't cover the query: amount isn't in it, so every row needs an extra lookup into the table. On a big table the optimiser may decide a plain scan plus a sort is cheaper, and keep the temp B-tree. An index on (customer_id, amount) covers the query and removes that doubt.
• With statistics (after ANALYZE), the optimiser might prefer the scan anyway.
• The ORDER BY or GROUP BY doesn't match the index order (a different column, or a different direction).

topics.name: Index-friendly queries: sargable filters and composite indexes
topics.definition: A filter is sargable when the database can use an index for it — the indexed column stands alone on one side of the comparison — and a composite index on (a, b) helps queries that filter on a, or on a and b, but not on b alone.
topics.problem: An index can exist and still not be used. `WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) = '2024-02'` reads every row even with an index on order_date. Knowing the rules lets you write the same filter in a way that uses the index.
topics.idea: The index stores the raw column values in order. If you wrap the column in a function (`UPPER(name)`, `strftime(…)`), do maths on it (`salary + 0 > 60000`), or start a LIKE with % ('%son'), the database can't search the sorted values, so it scans. Rewrite the condition so the bare column is compared with a value: a date range instead of a function. A composite index on (customer_id, order_date) is sorted by customer, then by date within each customer — like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. It helps `customer_id = 1`, and `customer_id = 1 AND order_date >= …`, but not `order_date >= …` alone: the leftmost-prefix rule. If the index contains every column the query needs, it is a covering index, and the table itself isn't touched.
topics.analogy: A phone book sorted by surname, then first name. Finding "Smith, John" is quick; finding all the Smiths is quick; finding everyone called John is not — you would have to read the whole book.
topics.breaks: A person might notice that the Johns are easy to find if there are only five surnames. Some databases can do a "skip scan" too, but don't count on it — design the column order for the queries you really run.
topics.syntax:
-- not sargable: the column is inside a function
WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) = '2024-02'
-- sargable: the bare column, compared with a range
WHERE order_date >= '2024-02-01' AND order_date < '2024-03-01'

CREATE INDEX idx ON orders (customer_id, order_date);
howItWorks: With an index on order_date, `strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) = '2024-02'` gives SCAN orders: the index can't be used.
The same filter as a range on the bare column gives SEARCH … (order_date>? AND order_date<?).
A composite index (customer_id, order_date) is searched for `customer_id = 1 AND order_date >= …`.
For `order_date >= …` alone, it can't be used: the dates are only sorted within each customer.
Selecting only customer_id and order_date lets the index answer on its own: a covering index.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR I["index on (customer_id, order_date)
1: 01-06, 01-07, 01-08, 02-02, 03-10
2: 01-21, 03-01
3: 02-12, 02-20"] --> A["customer_id = 1
uses it"] I --> B["customer_id = 1 AND date from Feb
uses it"] I --> C["date from Feb only
can't use it: scan"]
diagram.caption: A composite index is sorted by its first column, then by the second within each value of the first. It helps when the query fixes the leftmost column(s), not when it skips them.

examples.title: A function on the column blocks the index
The same filter as a range uses it

rows: SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_date (order_date>? AND order_date<?)

examples.title: Composite index: leftmost column fixed

rows: SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_cust_date (customer_id=? AND order_date>?)

examples.title: Composite index: leftmost column skipped
examples.note: Dates are only in order within each customer, so the index can't help a date-only filter.

keyPoints: Keep the indexed column bare: no functions, no maths, no leading % in LIKE.
Rewrite "same month" or "same year" filters as half-open ranges: >= start AND < next start.
A composite index (a, b) serves filters on a, or a and b — not b alone (leftmost prefix).
Put the column you test with = first, and the range column after it.
A covering index holds every column a query needs, so the table isn't read at all.
mistakes: `WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024` on an indexed date column.
Creating (order_date, customer_id) when the queries filter by customer first.
Comparing a column with a value of another type (a number column with '42'), which can force a conversion on every row.
dialects: PostgreSQL and Oracle support expression indexes, such as `CREATE INDEX ON customers (LOWER(email))`, which make that exact function sargable. MySQL 8 has functional indexes too.
PostgreSQL and SQL Server let you add extra non-key columns to make an index covering: `INCLUDE (amount)`.
topics.interviewAnswer: An index can only be used when the predicate is sargable — the indexed column appears bare, compared with a constant or range — so I avoid functions or arithmetic on indexed columns and rewrite things like `YEAR(date) = 2024` as a date range. For composite indexes the leftmost-prefix rule applies: an index on customer_id then order_date serves filters on customer, or customer and date, but not date alone, so I put equality columns first and range columns last, and make the index covering when a hot query only needs a few columns.

followUps.q: What does sargable mean?
followUps.a: Search-ARGument-ABLE: written so the database can use an index to evaluate it.

followUps.q: Index (a, b) or (b, a)?
followUps.a: Match the queries: the column filtered with = in most queries goes first; a column used for ranges or sorting goes after it.

followUps.q: How do you make a case-insensitive email lookup fast?
followUps.a: Store emails lower-cased and index them, or create an expression index on `LOWER(email)` and query with `LOWER(email)` = 'x'.

practice.write: Rewrite `WHERE strftime('%Y', hire_date) = '2021'` so an index on hire_date could be used, and check the plan.
practice.predict: With an index on employees(salary), is `WHERE salary + 0 > 60000` sargable? What about `WHERE salary > 60000 - 0`?
practice.edge: Design one index that helps both "orders for customer 1, newest first" and "orders for customer 1 in March".

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — a guide to database performance for developers

explain.answer:
A phone book is sorted by surname, then by first name: an index on (surname, first_name).

• "Smith, John": quick. Find the Smiths, then John among them.
• All the Smiths: quick. They are all together.
• Everyone called John: no help at all. The Johns are scattered through every surname, so you would have to read the whole book.

That is the leftmost-prefix rule. A composite index on (a, b) helps a query that fixes a, or a and b, but not one that only filters on b, because b is only sorted within each value of a.

write.answer: Wrapping the column in a function (`strftime('%Y', hire_date)`) hides it from the index: the database would have to work out the year for every row, so the plan is a SCAN. Say the same thing as a range on the bare column, and the plan becomes a SEARCH on the index. It finds the same people, Chen and Fatima.

rows: SEARCH employees USING INDEX idx_employees_hire (hire_date>? AND hire_date<?)

predict.answer:
`WHERE salary + 0 > 60000` is not sargable: the column is inside a calculation, so the database can't look it up in the index and scans (`SCAN employees`). (Adding + 0 is in fact an old trick to stop an index being used on purpose.)

`WHERE salary > 60000 - 0` is sargable: salary stands alone, and the arithmetic is on the constant side, which is worked out once. The plan is a SEARCH.

query.sql:
CREATE INDEX idx_employees_salary ON employees(salary);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > 60000 - 0;

edge.answer:
One composite index on (customer_id, order_date), customer first.

• "Customer 1, newest first": fix customer_id = 1, then read that customer's entries backwards. They are already sorted by date, so there is no sort step (no temp B-tree in the plan, below).
• "Customer 1 in March": fix customer_id = 1, then take a range on the second column: `order_date >= '2024-03-01' AND order_date < '2024-04-01'`. Its plan is `SEARCH … (customer_id=? AND order_date>? AND order_date<?)`.

The order matters: (order_date, customer_id) would only help the second query, and badly. Both plans even say COVERING here, because order_id is the rowid, which every SQLite index carries.

rows: SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX idx_orders_cust_date (customer_id=?)

topics.name: How a database runs a join: nested loop, hash join, merge join
topics.definition: Databases use three main join methods — a nested loop (for each row of one table, look up matches in the other), a hash join (build a hash table of one side, probe it with the other), and a merge join (walk two sorted inputs together) — and the optimiser picks one per join.
topics.problem: In senior interviews you may be asked why a join is slow or what a plan line like "Hash Join" means. Knowing the three methods tells you which index or memory setting will help.
topics.idea: Nested loop: for each row of the outer table, find matching rows in the inner table — fast when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index on the join key (that is what SQLite did in the last lesson). Hash join: read the smaller table into a hash table keyed on the join column, then stream the bigger table past it, checking each row — great for big, unindexed equality joins, but it needs memory. Merge join: if both sides are sorted on the key (by an index, or by sorting first), walk them side by side like zipping a zip — good for big inputs already in order.
topics.analogy: Matching wedding guests to tables. Nested loop: take each guest and look their name up in the seating plan. Hash join: first make a quick lookup card per surname, then let every guest find their card. Merge join: line up the guests alphabetically and the seating list alphabetically, then walk down both together.
topics.breaks: At a wedding you would pick the method by eye. A database picks it from estimates of how many rows each side has — wrong estimates are the main reason it picks badly.
howItWorks: Nested loop: outer has N rows, and each inner lookup is an index search, so the cost is about N × log(M). Bad if there is no index on the inner side: N × M.
Hash join: build a hash table on the smaller input (one pass), probe it with the larger (one pass): about N + M, using memory.
Merge join: if both inputs are already sorted, one pass over each: about N + M; otherwise a sort first.
Equality joins can use any method; only nested loops handle conditions like `a.x < b.y`.
You influence the choice through indexes, statistics and (in PostgreSQL) memory settings like work_mem.

diagram.code:
flowchart TD J["a join"] --> NL["nested loop
small outer side + index on inner"] J --> HJ["hash join
big inputs, equality, no useful index"] J --> MJ["merge join
both inputs already sorted on the key"]
diagram.caption: The optimiser chooses a join method per join, based on how many rows it expects on each side, whether indexes exist, and whether the inputs are already sorted.

examples.title: A nested loop: scan one side, search the other by key
examples.sql:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT p.category, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price)
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.category;

rows: SEARCH p USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)
USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY

examples.note: SQLite mostly uses nested loops: for each order item, it looks the product up by its primary key. PostgreSQL would likely show a Hash Join here on bigger tables.

keyPoints: Nested loop: best for a small outer input with an index on the inner join key.
Hash join: best for large, unsorted equality joins; needs memory for the hash table.
Merge join: best when both inputs are already sorted on the join key.
The optimiser chooses using row-count estimates; stale statistics cause bad choices.
Indexing join keys (especially foreign keys) is the single most useful join optimisation.
mistakes: Thinking an index always makes a join faster: for a hash join over whole tables it may not be used at all.
Ignoring a nested loop over two large tables without an index — it grows as N × M.
Forcing a join method with hints instead of fixing the statistics or indexes.
dialects: PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle use all three methods. SQLite uses nested loops (with automatic temporary indexes). MySQL added hash joins in 8.0.18.
topics.interviewAnswer: There are three main physical join algorithms. Nested loop iterates the outer input and looks up matches in the inner — ideal when the outer side is small and the inner join key is indexed. Hash join builds an in-memory hash table on the smaller input and probes it with the larger — ideal for big equality joins without useful indexes. Merge join walks two inputs sorted on the key. The optimiser chooses based on estimated cardinalities, so bad statistics are a common cause of a poor join plan.

followUps.q: Which join method can handle a non-equality condition like a.start < b.end?
followUps.a: Only a nested loop. Hash and merge joins need an equality condition.

followUps.q: When does a hash join go to disk?
followUps.a: When the hash table doesn't fit in the memory allowed (work_mem in PostgreSQL), it spills to disk in batches and slows down.

practice.explain: Explain the three join methods with the wedding-guest analogy.
practice.write: Write a query joining orders and customers, run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, and name the join method SQLite used.
practice.predict: Joining a 10-row table to a 10-million-row table with an index on the big table's join key — which method would you expect?
practice.edge: Two 100-million-row tables are joined on a column with no index on either side. Which method should the optimiser pick, and what resource does it need?

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — a guide to database performance for developers
Nested loop, hash and merge joins (video)

explain.answer:
Matching wedding guests to their tables:

• Nested loop: take each guest in turn and look their name up in the seating plan. Quick if the seating plan has an index (sorted by name, so each lookup is fast) or if there are only a few guests. Without an index, every guest reads the whole plan: very slow for big lists.
• Hash join: first make a quick lookup card for every name in the seating plan (a hash table, kept in memory), then let each guest find their card in one step. Great for two big lists with no index; it needs memory for the cards.
• Merge join: line the guests up alphabetically, line the seating plan up alphabetically, then walk down both lists together, matching as you go. Great when both are already sorted (by an index); otherwise both must be sorted first.

The optimiser picks one per join, from the sizes, the indexes and the memory available.

write.answer: The plan reads: SCAN o, then SEARCH c using the primary key. That is a nested loop: for each order (the outer loop), look up its customer by key (the inner step). SQLite only does nested loops; it makes them fast with indexes, and builds a temporary index itself when none exists. PostgreSQL would show "Nested Loop", "Hash Join" or "Merge Join" by name.

query.sql:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT o.order_id, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

rows: SEARCH c USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)

predict.answer:
A nested loop, with the small table outside. Loop over the 10 rows, and for each one search the big table's index: 10 index lookups of a few steps each, a few dozen page reads in all.

A hash join would have to read all 10 million rows of the big table (to build or to probe), and a merge join would need it sorted. Neither can compete with 10 index lookups.

edge.answer:
A hash join. A nested loop with no index would compare every row with every row: 100 million × 100 million = 10¹⁶ comparisons, which never finishes. A merge join would first have to sort both 100-million-row tables.

A hash join reads one side (ideally the smaller after filters) and builds a hash table on the join column, then reads the other side once and probes it: about two passes over the data.

The resource it needs is memory, for the hash table. If it doesn't fit, the database splits both sides into batches by hash and writes them to temporary disk space, then joins batch by batch (a "grace" hash join), which is slower but still linear. Big analytical joins are often limited by memory, so the work_mem (PostgreSQL) or join buffer settings matter.

phases.title: SQL interview problems, from easy to hard
phases.goal: Solve the classic SQL interview questions from a blank page, explain your approach while you write, and name the edge cases before the interviewer does.
phases.bigPicture: Most SQL interview questions are one of about a dozen patterns: Nth highest, top N per group, rows with no match, duplicates, comparisons with a group average, period-over-period change, first event per user, streaks, retention. Learn to spot the pattern from the wording, and the query almost writes itself.

topics.name: How to answer any SQL interview question
topics.definition: A repeatable method: restate the question, look at the tables and their grain, ask about edge cases, plan the steps out loud, write the query as small CTEs, then check the result against a few rows you can work out by hand.
topics.problem: Under pressure, people jump straight into typing, write one giant query, and miss the NULLs or ties the interviewer planted. Interviewers grade the process as much as the answer: do you clarify, structure, and verify?
topics.idea: Step 1, clarify: say the question back in your own words, and ask about ties, NULLs, duplicates and what "per" means. Step 2, look at the data: what is one row of each table (the grain), what are the keys, how do they join? Step 3, plan out loud: "First I'll get delivered orders, then total them per customer, then join the city." Step 4, write it as CTEs, one step each, running each one if you can. Step 5, check: does the row count make sense? Does a total match a number you can work out by hand? Then say the edge cases and how your query handles them.
