topics.analogy: A pilot's checklist. Experienced pilots still run it every flight — not because they forget how to fly, but because the checklist catches the one thing that pressure makes you skip.
topics.breaks: A checklist is the same every flight. Interviews vary: if the question is simple, go through the steps quickly; don't spend five minutes clarifying "count the rows".
topics.syntax:
-- 1 clarify  2 look at the grain  3 plan out loud
WITH step_one AS (...),   -- 4 one CTE per step
     step_two AS (...)
SELECT ... FROM step_two; -- 5 check against rows you know
howItWorks: Question: "Which city brings in the most delivered revenue?"
Clarify: delivered orders only? Customers with no city — drop them or show them as unknown? Ties?
Grain: one row of orders is one order; customers holds the city; join on customer_id.
Sanity-check the data first: 10 orders, 4 customers who ordered, 1 order with no amount.
Plan and write: a CTE of delivered orders → join customers → group by city → sort. Check: London = Priya 275 + Lena 60 = 335.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["1 clarify
ties? NULLs? per what?"] --> B["2 look at tables
grain, keys, joins"] --> C["3 plan out loud"] --> D["4 write CTEs
one step each"] --> E["5 check
row counts, a known total,
edge cases"]
diagram.caption: Five steps, every time. The talking in steps 1, 3 and 5 is what the interviewer is grading; the CTEs in step 4 make your thinking easy to follow.

examples.title: Step 2: look at the data before you write the answer
examples.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers_who_ordered,
       SUM(CASE WHEN amount IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS missing_amounts
FROM orders;
examples.note: Thirty seconds of this tells you there are missing amounts to mention, and how many rows to expect.

examples.title: Steps 4 and 5: write it in steps, then check a number
examples.sql:
WITH delivered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, amount
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'delivered'
)
SELECT COALESCE(c.city, 'unknown') AS city,
       SUM(d.amount) AS delivered_revenue
FROM delivered d
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = d.customer_id
GROUP BY COALESCE(c.city, 'unknown')
ORDER BY delivered_revenue DESC;
examples.note: Check by hand: London is Priya's 275 delivered plus Lena's 60. Zoe (no city) has no delivered order, so "unknown" doesn't appear.

keyPoints: Clarify first: ties, NULLs, duplicates, date ranges, and what "per" means.
Know each table's grain and keys before joining.
Think out loud — the interviewer is grading your reasoning.
Write CTEs, one step each, named after what they hold.
Verify: a row count, one total worked out by hand, and the edge cases said out loud.
mistakes: Typing straight away and writing one huge nested query.
Not asking about ties, then using LIMIT 1 when two rows tie.
Stopping when the query runs, without checking that the answer is right.
dialects: If the interviewer doesn't name a database, say "I'll write PostgreSQL" — it is the most common choice, and it means DATE_TRUNC, ::date casts and FILTER are all available.
topics.interviewAnswer: I start by restating the question and asking about edge cases — ties, NULLs, duplicates, the time window. Then I look at the tables to understand the grain and how they join, explain my plan in steps, and write it as a chain of CTEs so each step is readable and testable. Finally I sanity-check the output — row counts and one number I can verify by hand — and walk through how the query handles the edge cases.

followUps.q: What do you do if you don't know the exact function name in their database?
followUps.a: Say so, write the closest version you know (for example DATE_TRUNC), and explain what it does. Interviewers care about the logic, not the exact spelling.

followUps.q: How do you check a query when you can't run it?
followUps.a: Walk two or three rows through each step by hand, especially a NULL row and a tie.

practice.explain: Say the five steps from memory, with one sentence on why each matters.
practice.write: Use the five steps on: "Which product category had the most units sold in February?" Write your clarifying questions first.
practice.predict: Before running the city query, predict its result if cancelled orders were included too.
practice.edge: List three edge cases you would raise for "What is the average order value per customer?" and how each changes the query.

resources.title: How to approach SQL interview questions (video)

explain.answer:
1. Restate the question and clarify it: "So you want delivered revenue per city, highest first?" It catches misunderstandings before you write anything, and shows you listen.
2. Look at the tables, their grain and the data: one row of orders is one order; the city is in customers; run a quick count. Joins and sums go wrong when you don't know what one row means.
3. Ask about the edge cases: ties, NULLs, duplicates, date ranges, what "per" means. Each answer changes the query, and asking is what interviewers grade.
4. Plan out loud, then write it as small CTEs, one step each, named after what they hold. Easy to follow, and easy to fix one step.
5. Check the result: a row count and one number worked out by hand ("London = 275 + 60 = 335"). It catches fan-out, missing rows and integer division before the interviewer does.

write.answer:
Clarifying questions first:
• Which orders count? I'll assume everything except cancelled (shipped and pending were still sold), and say so.
• "February" means February 2024, by order_date.
• Units means the quantity in order_items, not the number of orders.
• What if two categories tie? I'll return both, rather than pick one.

Grain: one order_items row is one product in one order; the category is in products; the date and status are in orders.

Plan: February's item lines with their category → units per category → keep the maximum. Check by hand: February has orders 105 (3 headphones, 1 backpack) and 107 (2 backpacks); 106 was cancelled and has no items. So Electronics = 3 and Bags = 1 + 2 = 3: a tie, and both come back.

query.sql:
WITH feb_items AS (
  SELECT p.category, oi.quantity
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-02-01' AND o.order_date < '2024-03-01'
    AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
),
by_category AS (
  SELECT category, SUM(quantity) AS units
  FROM feb_items
  GROUP BY category
)
SELECT category, units
FROM by_category
WHERE units = (SELECT MAX(units) FROM by_category)
ORDER BY category;

predict.answer:
Exactly the same: London 335, Leeds 275.

The only cancelled order is 106 (Lena, London), and its amount is NULL. SUM skips NULLs, so adding it changes nothing. A good prediction checks the data, not just the logic: "include cancelled orders" sounds like a big change, but here it adds one row with nothing to add.

query.sql:
WITH delivered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, amount
  FROM orders
  WHERE status IN ('delivered', 'cancelled')
)
SELECT COALESCE(c.city, 'unknown') AS city,
       SUM(d.amount) AS delivered_revenue
FROM delivered d
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = d.customer_id
GROUP BY COALESCE(c.city, 'unknown')
ORDER BY delivered_revenue DESC;

edge.answer:
1. Orders with no amount, or cancelled orders. Order 106 has a NULL amount. AVG skips it (Lena's average is 60, from one order); treating it as £0 gives 30. Ask which is meant, then either filter `WHERE status <> 'cancelled'`, or use `AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0))`.

2. Customers with no orders. Omar has none. Starting from orders, he simply isn't there; if the question means "per customer, all of them", start from customers with a LEFT JOIN, and decide whether he shows NULL or 0.

3. Duplicate customers. Tom signed up twice (ids 2 and 6). Grouping by customer_id gives two Toms, one with no orders. If they are one person, group by the email instead (after cleaning it).

(A fourth worth asking: does "average order value per customer" mean each customer's own average, or one overall figure, which is total revenue ÷ number of orders?)

topics.name: Quick-fire SQL theory questions
topics.definition: Short "what is the difference between…" questions that open many SQL interviews; each is best answered with a one-line definition of both sides, the key difference, and when you would use each.
topics.problem: These questions take thirty seconds each but set the tone for the interview. A crisp answer shows you really understand the tool; a vague one makes the interviewer dig deeper. They are collected here so you can revise them in one place.
topics.idea: Use the same three-part shape every time. One: define both things in a sentence each. Two: state the difference that matters. Three: say when you would choose each, ideally with an example. Keep it under thirty seconds, then stop — let them ask for more. Open the follow-up questions below and answer each one out loud before showing the answer.
topics.analogy: Penalty practice. You don't learn penalties by thinking about them; you take the same kick again and again until it is automatic, so it holds up under pressure.
topics.breaks: A penalty is the same every time. Interviewers rephrase questions, so learn the idea behind each answer, not just the words.
howItWorks: Define both sides: "WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups."
Give the difference that matters: "WHERE runs before grouping, so it can't use aggregates."
Say when to use each: "Row conditions in WHERE, aggregate conditions in HAVING."
Offer a tiny example if it helps, then stop talking.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR Q["a difference-between
question"] --> D["1 define both"] --> K["2 the key difference"] --> W["3 when to use each
plus a tiny example"]
diagram.caption: One shape for every theory question: define both, give the difference that matters, say when you would use each — in under thirty seconds.

examples.title: Four classic answers, checked in one query
examples.sql:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees) AS count_star,
       (SELECT COUNT(manager_id) FROM employees) AS count_column,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT location FROM departments
                              UNION SELECT city FROM customers) AS u) AS union_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT location FROM departments
                              UNION ALL SELECT city FROM customers) AS ua) AS union_all_rows;
examples.note: `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(column)` skips NULLs; UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps them.

keyPoints: Shape: define both, the key difference, when to use each.
Keep it under thirty seconds, then stop.
Use a tiny example from tables you know, like employees and orders.
Revise the follow-up questions below out loud until each answer is automatic.
mistakes: Rambling for two minutes on a thirty-second question.
Giving only one side ("HAVING is for groups") without the contrast.
Memorising words without the reason, then freezing when the question is rephrased.
topics.interviewAnswer: For any "what's the difference" question I give a one-line definition of each, the difference that matters in practice, and when I would choose each. For example: WHERE filters rows before grouping and can't use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can — so row conditions go in WHERE and aggregate conditions in HAVING.

followUps.q: WHERE vs HAVING?
followUps.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping and can't use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can.

followUps.q: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN?
followUps.a: INNER keeps only rows that match on both sides; LEFT keeps every left row and fills NULLs where the right has no match.

followUps.q: UNION vs UNION ALL?
followUps.a: UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster.

followUps.q: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP?
followUps.a: DELETE removes chosen rows (WHERE, logged, can roll back); TRUNCATE empties the whole table fast; DROP removes the table itself.

followUps.q: Primary key vs unique key?
followUps.a: Both forbid duplicates. One primary key per table and never NULL; many unique keys allowed, and they usually allow NULLs.

followUps.q: RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER?
followUps.a: ROW_NUMBER: 1, 2, 3, 4. RANK: ties share, then a gap (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK: ties share, no gap (1, 2, 2, 3).

followUps.q: `COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(column)`?
followUps.a: `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(column)` counts rows where that column isn't NULL.

followUps.q: What does NULL = NULL return?
followUps.a: NULL (unknown), not true. Use IS NULL.

followUps.q: Subquery vs CTE?
followUps.a: Both are queries inside a query. A CTE is named, defined at the top, reusable within the statement, can be recursive, and reads top to bottom.

followUps.q: Correlated vs non-correlated subquery?
followUps.a: A non-correlated subquery runs once on its own; a correlated one uses columns from the outer row, so logically it runs once per outer row.

followUps.q: Clustered vs non-clustered index?
followUps.a: A clustered index is the table itself stored in key order (one per table); a non-clustered index is a separate sorted structure pointing to rows.

followUps.q: Why not index every column?
followUps.a: Each index slows down every insert, update and delete and uses space; index the columns you filter, join and sort by.

followUps.q: What is normalisation?
followUps.a: Designing tables so each fact is stored once (usually to 3NF), which prevents update anomalies, at the cost of more joins.

followUps.q: What does ACID stand for?
followUps.a: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees of a database transaction.

followUps.q: View vs materialised view?
followUps.a: A view is a saved query, always fresh, no stored data; a materialised view stores the result, fast to read, stale until refreshed.

followUps.q: OLTP vs OLAP?
followUps.a: OLTP systems handle many small, fast reads and writes (an app's database, normalised); OLAP systems handle big analytical queries over lots of history (a data warehouse, often denormalised).

practice.explain: Answer five follow-up questions below out loud, without opening the answers, each in under thirty seconds.
practice.write: Write one query that shows the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN on departments and employees, as two counts in one row.
practice.predict: What does `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city), COUNT(city), COUNT(*) FROM customers;` return?
practice.edge: Explain why `SELECT DISTINCT` and `GROUP BY` can give the same rows, and when they don't.

resources.title: Mode SQL Tutorial — The SQL Tutorial for Data Analysis

explain.answer:
Five, each in one breath:

• WHERE vs HAVING: WHERE filters rows before grouping and can't use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, so it can use COUNT and SUM.
• INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN: INNER keeps only rows that match on both sides; LEFT keeps every row of the left table and fills NULLs where the right has no match. Use LEFT for "including the ones with none".
• UNION vs UNION ALL: both stack two results; UNION removes duplicate rows (extra work), UNION ALL keeps them all and is faster. Default to UNION ALL unless you need distinct rows.
• DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP: DELETE removes chosen rows and can be rolled back; TRUNCATE empties the whole table fast; DROP removes the table itself.
• RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER: ROW_NUMBER gives 1, 2, 3, 4 with no ties; RANK lets ties share and then skips (1, 2, 2, 4); DENSE_RANK lets ties share without skipping (1, 2, 2, 3).

write.answer:
Each count is a scalar subquery, so both fit in one row.

The INNER JOIN gives 7: every employee who has a department (Gus has none, so he isn't paired). The LEFT JOIN from departments gives 8: the same 7, plus one row for HR, which has nobody, with NULL employee columns. The difference is exactly the unmatched rows on the left side.

query.sql:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM departments d
          JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS inner_join_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM departments d
          LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS left_join_rows;

predict.answer:
3, 5 and 6.

• `COUNT(DISTINCT city)`: London, Leeds and Bristol. The NULL is not counted.
• `COUNT(city)`: every city that isn't NULL, duplicates included: Zoe is the only one missing, so 5.
• `COUNT(*)`: every row, 6.

query.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city), COUNT(city), COUNT(*) FROM customers;

edge.answer:
When you select only the grouped columns, they mean the same thing: `SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees` and `SELECT dept_id FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id` both give one row per department (with one row for NULL). Many databases even run them the same way.

They differ when:
• You want something per group. GROUP BY can count, sum or average each group (below); DISTINCT can only remove duplicates.
• You filter groups. HAVING works with GROUP BY; DISTINCT has nothing like it.
• DISTINCT applies to every selected column, including calculated ones, and runs after SELECT. GROUP BY groups by what you list, and everything else in SELECT must be aggregated.
• The output order: neither guarantees one without ORDER BY.

query.sql:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS people
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;

topics.name: The second highest salary (and the Nth)
topics.definition: Return the second highest salary from employees. If there is no second highest salary, return NULL.
topics.problem: Whether you think about ties and about "no answer". LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 is wrong when two people share the top salary, and many answers return no row at all instead of NULL.
topics.spot: The words "second highest", "Nth largest", "third most recent". The answer is a value, not a person, so ties must collapse: think DENSE_RANK or DISTINCT.
approach: Ask: if two people tie for the highest salary, is the "second highest" the next different amount? (Usually yes.)
Rank the distinct salaries from highest down, so ties share a rank and no number is skipped.
Keep the salary ranked 2.
Wrap it so that "no such salary" gives one row containing NULL, not an empty result — an aggregate like MAX does this.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR S["salaries high to low
95000 · 80000 · 70000 · 70000 · 60000 …"] --> R["DENSE_RANK
1 · 2 · 3 · 3 · 4 …"] R --> K["keep rank 2
80000"]
diagram.caption: DENSE_RANK gives tied salaries the same rank without leaving gaps, so "rank 2" is always the second-highest different amount.

solution.title: Solution: DENSE_RANK, wrapped in MAX
solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
)
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 2;
solution.note: MAX over no rows returns NULL, so if there were no second salary you would still get one row with NULL. Change 2 to N for the Nth highest.

alternatives.title: Without window functions: the highest below the highest
alternatives.note: Short and clear for "second", but it doesn't generalise neatly to the Nth.

alternatives.title: DISTINCT with LIMIT and OFFSET, inside a scalar subquery
alternatives.note: DISTINCT makes ties collapse; the outer SELECT turns "no row" into NULL.

edgeCases: Ties for first: two people on 95000 — the answer is still the next different salary, 80000.
Fewer than two different salaries: return NULL, not an empty result.
NULL salaries: ignored by ranking and MAX, which is usually what you want — say so.
mistakes: `ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1` without DISTINCT: returns the top salary again when two people tie for first.
Using RANK: after a tie for first, there is no rank 2.
Returning an empty result when the question asked for NULL.
topics.interviewAnswer: I first confirm that ties should collapse, so the second highest is the second different amount. Then I rank salaries with DENSE_RANK in descending order — dense so a tie doesn't skip a number — and take rank 2. I wrap it in MAX so that if there is no second salary I return a single NULL instead of no rows, and for the Nth highest I just change the 2.

followUps.q: How would you return the employees who earn the second highest salary?
followUps.a: Keep the DENSE_RANK CTE with names in it and select every row `WHERE rnk = 2`.

followUps.q: Why DENSE_RANK and not RANK?
followUps.a: With RANK, a tie at the top makes the next rank 3, so rank 2 would not exist.

practice.explain: Explain why LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 can give the wrong answer here, using a tie example.
practice.write: Return the third highest salary, and then the second highest salary within each department.
practice.predict: If Hana's salary were changed to 95000, what would the solution return?
practice.edge: What does your query return on an empty employees table? Make sure it is one row with NULL.

explain.answer:
`ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1` takes the second row, not the second salary. With a tie at the top, the second row has the same salary as the first.

If Hana's salary were 95,000 too, the sorted salaries would be 95,000, 95,000, 70,000… The second row is 95,000: the highest again, not the second highest (which is 70,000). The query below makes that change and shows the wrong answer.

It has a second problem: when there is no second row, it returns no rows at all, while the question asks for NULL. `SELECT DISTINCT` inside a scalar subquery fixes both, and DENSE_RANK = 2 is clearer still.

write.answer:
The third highest is the same query with `WHERE rnk = 3`: 70,000 (after 95,000 and 80,000; Ben and Chen share it, and DENSE_RANK counts it once).

Per department, add PARTITION BY dept_id so each department ranks its own salaries. Starting from departments with a LEFT JOIN, and putting `rnk = 2` in the ON, keeps departments with no second salary: Marketing (only Fatima) and HR (nobody) show NULL, as the original question asks.

query.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT dept_id, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
  WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT d.dept_name, MAX(r.salary) AS second_highest
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN ranked r ON r.dept_id = d.dept_id AND r.rnk = 2
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
ORDER BY d.dept_id;

predict.answer: 70,000. Asha and Hana would both be on 95,000, and DENSE_RANK gives them both rank 1. The next different salary, 70,000 (Ben and Chen), gets rank 2.

edge.answer:
One row, with NULL. That is why the solution wraps the result in MAX: an aggregate with no GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, even when no rows match, and MAX of nothing is NULL.

Without the MAX (`SELECT salary FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 2`), an empty table would return no rows at all. Below, every employee is deleted first.

topics.name: Employees who earn more than their manager
topics.definition: Find every employee who earns more than their own manager. Show the employee's name and salary, and the manager's name and salary.
topics.problem: Whether you can treat one table as two — a self join — and read a self-referencing key the right way round.
topics.spot: "Their manager", "their parent", "the person who referred them" — a column pointing at another row of the same table.
approach: Notice that manager_id points to another row of employees.
Use the table twice: e for the employee, m for the manager.
Join with `m.emp_id = e.manager_id` (m is e's manager).
Keep rows where e.salary > m.salary. An inner join is fine here: people with no manager can't earn more than one.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR H["e: Hana · 80000
manager_id 2"] -->|"m.emp_id = e.manager_id"| B["m: Ben · 70000"] B --> C{"80000 more than 70000?"} C -->|"yes"| K["keep Hana"]
diagram.caption: Each employee row is paired with its manager's row from the same table, and the two salaries are compared side by side.

solution.title: Solution: a self join
solution.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary,
       m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary
ORDER BY e.name;

alternatives.title: A correlated subquery
alternatives.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT m.salary
  FROM employees m
  WHERE m.emp_id = e.manager_id
)
ORDER BY e.name;
alternatives.note: Works, but can't show the manager's name without another subquery. The self join is clearer.

edgeCases: Employees with no manager (Asha): the inner join drops them, which is correct here.
Equal salaries: "more than" means strictly greater, so a tie is not included — confirm with the interviewer.
A manager_id that points to a deleted employee: the inner join drops the row; a foreign key should prevent it.
mistakes: Joining the wrong way round (`e.emp_id = m.manager_id`), which compares people with their reports.
Leaving columns unprefixed, so name and salary are ambiguous.
topics.interviewAnswer: manager_id references the same table, so I self-join employees as e and m, matching the manager alias's emp_id to the employee's manager_id, and filter where the employee's salary is greater than the manager's. An inner join is right here because someone without a manager can't out-earn one.

followUps.q: How would you include the manager's manager?
followUps.a: Join employees a third time: `JOIN employees mm ON mm.emp_id = m.manager_id`, as a LEFT JOIN if the chain can end.

followUps.q: How would you count, per manager, how many reports earn more than them?
followUps.a: Same self join and filter, then GROUP BY m.emp_id, m.name with `COUNT(*)`.

practice.explain: Explain what each alias stands for and why the join condition is written that way round.
practice.write: Find employees who were hired before their manager.
practice.predict: If Eli's salary rose to 61000, which rows would the solution return?
practice.edge: Change the solution to also list employees with no manager, showing NULL for the manager columns.

explain.answer:
The table is used twice. e is the employee: the row we are asking about. m is the manager: a second copy of the same table, used to look up the boss.

`m.emp_id = e.manager_id` reads: "find the row in m whose id is the manager_id written on the employee's row". For Hana, manager_id is 2, so m is Ben's row.

Written the other way round, `e.emp_id = m.manager_id`, the roles swap: m becomes someone who reports to e. Then `e.salary > m.salary` would find managers who earn more than their reports, which is nearly everyone.

write.answer: The same self join, comparing hire dates instead of salaries. In this data nobody was hired before their manager: Asha (2019) came before everyone she manages, and so did Dara and Ben (2020). An empty result is the right answer here.

query.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.hire_date,
       m.name AS manager, m.hire_date AS manager_hired
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.hire_date < m.hire_date
ORDER BY e.name;

predict.answer: Two rows: Eli (61,000) over his manager Dara (60,000), and Hana (80,000) over Ben (70,000), as before. Sorted by name, Eli comes first.

query.sql:
UPDATE employees SET salary = 61000 WHERE name = 'Eli';
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary,
       m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary
ORDER BY e.name;

edge.answer: Use a LEFT JOIN so employees with no manager keep their row (with NULLs), and let them through the WHERE on purpose: `e.salary > m.salary` is unknown when m is NULL, so add `OR m.emp_id IS NULL`. Asha now appears with NULL manager columns, next to Hana.

query.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary,
       m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary OR m.emp_id IS NULL
ORDER BY e.name;

topics.name: Customers who have never had an order delivered
topics.definition: List every customer who has never had an order delivered — including customers who have never ordered at all.
topics.problem: Anti-joins, and the classic trap of putting a condition on the right-hand table in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN, which silently removes the customers you are looking for.
topics.spot: "Never", "no", "without", "haven't" — you are looking for something that isn't there.
approach: Start from customers, because every customer must be considered — including ones with no orders.
Look for a delivered order belonging to each customer.
Keep the customers for whom none exists: NOT EXISTS, or a LEFT JOIN with the status test inside ON and `WHERE o.order_id IS NULL`.
Check: Omar and the second Tom never ordered; Zoe only has a pending order.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["every customer"] --> Q{"any delivered order
for this customer?"} Q -->|"yes: Priya, Tom, Lena"| X["dropped"] Q -->|"no: Omar, Zoe, Tom 6"| K["kept"]
diagram.caption: For each customer, ask one question: does a delivered order exist? Keep the customers where the answer is no.

solution.title: Solution: NOT EXISTS
solution.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND o.status = 'delivered'
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

alternatives.title: LEFT JOIN with the condition in ON
alternatives.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
 AND o.status = 'delivered'
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
alternatives.note: The status test must be in ON. In WHERE, `o.status = 'delivered' AND o.order_id IS NULL` could never both be true, and the query would return nothing.

edgeCases: Customers with no orders at all: must be included — that is why we start from customers.
Customers whose only orders are cancelled or pending (Zoe): included.
Orders with a NULL status: they are not delivered, so they don't count — NOT EXISTS handles this correctly.
mistakes: `LEFT JOIN … WHERE o.status <> 'delivered'`: drops customers with no orders and keeps customers who also have delivered orders.
`WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered')` is fine here only because customer_id is NOT NULL in orders — say that out loud.
Starting from orders, which can never return customers who have no orders.
topics.interviewAnswer: This is an anti-join. I drive it from customers so customers with no orders are included, and keep those for which NOT EXISTS finds a delivered order. Equivalently, a LEFT JOIN with the status filter inside the ON clause and WHERE the order id IS NULL. The trap is putting the status filter in WHERE, which turns the left join into an inner join.

followUps.q: Why not NOT IN?
followUps.a: If the subquery could return a NULL, NOT IN returns nothing. NOT EXISTS is always safe.

followUps.q: How would you also show how many orders each of these customers has?
followUps.a: LEFT JOIN orders (all statuses) and `COUNT(o.order_id)`, grouped by customer, keeping the anti-join as a filter.

practice.explain: Explain why the status condition must go in ON, not WHERE, in the LEFT JOIN version.
practice.write: List products that have never been part of a delivered order.
practice.predict: What does the LEFT JOIN version return if you move the status test into WHERE?
practice.edge: What should happen to a customer whose only order has a NULL status? Does your query do that?

explain.answer:
In the LEFT JOIN version, the ON decides what counts as a match: "an order of this customer that was delivered". A customer with no delivered order finds no match, so they get one row with NULLs, and `WHERE o.order_id IS NULL` keeps exactly those customers.

Move the status test into the WHERE and it runs after the join, on every row. A customer whose orders are all pending gets matched to those orders (not NULL, so `IS NULL` drops them), and a customer with no orders has a NULL status, which fails `o.status = 'delivered'`. Every row fails one test or the other, so nothing comes back.

write.answer: For each product, look for any item line in a delivered order. Only the phone case has none: it has never been sold at all. Every other product appears in at least one delivered order.

query.sql:
SELECT p.product_name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id
    AND o.status = 'delivered'
)
ORDER BY p.product_name;

predict.answer: No rows at all. After the LEFT JOIN, every row either has an order (so order_id is not NULL) or has no order (so status is NULL, and `NULL = 'delivered'` isn't true). A row would need a delivered status and a NULL order_id at once, which is impossible. A filter on the right-hand table in WHERE quietly cancels the LEFT JOIN.

query.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered' AND o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

edge.answer:
They have never had an order delivered, so they should be listed. (In this database status is NOT NULL, so it can't happen, but it is worth checking.)

The NOT EXISTS solution gets it right: inside the subquery, `NULL = 'delivered'` is not true, so no delivered order is found, NOT EXISTS is true, and the customer is listed. The LEFT JOIN version also lists them, because the ON finds no match.

The version that gets it wrong flips the logic: "customers who have an order WHERE status <> 'delivered'". `NULL <> 'delivered'` is not true either, so that customer would be missed. Whenever you write a negative test, ask what it does with NULL.

topics.name: Find duplicate emails, then remove the duplicates
topics.definition: Find every email that belongs to more than one customer, with how many sign-ups it has. Then delete the duplicates, keeping the row with the lowest customer_id.
topics.problem: GROUP BY with HAVING, the ROW_NUMBER pattern for picking one row per group, and writing a safe DELETE.
approach: Group by the column that should be unique (email).
Keep groups with more than one row: HAVING `COUNT(*) > 1`.
To see the extra rows themselves, number the rows in each email group by customer_id and keep row numbers above 1.
To delete them, keep the `MIN(customer_id)` per email and delete everything else. Run it as a SELECT first.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR A["customers grouped by email"] --> T["tom@mail.com
id 2 · id 6"] A --> O["other emails
one row each"] T -->|"COUNT is 2"| D["duplicate:
keep id 2, remove id 6"]
diagram.caption: Grouping by email puts both of Tom's sign-ups in one group. A group of two is a duplicate; keep the lowest id and remove the rest.

solution.title: Solution: find them with GROUP BY and HAVING
solution.sql:
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS sign_ups
FROM customers
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY email;

alternatives.title: Show the extra rows with ROW_NUMBER
alternatives.sql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, name, email,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY customer_id) AS rn
  FROM customers
)
SELECT customer_id, name, email
FROM numbered
WHERE rn > 1
ORDER BY customer_id;
alternatives.note: These are the rows to remove: every row except the first in its email group.

alternatives.title: Delete the duplicates, keeping the lowest id
alternatives.note: NOT IN is safe here because `MIN(customer_id)` is never NULL. Then add a UNIQUE constraint on email so it can't happen again.

edgeCases: Case and spaces: 'Tom@mail.com ' and 'tom@mail.com' are different strings — normalise with `LOWER(TRIM(email))` if they should match.
NULL emails group together in GROUP BY: decide whether they count as duplicates.
If the duplicate rows have orders, the foreign key blocks the delete — re-point those orders to the kept id first.
mistakes: Using WHERE `COUNT(*) > 1` instead of HAVING.
Deleting without checking the rows first with a SELECT.
Fixing the data but not adding a UNIQUE constraint, so duplicates come straight back.
dialects: MySQL can't delete from a table while selecting from it in a subquery; wrap the subquery in another SELECT or use a DELETE … JOIN.
topics.interviewAnswer: To find duplicates I group by the column that should be unique and keep groups with HAVING COUNT star greater than one. To remove them I number the rows within each group with ROW_NUMBER — or take the minimum id per group — and delete every row that isn't the keeper, checking it as a SELECT first. Then I'd add a unique constraint, and I'd ask whether emails need normalising for case and spaces before comparing.

followUps.q: How would you keep the most recent sign-up instead?
followUps.a: Order the ROW_NUMBER by signup_date DESC (with customer_id as a tiebreaker), or keep `MAX(customer_id)` if ids grow over time.

followUps.q: What if the duplicate customer has orders?
followUps.a: Update those orders to point at the kept customer_id first, in the same transaction, then delete.

practice.explain: Explain why HAVING and not WHERE is used to find duplicates.
practice.write: Find customers who share the same name and city, and how many rows each pair has.
practice.predict: What would the first query return if Zoe's email were changed to 'priya@mail.com'?
practice.edge: Rewrite the duplicate check so 'TOM@mail.com' and 'tom@mail.com' count as the same email.

explain.answer:
A duplicate email is a fact about a group of rows ("this email appears more than once"), not about any single row. Looking at one row on its own, you can't tell whether its email is repeated.

WHERE runs before GROUP BY, one row at a time, so `COUNT(*)` doesn't exist yet there. GROUP BY email makes one group per email, and HAVING runs after it, so `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` can keep only the groups with more than one row.

write.answer:
Group by both columns and keep groups with more than one row. Only Tom in Leeds appears twice.

Note: GROUP BY puts NULLs together, so two people with the same name and no city would count as a pair. Usually that is what you want for finding duplicates, but say it out loud.

query.sql:
SELECT name, city, COUNT(*) AS sign_ups
FROM customers
GROUP BY name, city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY name, city;

predict.answer: Two rows: priya@mail.com with 2 sign-ups (Priya and now Zoe), and tom@mail.com with 2, as before. The query doesn't care that the names differ; it only groups by email.

edge.answer:
Group by a cleaned-up version of the email: `LOWER(TRIM(email))`. LOWER makes the case the same; TRIM removes stray spaces, another common cause of fake "different" emails. Below, Tom's second sign-up is changed to 'TOM@mail.com' and the two still count as one.

To stop it happening again, store emails lower-cased, and put a unique index on the lower-cased value (`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON customers (LOWER(email))`, or a COLLATE NOCASE column in SQLite).

topics.name: The highest-paid employee in each department
topics.definition: For each department, return the employee (or employees, if tied) with the highest salary. Show the department name, the employee's name and their salary.
topics.problem: The most common window-function question: top N per group, including how to handle ties and how to filter on a window function.
approach: Ask: if two people tie for top salary in a department, show both? (Yes here.)
Rank employees within each department by salary, highest first: `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC)`.
RANK keeps ties together; ROW_NUMBER would pick one at random.
Do the ranking in a CTE, then keep rank 1 outside it, and join departments for the name.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR E["employees"] --> P["PARTITION BY dept_id
ORDER BY salary DESC"] P --> D1["Engineering: Asha 1, Hana 2, Ben 3, Chen 3"] P --> D2["Sales: Dara 1, Eli 2"] P --> D3["Marketing: Fatima 1"] D1 --> K["keep rank 1 in each"] D2 --> K D3 --> K
diagram.caption: Rank inside each department separately, then keep the rows ranked 1. Every department gets its own number one.

solution.title: Solution: RANK in a CTE, filter outside
solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT d.dept_name, e.name, e.salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees e
  JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
)
SELECT dept_name, name, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY dept_name;

alternatives.title: Without window functions: match the department maximum
alternatives.sql:
SELECT d.dept_name, e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary = (
  SELECT MAX(e2.salary)
  FROM employees e2
  WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id
)
ORDER BY d.dept_name;
alternatives.note: Also keeps ties. Harder to extend to "top 3" than the window version.

edgeCases: Ties for the top: RANK (or DENSE_RANK) returns all of them; ROW_NUMBER returns one.
Departments with no employees (HR): not in the result. Ask whether they should appear with NULLs (then LEFT JOIN from departments).
Employees with no department (Gus): dropped by the inner join to departments.
mistakes: Putting the window function in WHERE.
`GROUP BY dept_id` with `MAX(salary)` and `name` in SELECT — the name isn't guaranteed to belong to the max.
Using ROW_NUMBER when ties should all be returned.
topics.interviewAnswer: This is top-N-per-group. I rank employees within each department with RANK partitioned by department and ordered by salary descending, in a CTE, then filter to rank one outside — window functions can't go in WHERE. I use RANK so tied top earners are all returned; if they wanted exactly one per department I'd switch to ROW_NUMBER with a tiebreaker. For "top three salaries" I'd use DENSE_RANK less than or equal to three.

followUps.q: How would you return the top 3 salaries in each department?
followUps.a: `DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) <= 3`, so that three different salary amounts are covered, with ties.

followUps.q: Why not GROUP BY dept_id with `MAX(salary)`?
followUps.a: That gives the top amount per department, but not who earns it. You would have to join back, and that is the alternative solution.

practice.explain: Explain why the rank must be computed in a CTE and filtered outside.
practice.write: Return the two highest-paid employees in each department, including ties.
practice.predict: What does the solution return if Hana's salary becomes 95000?
practice.edge: Change the query so HR appears with NULL name and salary.

resources.title: DataLemur — top N per group questions
Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL Window Functions

explain.answer:
Because of the order a query runs in. WHERE runs before SELECT, and window functions like RANK are worked out in the SELECT step. So when WHERE runs, the rank doesn't exist yet, and `WHERE RANK() OVER (…) = 1` is an error.

The fix is two steps: a CTE (or subquery) works out the rank for every row, and the outer query, which runs afterwards, filters on it like an ordinary column. (Some databases, such as Snowflake and BigQuery, add QUALIFY to filter on a window function directly.)

write.answer: Same as the solution, with `rnk <= 2`. RANK keeps ties: if two people shared second place, both would be included. Here Engineering gives Asha and Hana (Ben and Chen tie for third, so they are out), Sales gives Dara and Eli, and Marketing has only Fatima.

query.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT d.dept_name, e.name, e.salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees e
  JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
)
SELECT dept_name, name, salary, rnk
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY dept_name, rnk, name;

predict.answer:
Engineering now has two rows: Asha and Hana both earn 95,000, so both get rank 1. Marketing (Fatima) and Sales (Dara) are unchanged. 4 rows in all.

The ORDER BY below adds name, so the two Engineering rows always come out in the same order.

query.sql:
UPDATE employees SET salary = 95000 WHERE name = 'Hana';
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT d.dept_name, e.name, e.salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees e
  JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
)
SELECT dept_name, name, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY dept_name, name;

edge.answer: Start from departments and LEFT JOIN employees, and partition by d.dept_id (not e.dept_id, which is NULL for HR). HR gets one row with NULL name and salary; it is the only row in its partition, so its rank is 1 and it survives the filter.

query.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT d.dept_name, e.name, e.salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d.dept_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM departments d
  LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
)
SELECT dept_name, name, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY dept_name;

topics.name: Employees paid above their department's average
topics.definition: List employees whose salary is above the average salary of their own department, showing that average next to them.
topics.problem: Comparing a row with an aggregate of its own group — three valid ways (window function, join to a grouped subquery, correlated subquery) and knowing when each fits.
topics.pattern: Compare a row with its group
topics.spot: "Above the average for their…", "more than their team's…", "compared with others in the same…".
approach: Work out each department's average salary.
Put that average next to each employee — a window function does both in one step.
Keep rows where salary > the department average, filtering outside the CTE.
Decide what to do with Gus, who has no department.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR E["each employee"] --> A["AVG(salary) OVER
(PARTITION BY dept_id)"] A --> C{"salary above
dept average?"} C -->|"yes"| K["Asha, Hana, Dara"]
diagram.caption: Every employee gets their own department's average beside them; then a simple comparison picks those above it.

solution.title: Solution: a window average, filtered outside
solution.sql:
WITH with_avg AS (
  SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
         AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
)
SELECT name, dept_id, salary, dept_avg
FROM with_avg
WHERE salary > dept_avg
ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC;
solution.note: Fatima is alone in Marketing, so she equals her own average. Gus forms a NULL group of one and also equals his average.

alternatives.title: Join to a grouped subquery
alternatives.sql:
SELECT e.name, e.dept_id, e.salary, a.dept_avg
FROM employees e
JOIN (
  SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
  GROUP BY dept_id
) AS a ON a.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary > a.dept_avg
ORDER BY e.dept_id, e.salary DESC;
alternatives.note: Works in any database, even without window functions. Gus drops out here because NULL = NULL is not true in the join.

edgeCases: An employee with no department: the window version groups NULLs together; the join version drops them. Ask which is wanted.
A department of one person can never be above its own average.
"Above" means strictly greater; say so.
mistakes: `WHERE salary > AVG(salary)` — an aggregate in WHERE is not allowed, and it would be the company average anyway.
Comparing with the company average when the question says "their department".
Filtering on the window function in the same SELECT's WHERE.
topics.interviewAnswer: I need each employee's department average next to their row, so I compute AVG of salary over a window partitioned by department in a CTE, and keep rows where salary exceeds it. An equivalent approach joins employees to a grouped subquery of averages per department. I'd mention the NULL-department case, since the two approaches treat it differently.

followUps.q: How would you show how far above the average each person is, as a percentage?
followUps.a: `ROUND(100.0 * (salary - dept_avg) / dept_avg, 1)` in the outer query.

followUps.q: Which approach is fastest?
followUps.a: Usually the window function, because it reads the table once. The optimiser often makes them similar; check the plan.

practice.explain: Explain the three ways to compare a row with its group's average.
practice.write: List orders whose amount is above that customer's average order amount.
practice.predict: If Chen's salary rose to 90000, who would the solution return?
practice.edge: Make the solution exclude employees with no department, and explain why the join version already does.

explain.answer:
1. A window function: `AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)` puts the department average on every row; a CTE then filters `salary > dept_avg`. One pass, and the average is right there to show.
2. Join to a grouped subquery: `SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) … GROUP BY dept_id` makes one row per department, then you join it to employees on dept_id and compare. Works in every database, even ones without window functions.
3. A correlated subquery: `WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id)`. Reads naturally, but is worked out once per row (good optimisers rewrite it), and the average isn't available to display.

write.answer: Partition the average by customer instead of department. Priya averages 85 (425 ÷ 5), so orders 101 (120) and 105 (150) are above it; Tom averages 137.5, so 104 (200) is. Lena's average is 60 (the NULL order is skipped), and her only amount equals it, so nothing of hers is above.

query.sql:
WITH with_avg AS (
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
         AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_avg
  FROM orders
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, customer_avg
FROM with_avg
WHERE amount > customer_avg
ORDER BY customer_id, order_id;

predict.answer: Asha, Chen and Dara. Engineering's average rises to (95,000 + 70,000 + 90,000 + 80,000) ÷ 4 = 83,750. Asha (95,000) and Chen (90,000) are above it; Hana (80,000) drops below. Sales is unchanged, so Dara is still above 52,500.

edge.answer:
Add `WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL` inside the CTE, so Gus is never given a "department" of his own. (In the window version, PARTITION BY puts all NULLs in one group, so Gus is compared with himself; he isn't above his own average, so he doesn't appear today, but only by luck: two employees with no department would be compared with each other.)

The join version excludes him already: it joins on `a.dept_id = e.dept_id`, and `NULL = NULL` is not true, so Gus's row finds no partner and the join drops it.

query.sql:
WITH with_avg AS (
  SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
         AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
  WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT name, dept_id, salary, dept_avg
FROM with_avg
WHERE salary > dept_avg
ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC;

topics.name: Month-over-month revenue growth
topics.definition: For each month, show the revenue and the percentage change from the previous month, rounded to one decimal place.
topics.problem: Aggregating to the right grain first, then LAG, then safe percentage maths — integer division and division by zero included.
topics.spot: "Growth", "change from the previous", "month over month", "compared with last week".
approach: Aggregate orders to one row per month first (a CTE).
Use `LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)` to bring last month's revenue onto each row.
Growth % = 100.0 × (this − last) ÷ last. Use 100.0 to avoid integer division and `NULLIF(last, 0)` to avoid dividing by zero.
The first month has no previous month, so its growth is NULL.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR O["orders"] --> M["monthly revenue
Jan 445 · Feb 210 · Mar 138"] M --> L["LAG brings the month before
Feb sees 445 · Mar sees 210"] L --> G["growth %
Feb −52.8 · Mar −34.3"]
diagram.caption: First shrink orders to one row per month, then let each month look back at the one before it with LAG, then do the percentage maths.

solution.title: Solution: monthly CTE, then LAG
solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

alternatives.title: A named window, and a guard against dividing by zero
alternatives.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER w)
             / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER w, 0), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY month)
ORDER BY month;
alternatives.note: WINDOW w AS (…) names the window once. NULLIF turns a previous revenue of 0 into NULL, so the growth is NULL instead of an error.

edgeCases: The first month: no previous month, so NULL.
A previous month with 0 revenue: divide by `NULLIF(…, 0)`.
A month with no orders at all has no row, so LAG would compare with two months ago — build a month list and LEFT JOIN if that matters.
mistakes: Using LAG on the order rows instead of the monthly totals.
`(revenue - prev) / prev * 100` with whole numbers: integer division gives 0 or -1.
Grouping by order_date instead of the month.
dialects: PostgreSQL: `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)` for the month. MySQL: `DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m')`. SQL Server: `FORMAT(order_date, 'yyyy-MM')` or `DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d), MONTH(d), 1)`.
topics.interviewAnswer: I aggregate to one row per month in a CTE, then use LAG over month order to bring the previous month's revenue alongside, and compute 100.0 times the difference divided by the previous value, rounded. I guard the division with NULLIF for zero months, note that the first month is NULL, and would fill in missing months with a calendar join if gaps are possible.

followUps.q: How would you do year-over-year growth on monthly data?
followUps.a: `LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month)` — twelve rows back — assuming every month is present.

followUps.q: How would you compute it per product category?
followUps.a: Group by category and month, then `LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY month)`.

practice.explain: Explain why you aggregate to months before using LAG.
practice.write: Compute month-over-month growth in the number of orders, not revenue.
practice.predict: What would growth_pct be for March if March revenue were 315?
practice.edge: Show what goes wrong if you remove the 100.0 and use whole-number maths, then fix it.

resources.title: Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL Window Functions: LAG and LEAD

explain.answer:
LAG returns the previous row, so the rows must be the things you want to compare: months. On the raw orders table, the previous row is the previous order, so "growth" would compare one order with another order.

So first collapse to one row per month (GROUP BY month, SUM(amount)) in a CTE, and only then use LAG over those monthly rows. The previous row is now the previous month.

(The order of the steps matters for a second reason too: window functions run after GROUP BY, so even in one query, LAG over a SUM is computed on the grouped rows.)

write.answer:
Swap SUM(amount) for COUNT(*). January has 4 orders, February 3 (−25%) and March 3 (0%).

One question to ask: do cancelled orders count? Order 106 is in February's 3. Excluding it would make February 2 and March +50%.

query.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
         COUNT(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)
)
SELECT month, orders,
       ROUND(100.0 * (orders - LAG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / LAG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

predict.answer:
+50.0. February's revenue is 210, so (315 − 210) ÷ 210 = 105 ÷ 210 = 0.5, which is 50%.

The query below makes March 315 by adding 177 to order 110 (138 + 177 = 315).

query.sql:
UPDATE orders SET amount = amount + 177 WHERE order_id = 110;
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

edge.answer:
Revenue is a whole number, so with whole-number maths the division throws away the fraction. (210 − 445) ÷ 445 is −0.53, which becomes 0, and 0 × 100 = 0: February shows 0% growth instead of −52.8%. March does the same. Nothing errors; the numbers are just wrong.

The fix is to make one side a decimal before dividing: multiply by 100.0 first, as the solution does. Multiplying by 100 (whole) first would be closer but still cut the decimals off: −52 instead of −52.8.

query.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
         / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) * 100 AS whole_number_maths,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

topics.name: Each customer's first order
topics.definition: For each customer who has ordered, show their first order — its id, date and amount — and how many days after signing up they placed it.
topics.problem: Picking exactly one row per group (the first event per user) with ROW_NUMBER, and joining back for extra columns. Used for activation, onboarding and funnel questions.
topics.spot: "First purchase", "most recent login", "latest status", "earliest", one per user.
approach: Number each customer's orders by date: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id)`.
Add order_id as a tiebreaker in case two orders share a date.
Keep row number 1 in an outer query.
Join customers for the name and sign-up date, and work out the days between.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR O["Priya's orders by date
101 · 102 · 103 · 105 · 109"] --> R["ROW_NUMBER
1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5"] R --> K["keep 1:
order 101 on 2024-01-06"]
diagram.caption: Number each customer's orders from oldest to newest, then keep number 1. The same pattern with DESC gives the latest order.

solution.title: Solution: ROW_NUMBER = 1
solution.sql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT c.name, n.order_id, n.order_date, n.amount,
       julianday(n.order_date) - julianday(c.signup_date) AS days_to_first_order
FROM numbered n
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = n.customer_id
WHERE n.rn = 1
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
solution.note: Lena's first order is the cancelled one with no amount. Ask whether "first order" should mean first delivered order.

alternatives.title: MIN date, then match it
alternatives.sql:
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date = (
  SELECT MIN(o2.order_date)
  FROM orders o2
  WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
alternatives.note: Returns two rows for a customer with two orders on their first day. ROW_NUMBER with a tiebreaker guarantees one.

edgeCases: Two orders on the same first day: the tiebreaker (order_id) decides; say which one you keep.
Cancelled first orders: confirm whether they count.
Customers with no orders: not in the result — LEFT JOIN from customers if they should appear.
mistakes: `GROUP BY customer_id` with `MIN(order_date)` and `amount` in SELECT — the amount isn't tied to the first order.
Forgetting PARTITION BY, so only one order in the whole table gets number 1.
No tiebreaker in ROW_NUMBER, so the answer can change between runs.
dialects: PostgreSQL has a shortcut: `SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) * FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, order_date, order_id`.
Days between: PostgreSQL `order_date - signup_date` for DATE columns; MySQL `DATEDIFF(order_date, signup_date)`.
topics.interviewAnswer: For first-per-group I number rows with ROW_NUMBER partitioned by customer and ordered by date with the order id as a tiebreaker, keep row number one in an outer query, and join customers for the sign-up date to compute days to first order. I'd confirm whether cancelled orders count, and mention that a MIN-date join can return duplicates on ties while ROW_NUMBER always returns exactly one.

followUps.q: How would you get each customer's latest order instead?
followUps.a: Order the ROW_NUMBER by order_date DESC, order_id DESC and keep row 1.

followUps.q: How would you find each customer's first delivered order?
followUps.a: Add `WHERE status = 'delivered'` inside the CTE, before numbering.

practice.explain: Explain why ROW_NUMBER needs a tiebreaker here, with an example.
practice.write: For each customer, show their latest order and its status.
practice.predict: What would the solution return for Lena if the CTE only numbered delivered orders?
practice.edge: Change the solution so customers with no orders appear with NULLs.

explain.answer:
ROW_NUMBER must give exactly one row number 1 per customer. If two orders share the earliest date, ordering by date alone leaves the tie unbroken, and the database may pick either one, and pick differently on another run or after an index changes. The answer looks fine but isn't repeatable.

Example: if Priya had placed orders 101 and 111 both on 2024-01-06, `ORDER BY order_date` could return either as her first order. Adding `order_id` as a second sort key (`ORDER BY order_date, order_id`) makes 101 win every time.

write.answer: Number each customer's orders newest first, with order_id as the tiebreaker, and keep number 1. Zoe's latest (and only) order is still pending.

query.sql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, status,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT c.name, n.order_id, n.order_date, n.status
FROM numbered n
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = n.customer_id
WHERE n.rn = 1
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

predict.answer:
Lena's first delivered order is 107 (20 February, £60), not the cancelled 106, so her days to first order become 21 instead of 13 (she signed up on 30 January).

And Zoe disappears: her only order is pending, so she has no delivered orders to number.

query.sql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS rn
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'delivered'
)
SELECT c.name, n.order_id, n.order_date, n.amount,
       julianday(n.order_date) - julianday(c.signup_date) AS days_to_first_order
FROM numbered n
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = n.customer_id
WHERE n.rn = 1
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

edge.answer: Start from customers and LEFT JOIN the numbered orders. The `n.rn = 1` test must go in the ON: in the WHERE, it would be NULL for customers with no orders and would drop them again. Omar and the second Tom now appear with NULLs.

query.sql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT c.name, n.order_id, n.order_date, n.amount,
       julianday(n.order_date) - julianday(c.signup_date) AS days_to_first_order
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN numbered n ON n.customer_id = c.customer_id AND n.rn = 1
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

topics.name: Streaks: orders on consecutive days (gaps and islands)
topics.definition: Find every streak where a customer ordered on two or more consecutive days. Show the customer, the first and last day of the streak, and its length in days.
topics.problem: The "gaps and islands" technique, which turns consecutive runs into groups — a favourite hard question for login streaks, consecutive wins and uninterrupted sessions.
approach: Reduce to one row per customer per day (DISTINCT), so two orders on one day don't break the count.
Number each customer's days in order with ROW_NUMBER.
Subtract the row number from the date (as a day number). Consecutive days give the same result — that value labels the island.
Group by customer and that label: MIN date, MAX date and COUNT give the streak. Keep streaks of 2 or more.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR D["Priya's days
01-06 · 01-07 · 01-08 · 02-02 · 03-10"] --> N["minus row number
1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5"] N --> G["labels
01-05 · 01-05 · 01-05 · 01-29 · 03-05"] G --> I["same label = one streak
01-06 to 01-08: 3 days"]
diagram.caption: Day by day the date goes up by 1 and so does the row number, so their difference stays the same across a run. A gap breaks the run and changes the label.

solution.title: Solution: date minus row number
solution.sql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, order_date
  FROM orders
),
labelled AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_date,
         julianday(order_date)
           - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS island
  FROM days
)
SELECT c.name, MIN(l.order_date) AS streak_start, MAX(l.order_date) AS streak_end,
       COUNT(*) AS days_in_a_row
FROM labelled l
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = l.customer_id
GROUP BY l.customer_id, c.name, l.island
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY days_in_a_row DESC, c.name;

alternatives.title: Flag each new streak with LAG, then number the streaks
alternatives.sql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, order_date
  FROM orders
),
flagged AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_date,
         CASE WHEN julianday(order_date)
                 - julianday(LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)) = 1
              THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS starts_streak
  FROM days
),
numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_date,
         SUM(starts_streak) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS streak_id
  FROM flagged
)
SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS streak_start, MAX(order_date) AS streak_end,
       COUNT(*) AS days_in_a_row
FROM numbered
GROUP BY customer_id, streak_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY days_in_a_row DESC;
alternatives.note: Longer, but easy to explain: a row starts a new streak when yesterday is missing, and a running SUM of those starts numbers the streaks.

edgeCases: Several orders on one day: DISTINCT first, or the row numbers jump and break the streak.
Streaks that cross a month or year: day numbers (julianday, or date arithmetic) handle that; string tricks don't.
"Longest streak per customer": wrap the result and keep the max length per customer, deciding how to break ties.
mistakes: Forgetting DISTINCT on (customer, day).
Subtracting the row number from a date string instead of a day number.
Using LAG alone, which finds pairs of consecutive days but not whole streaks.
dialects: PostgreSQL: `order_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…))::int` works directly on DATE values. SQL Server: `DATEADD(day, -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…), order_date)`.
topics.interviewAnswer: This is gaps and islands. I first reduce to distinct customer-days, number each customer's days with ROW_NUMBER, and subtract that number from the date: within a run of consecutive days both go up by one, so the difference is constant and labels the island. Grouping by customer and that label gives each streak's start, end and length, and HAVING keeps the ones of two days or more.

followUps.q: How would you find each customer's longest streak?
followUps.a: Wrap the streak query and use `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY days_in_a_row DESC) = 1`, or MAX per customer.

followUps.q: How would you find gaps — periods with no orders?
followUps.a: Use `LEAD(order_date)` to get the next date, and keep rows where the next date is more than one day later; the gap runs between them.

practice.explain: Explain, with Priya's dates, why date minus row number is constant inside a streak.
practice.write: Find the longest run of consecutive order days across all customers combined.
practice.predict: If Priya also ordered on 2024-01-09, what would the solution return?
practice.edge: Add a second order for Priya on 2024-01-07 and show that the solution still gives a 3-day streak. Then remove DISTINCT and see what breaks.

explain.answer:
Priya ordered on 6, 7 and 8 January, 2 February and 10 March. Number them 1 to 5 in date order, and subtract the number from the date:

• 6 Jan − 1 = 5 Jan
• 7 Jan − 2 = 5 Jan
• 8 Jan − 3 = 5 Jan
• 2 Feb − 4 = 29 Jan
• 10 Mar − 5 = 5 Mar

Inside a streak, the date goes up by one day and the row number goes up by one, so their difference stays the same: 5 January for all three. A gap makes the date jump by more than one while the row number still only goes up by one, so the difference changes. That difference is a label for each island: group by it, and each group is one streak.

write.answer: Same trick, without PARTITION BY: take every distinct date on which anyone ordered, number them in order, and group by date minus row number. The longest run is 6 to 8 January (3 days, all Priya's). Every other order date stands alone.

query.sql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT order_date
  FROM orders
),
labelled AS (
  SELECT order_date,
         julianday(order_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS island
  FROM days
)
SELECT MIN(order_date) AS run_start, MAX(order_date) AS run_end,
       COUNT(*) AS days_in_a_row
FROM labelled
GROUP BY island
ORDER BY days_in_a_row DESC, run_start
LIMIT 1;

predict.answer: One streak for Priya, now 4 days long: 6 to 9 January. 9 January is row 4, and 9 Jan − 4 = 5 Jan, the same label as the other three, so it joins their island.

query.sql:
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (111, 1, '2024-01-09', 10, 'delivered');
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, order_date
  FROM orders
),
labelled AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_date,
         julianday(order_date)
           - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS island
  FROM days
)
SELECT c.name, MIN(l.order_date) AS streak_start, MAX(l.order_date) AS streak_end,
       COUNT(*) AS days_in_a_row
FROM labelled l
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = l.customer_id
GROUP BY l.customer_id, c.name, l.island
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY days_in_a_row DESC, c.name;

edge.answer:
With DISTINCT, the second order on 7 January collapses into the same day, so the dates are still 6, 7, 8 and the solution still reports one 3-day streak.

Without DISTINCT (below), the days are 6, 7, 7, 8 numbered 1 to 4. The labels become 5 Jan, 5 Jan, 4 Jan, 4 Jan: the repeated day pushes the row number ahead of the date, so the streak splits into two "2-day streaks" (6–7 and 7–8), and 7 January is counted twice. DISTINCT matters because the trick assumes one row per day.

query.sql:
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (111, 1, '2024-01-07', 10, 'delivered');
WITH days AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_date
  FROM orders
),
labelled AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_date,
         julianday(order_date)
           - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS island
  FROM days
)
SELECT c.name, MIN(l.order_date) AS streak_start, MAX(l.order_date) AS streak_end,
       COUNT(*) AS days_in_a_row
FROM labelled l
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = l.customer_id
GROUP BY l.customer_id, c.name, l.island
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY streak_start;

topics.name: Products bought together
topics.definition: Find every pair of different products that appear in the same order, and count how many orders contain each pair. List each pair once.
topics.problem: A self join on a link table, and the trick for listing each pair once — the basis of "customers who bought this also bought…".
topics.pattern: Pairs within a group (self join with a < b)
topics.spot: "Bought together", "pairs", "in the same order / session / team", "co-occurrence".
approach: Join order_items to itself on the same order_id: every product paired with every other product in that order.
Keep only pairs where the first product's name is less than the second's — this removes self-pairs and mirrored duplicates (A–B and B–A).
Join products twice to get both names.
Group by the pair and count the orders.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR O["order 102
Desk lamp, Backpack"] --> P["self join on order_id
Backpack–Desk lamp
Desk lamp–Backpack
Backpack–Backpack …"] P -->|"keep name a less than name b"| K["Backpack–Desk lamp
once"]
diagram.caption: Joining an order's items to themselves makes every combination, including each item with itself and each pair twice. "a < b" keeps exactly one copy of each real pair.

solution.title: Solution: self join with a < b
solution.sql:
SELECT p1.product_name AS product_a, p2.product_name AS product_b,
       COUNT(*) AS orders_together
FROM order_items a
JOIN order_items b ON b.order_id = a.order_id
JOIN products p1   ON p1.product_id = a.product_id
JOIN products p2   ON p2.product_id = b.product_id
WHERE p1.product_name < p2.product_name
GROUP BY p1.product_name, p2.product_name
ORDER BY orders_together DESC, product_a, product_b;
solution.note: Each pair appears in one order in this small data set. On real data you would sort by orders_together and take the top pairs.

edgeCases: The same product twice in one order: order_items has one row per product per order, so it can't pair with itself here — but say how you would handle it.
Big orders make many pairs (n items → n × (n − 1) / 2 pairs), so this can get expensive on real data.
Pairs vs. lift: "bought together most" favours popular products; analysts often normalise by each product's own popularity.
mistakes: Using `<>` instead of `<`, which lists every pair twice.
Joining on product_id instead of order_id, which pairs a product with itself across orders.
Counting rows when an order could contain a pair more than once — use `COUNT(DISTINCT a.order_id)` if so.
topics.interviewAnswer: I self-join the order items table on order_id so every product is paired with every other product in the same order, filter with product a less than product b to drop self-pairs and mirrored duplicates, join product names, and count orders per pair. I'd note that the number of pairs grows quadratically with basket size, so on big data I might limit to recent orders or popular products.

followUps.q: Why `<` and not `<>`?
followUps.a: `<>` removes self-pairs but keeps both A–B and B–A. `<` keeps exactly one ordering of each pair.

followUps.q: How would you find triples bought together?
followUps.a: Join order_items three times on order_id with a < b < c, then group by all three.

practice.explain: Explain what the self join produces before the WHERE, for order 102.
practice.write: For each product, list how many different products it has ever been bought with.
practice.predict: How many rows does the self join `order_items a JOIN order_items b ON b.order_id = a.order_id` produce before any WHERE?
practice.edge: If an order could contain the same product on two rows, how would you stop it pairing with itself and double-counting?

explain.answer:
Order 102 has two item lines: product 4 (desk lamp) and product 5 (backpack). Joining order_items to itself on order_id pairs every line of the order with every line of the same order, 2 × 2 = 4 rows: (lamp, lamp), (lamp, backpack), (backpack, lamp), (backpack, backpack).

Two of those are a product paired with itself, and the other two are the same pair in both orders. `WHERE p1.product_name < p2.product_name` removes both problems at once: a name is never less than itself, and of (lamp, backpack) and (backpack, lamp) only one has the names in alphabetical order. One row is left: (Backpack, Desk lamp).

query.sql:
SELECT a.order_id, a.product_id AS a_product, b.product_id AS b_product
FROM order_items a
JOIN order_items b ON b.order_id = a.order_id
WHERE a.order_id = 102
ORDER BY a.product_id, b.product_id;

write.answer: Pair each product's item lines with the other lines of the same order (`b.product_id <> a.product_id`), and count distinct partners. LEFT JOINs keep the products with no partners: the headphones are often bought alone, and the phone case has never been bought at all.

query.sql:
SELECT p.product_name, COUNT(DISTINCT b.product_id) AS bought_with
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items a ON a.product_id = p.product_id
LEFT JOIN order_items b ON b.order_id = a.order_id AND b.product_id <> a.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
ORDER BY bought_with DESC, p.product_name;

predict.answer: 24. Each order contributes (its number of item lines)², because every line is paired with every line of the same order, itself included. Orders 101, 104, 107 and 108 have 1 line each (1 row each); orders 102, 103, 105, 109 and 110 have 2 lines each (4 rows each). 4 × 1 + 5 × 4 = 24.

edge.answer:
Two separate problems, two fixes:

• Self-pairs: compare product ids, not rows. `a.product_id < b.product_id` can never pair a product with itself, even if it appears on two rows of the order (two lines with the same product have equal ids, so `<` is false).
• Double counting: the same pair would come out several times for one order (2 lines × 1 line = 2 rows). Count orders, not rows: `COUNT(DISTINCT a.order_id)`. Or remove the duplicates first, in a CTE: `SELECT DISTINCT order_id, product_id FROM order_items`, then self-join that.

In this database it can't happen, because the primary key (order_id, product_id) allows one row per product per order. But many real order tables have no such key.

topics.name: Which products make up 80% of revenue? (share of total)
topics.definition: Show each product's revenue, its percentage of total revenue, and the running (cumulative) percentage from the best seller down. Then list the products that bring in the first 80% of revenue.
topics.problem: Window aggregates over the whole result (share of total), a running total with an explicit ROWS frame, and turning a cumulative share into a filter — the classic Pareto analysis.
topics.pattern: Share of total and cumulative share
topics.spot: "Percentage of total", "share", "contribution", "cumulative", "top products making up X%".
approach: Total revenue per product in a CTE: `SUM(quantity × price)`.
Share of total: revenue ÷ `SUM(revenue) OVER ()`, times 100.0.
Cumulative share: a running SUM ordered by revenue descending, with ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, divided by the total.
For "the first 80%": keep products whose revenue before them is still under 80% of the total.

diagram.code:
xychart-beta
  title "Cumulative share of revenue"
  x-axis ["Headphones", "Desk lamp", "Backpack", "Mug", "Notebook", "Pen"]
  y-axis "Cumulative %" 0 --> 100
  bar [55.5, 74.4, 89.5, 95.6, 98.7, 100]
diagram.caption: Sorted from best seller down, the running share climbs fast and then flattens. The first three products already pass 80% — that is the Pareto pattern.

solution.title: Solution: share and running share with window functions
solution.sql:
WITH product_revenue AS (
  SELECT p.product_name, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  GROUP BY p.product_name
)
SELECT product_name, revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
             / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1) AS cumulative_pct
FROM product_revenue
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

alternatives.title: The products that make up the first 80%
alternatives.sql:
WITH product_revenue AS (
  SELECT p.product_name, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  GROUP BY p.product_name
),
running AS (
  SELECT product_name, revenue,
