         SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) - revenue AS revenue_before
  FROM product_revenue
)
SELECT product_name, revenue
FROM running
WHERE revenue_before < 0.8 * (SELECT SUM(revenue) FROM product_revenue)
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
alternatives.note: A product is in the first 80% if the revenue before it hadn't reached 80% yet. Backpack starts at 74.4%, so it is the one that crosses the line.

edgeCases: Ties in revenue: the running total needs a tiebreaker (e.g. product name), or tied products share a RANGE frame.
Products that never sold (the phone case) don't appear; LEFT JOIN from products if they should show 0%.
Rounding: the rounded percentages may not add up to exactly 100.
mistakes: Integer division: `revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER ()` is 0 without the 100.0.
Leaving the frame as the default RANGE, so tied revenues get the same cumulative value.
Filtering `cumulative_pct <= 80`, which drops the product that crosses 80% — usually it should be included.
topics.interviewAnswer: I total revenue per product in a CTE, then divide each by SUM over an empty window for the share of total, and use a running SUM ordered by revenue descending with an explicit ROWS frame for the cumulative share. To list the products making up the first 80%, I keep those whose revenue before them is still under 80% of the total, which includes the product that crosses the line.

followUps.q: How would you show each product's share within its own category?
followUps.a: Divide by `SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category)` instead of `OVER ()`.

followUps.q: Why ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING rather than the default?
followUps.a: The default RANGE frame lumps tied values together; ROWS adds one product at a time.

practice.explain: Explain the difference between the pct_of_total and cumulative_pct columns.
practice.write: Do the same analysis for customers: each customer's share of total spend and the cumulative share.
practice.predict: Which products would be in "the first 90% of revenue"?
practice.edge: Make the phone case appear with 0 revenue and 0%, without breaking the cumulative column.

resources.title: Mode SQL Tutorial — SQL Window Functions

explain.answer:
pct_of_total is each product on its own: its revenue ÷ total revenue. The headphones bring in 440 of 793, so 55.5%. These add up to 100% across all rows.

cumulative_pct is a running total: this product plus every product above it in the list, ÷ total revenue. It only grows as you go down: 55.5% after the headphones, 74.4% once the desk lamp is added, 89.5% after the backpack, and 100% at the last row. It answers "how much of revenue do the top N products bring in?", which is what the 80% question needs.

write.answer: Same structure, with customers instead of products: total each customer's spend, then divide by the grand total (empty OVER) and by the running total (ordered OVER). Priya alone is 53.6% of all spending, and Priya and Tom together are 88.3%.

query.sql:
WITH customer_spend AS (
  SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS spend
  FROM orders o
  JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
)
SELECT name, spend,
       ROUND(100.0 * spend / SUM(spend) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(spend) OVER (ORDER BY spend DESC ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
             / SUM(spend) OVER (), 1) AS cumulative_pct
FROM customer_spend
ORDER BY spend DESC;

predict.answer:
Headphones, desk lamp, backpack and mug.

The first three only reach 89.5%, just short of 90%, so you need the mug too (it takes the total to 95.6%). The rule in the alternative query is "keep a product if the revenue before it was still under the target"; with 0.9 instead of 0.8, the mug passes (89.5% before it) and the notebook doesn't (95.6% before it).

query.sql:
WITH product_revenue AS (
  SELECT p.product_name, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  GROUP BY p.product_name
),
running AS (
  SELECT product_name, revenue,
         SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) - revenue AS revenue_before
  FROM product_revenue
)
SELECT product_name, revenue
FROM running
WHERE revenue_before < 0.9 * (SELECT SUM(revenue) FROM product_revenue)
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

edge.answer:
Start from products with a LEFT JOIN, so the phone case has a row, and COALESCE its NULL revenue to 0. A zero adds nothing to any sum, so the totals and the running column are unchanged: the phone case sorts last, with 0% and a cumulative 100%.

Add product_name to both ORDER BYs (the window's and the query's). That way two products with equal revenue, such as several unsold ones at 0, always come out in the same order, and the running total doesn't depend on chance.

query.sql:
WITH product_revenue AS (
  SELECT p.product_name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * p.price), 0) AS revenue
  FROM products p
  LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  GROUP BY p.product_name
)
SELECT product_name, revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_name ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
             / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1) AS cumulative_pct
FROM product_revenue
ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_name;

topics.name: Retention: who came back within 30 days?
topics.definition: Of the customers who placed an order, what percentage placed another order within 30 days of their first one?
topics.problem: Cohort-style thinking: anchor each user on their first event, look for a later event within a window, and compute a rate — the core of product and growth analytics interviews.
topics.pattern: Retention (first event, then a later event within N days)
approach: Find each customer's first order date (MIN per customer).
For each customer, check whether any later order falls within 30 days of that first date.
Turn that into 1 or 0 per customer (MAX of a CASE).
Rate = 100.0 × customers who came back ÷ customers who ordered.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR F["first order per customer"] --> P["Priya: next order after 1 day"] F --> T["Tom: after 40 days"] F --> L["Lena: after 8 days"] F --> Z["Zoe: no second order"] P --> R["came back within 30 days:
Priya, Lena
2 of 4 = 50%"] L --> R
diagram.caption: Anchor each customer on their first order, then ask one yes-or-no question: was there another order within 30 days? The share of yeses is the retention rate.

solution.title: Solution: first date, then a flag per customer
solution.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
flags AS (
  SELECT f.customer_id,
         MAX(CASE WHEN o.order_date > f.first_date
                   AND julianday(o.order_date) - julianday(f.first_date) <= 30
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS came_back
  FROM firsts f
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = f.customer_id
  GROUP BY f.customer_id
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers,
       SUM(came_back) AS came_back_within_30_days,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(came_back) / COUNT(*), 1) AS retention_pct
FROM flags;

alternatives.title: See it per customer with LEAD
alternatives.sql:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS rn,
         LEAD(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS next_date
  FROM orders
)
SELECT c.name, n.order_date AS first_order, n.next_date AS second_order,
       julianday(n.next_date) - julianday(n.order_date) AS gap_days
FROM numbered n
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = n.customer_id
WHERE n.rn = 1
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
alternatives.note: The gap to the second order shows the answer at a glance: 1 and 8 days are within 30; 40 isn't; Zoe never came back.

edgeCases: A second order on the same day as the first: does it count as "coming back"? The solution says no (`>`); ask.
Customers whose first order is less than 30 days before the end of the data haven't had a full 30 days yet — exclude them from the denominator for a fair rate.
Should cancelled orders count as activity? Filter by status if not.
mistakes: Counting any second order, regardless of how long after.
Dividing whole numbers and getting 0.
Measuring from sign-up date when the question says first order (or the other way round).
topics.interviewAnswer: I anchor each customer on their first order with MIN per customer, join back to their orders, and flag whether any later order falls within 30 days, taking MAX of a CASE so each customer is one or zero. The retention rate is the sum of flags over the number of customers, times 100.0. I'd raise two definitional points: whether a same-day second order counts, and excluding customers who haven't had a full 30 days yet.

followUps.q: How would you compute retention by sign-up month (a cohort table)?
followUps.a: Add the first-order month to the firsts CTE, group the flags by that month, and compute the rate per cohort.

followUps.q: Why exclude recent customers from the denominator?
followUps.a: Someone who ordered yesterday hasn't had 30 days to come back; counting them as "not retained" makes the rate look worse than it is.

practice.explain: Explain why each customer is reduced to a single 1 or 0 before the rate is calculated.
practice.write: Compute the share of customers who came back within 7 days.
practice.predict: What would retention_pct be with a 45-day window?
practice.edge: Change the solution so only delivered orders count as activity. Who changes?

resources.title: Retention and cohort analysis in SQL (video)

explain.answer:
Because the question is about customers, not orders: "what share of customers came back?". Every customer must count exactly once.

If you worked on order rows instead, Priya, with 5 orders, would count five times and her habits would swamp everyone else's. So each customer is first reduced to one row with a single flag: 1 if they came back within 30 days, 0 if not (MAX over their orders turns "any qualifying order" into one 1). Then the rate is simple: the sum of the flags (customers who came back) ÷ the count of rows (customers).

write.answer: Change 30 to 7. Only Priya came back within a week (her second order was the next day). Lena's came 8 days later and Tom's 40 days later, and Zoe has only one order. 1 out of 4 is 25.0%.

query.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
flags AS (
  SELECT f.customer_id,
         MAX(CASE WHEN o.order_date > f.first_date
                   AND julianday(o.order_date) - julianday(f.first_date) <= 7
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS came_back
  FROM firsts f
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = f.customer_id
  GROUP BY f.customer_id
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers,
       SUM(came_back) AS came_back_within_7_days,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(came_back) / COUNT(*), 1) AS retention_pct
FROM flags;

predict.answer: 75.0. Tom now counts as well: his second order (1 March) came 40 days after his first (21 January), inside 45 days but outside 30. With Priya and Lena, that is 3 of the 4 customers. Zoe still has only one order.

query.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
flags AS (
  SELECT f.customer_id,
         MAX(CASE WHEN o.order_date > f.first_date
                   AND julianday(o.order_date) - julianday(f.first_date) <= 45
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS came_back
  FROM firsts f
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = f.customer_id
  GROUP BY f.customer_id
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers,
       SUM(came_back) AS came_back_within_45_days,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(came_back) / COUNT(*), 1) AS retention_pct
FROM flags;

edge.answer:
Filter to delivered orders once, in a first CTE, and use it in both later steps, so the first order and the return visit are both delivered ones.

Who changes:
• Lena: her first order (106) was cancelled, so her first delivered order is 107, and she has none after it. She no longer came back.
• Zoe: her only order is pending, so she has no delivered orders and drops out of the customers counted entirely.
• Priya (came back) and Tom (didn't) are unchanged.

The rate becomes 1 of 3: 33.3%. The query below shows the flags per customer, to make the change visible.

query.sql:
WITH delivered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, order_date
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'delivered'
),
firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date
  FROM delivered
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
flags AS (
  SELECT f.customer_id,
         MAX(CASE WHEN d.order_date > f.first_date
                   AND julianday(d.order_date) - julianday(f.first_date) <= 30
                  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS came_back
  FROM firsts f
  JOIN delivered d ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id
  GROUP BY f.customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, fl.came_back
FROM flags fl
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = fl.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

topics.name: The median salary
topics.definition: Find the median salary of all employees, and then the median salary in each department.
topics.problem: Whether you can build a statistic that SQL doesn't always provide, using row numbers and counts — and handle both odd and even group sizes.
approach: Sort the salaries and number them 1 to n with ROW_NUMBER; get n with `COUNT(*) OVER ()`.
The middle positions are (n + 1) / 2 and (n + 2) / 2 using whole-number division: the same row when n is odd, the two middle rows when n is even.
Average the salaries at those positions.
For each department, add PARTITION BY dept_id to both window functions and GROUP BY dept_id.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR S["8 salaries sorted
38k 45k 52k 60k 70k 70k 80k 95k"] --> M["middle positions
(8+1)/2 = 4 and (8+2)/2 = 5"] M --> A["average of 60000 and 70000
= 65000"]
diagram.caption: With an even number of rows there are two middle values, and the median is their average. With an odd number, both formulas point at the same single row.

solution.title: Solution: row numbers and a count
solution.sql:
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS n
  FROM employees
)
SELECT AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM ordered
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2);
solution.note: n = 8, so positions 4 and 5: 60000 and 70000, averaging 65000. The average salary is 63750 — the median and the mean are different things.

alternatives.title: The median in each department
alternatives.sql:
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT dept_id, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS n
  FROM employees
  WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM ordered
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2)
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;
alternatives.note: Engineering has 4 people (70000, 70000, 80000, 95000): the middle two average 75000.

edgeCases: Even vs odd counts: the two-position trick covers both.
NULL salaries: filter them out before numbering, or they shift the positions.
Ties in salary don't matter: whichever tied row gets which number, the values at the middle positions are the same.
mistakes: Using AVG — that is the mean, not the median.
Taking only position n / 2, which is wrong for odd counts and only half the answer for even counts.
Decimal division in the position maths ((n + 1) / 2.0), which gives 4.5 and matches no row.
dialects: PostgreSQL and Oracle: `PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary)` gives the median directly; SQL Server has PERCENTILE_CONT as a window function. MySQL and SQLite have no built-in median, so use this pattern.
topics.interviewAnswer: If the database has PERCENTILE_CONT, the median is PERCENTILE_CONT 0.5 within group ordered by salary. Otherwise I number the sorted values with ROW_NUMBER, get the count with COUNT over the same window, and average the values at positions n plus one over two and n plus two over two with integer division — that's the single middle row for odd n and the two middle rows for even n. Partitioning both window functions gives a median per group.

followUps.q: Median or mean — when does the difference matter?
followUps.a: When the data is skewed: one very high salary pulls the mean up but barely moves the median.

followUps.q: How would you get the 90th percentile?
followUps.a: `PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary)` where available; otherwise the row at position `CEIL(0.9 × n)` with the same ROW_NUMBER pattern.

practice.explain: Explain why positions (n + 1) / 2 and (n + 2) / 2 work for both odd and even n.
practice.write: Find the median order amount, ignoring the order with no amount.
practice.predict: What is the median salary if Asha leaves (7 employees)?
practice.edge: What happens to the median calculation if one salary is NULL and you don't filter it out?

explain.answer:
Both use whole-number division, which drops the fraction.

• Odd n, say 7: (7 + 1) / 2 = 4 and (7 + 2) / 2 = 9 / 2 = 4. Both point at row 4, the single middle row, and the average of one value is that value.
• Even n, say 8: (8 + 1) / 2 = 9 / 2 = 4 and (8 + 2) / 2 = 5. They point at rows 4 and 5, the two middle rows, and AVG gives the halfway point between them, which is the median of an even list.

So one formula covers both cases, with no CASE needed.

write.answer: Filter the NULL out before numbering, so it neither takes a position nor counts in n. 9 amounts remain: 30, 33, 45, 60, 75, 80, 120, 150, 200. n is 9, so the median is row 5: 75.

query.sql:
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS n
  FROM orders
  WHERE amount IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT AVG(amount) AS median_amount
FROM ordered
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2);

predict.answer:
60,000. The 7 remaining salaries in order are 38,000, 45,000, 52,000, 60,000, 70,000, 70,000 and 80,000. n is odd, so the median is the 4th: Dara's 60,000. (With all 8 it was 65,000, the average of 60,000 and 70,000.)

Asha can't simply be deleted below, because other employees' manager_id points at her, so the query leaves her out with a WHERE instead.

query.sql:
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS n
  FROM employees
  WHERE name <> 'Asha'
)
SELECT AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM ordered
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2);

edge.answer:
The median comes out wrong, without any error. The NULL still gets a row number (SQLite sorts NULLs first, so it takes position 1) and is counted in n, so every real value is pushed one place along and the middle is picked at the wrong spot. If the NULL itself lands in the middle, AVG skips it and averages whatever else is there.

The salary column can't be NULL here, so the query below does it with order amounts, which have one NULL. With it, n is 10 and the middle rows are 60 and 75, giving 67.5; the true median of the 9 real amounts is 75. Always filter `WHERE x IS NOT NULL` first, as AVG and COUNT(column) do automatically.

query.sql:
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS n
  FROM orders
)
SELECT AVG(amount) AS median_with_the_null
FROM ordered
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2);

topics.name: Customers who bought every product in a category
topics.definition: Find the customers who have bought every product in the Stationery category.
topics.problem: "Every" questions — relational division — which can't be answered with a plain join. They test counting distinct matches against a total, or thinking in double negatives.
topics.spot: "Every", "all of the", "each one of", "the complete set".
approach: Count how many products the category has (here 2: Pen and Notebook).
For each customer, count the different products from that category they have bought.
Keep customers whose count equals the category's total: GROUP BY with HAVING `COUNT(DISTINCT …)` = (subquery).
Or say it as a double negative: there is no Stationery product this customer has not bought.

diagram.code:
flowchart LR C["Stationery has 2 products
Pen, Notebook"] --> Q{"customer bought
2 different ones?"} Q -->|"Priya: Notebook and Pen"| K["kept"] Q -->|"everyone else: 0"| X["dropped"]
diagram.caption: Count the distinct category products each customer bought and compare with the size of the category. Equal means they bought every one.

solution.title: Solution: count distinct matches and compare with the total
solution.sql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE p.category = 'Stationery'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) = (
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products WHERE category = 'Stationery'
)
ORDER BY c.name;
solution.note: Priya bought notebooks in two orders and pens in one; DISTINCT stops the repeat notebook counting twice.

alternatives.title: The double negative: no product they haven't bought
alternatives.sql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM products p
  WHERE p.category = 'Stationery'
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM orders o
      JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
      WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
        AND oi.product_id = p.product_id
    )
)
ORDER BY c.name;
alternatives.note: Read it as: keep the customer if there is no Stationery product that this customer has not bought.

edgeCases: An empty category: the counting version returns nobody, while the double-negative version returns every customer ("bought all of nothing"). Ask which is wanted.
Buying the same product twice must not count twice: use `COUNT(DISTINCT)`.
Products added to the category later change the answer for past customers — that is usually intended.
mistakes: `COUNT(*)` instead of `COUNT(DISTINCT product_id)`, so two notebooks look like two different products.
Hard-coding the total (= 2) instead of counting the category.
Using IN ('Pen', 'Notebook'), which finds customers who bought any of them, not all.
topics.interviewAnswer: This is relational division — "bought all of". I join each customer to the category's products they bought, group by customer, and keep those whose count of distinct products equals the category's product count from a subquery. An equivalent formulation is a double NOT EXISTS: there's no product in the category that the customer hasn't bought. I'd mention the empty-category case, where the two versions disagree.

followUps.q: How would you find customers who bought at least 2 of the 3 products in a category?
followUps.a: Same query, with HAVING `COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) >= 2`.

followUps.q: How would you find customers who bought exactly the Stationery products and nothing else?
followUps.a: Count distinct stationery products = category size, and also count of non-stationery products = 0 (conditional aggregation over all their items).

practice.explain: Explain the double NOT EXISTS version in plain words.
practice.write: Find customers who bought every product in the Electronics category. (Who bought the phone case?)
practice.predict: If Tom had also bought a pen and a notebook, what would the solution return?
practice.edge: Show what each version returns for a category with no products, and explain why they differ.

explain.answer:
It turns "bought every product" into a double negative: "there is no Stationery product that this customer has not bought".

• The outer NOT EXISTS goes through each Stationery product, looking for one this customer is missing.
• The inner NOT EXISTS answers, for one product: "has this customer never bought it?" (no item line of theirs has that product).
• If the search finds no missing product, the customer has bought them all, and they are kept.

It reads oddly, but it works without counting, and it handles products bought several times naturally.

write.answer: Change the category in both places. Nobody qualifies: Electronics has two products, the headphones and the phone case, and nobody has ever bought the phone case. Priya and Tom bought headphones, but one product out of two isn't "every product". An empty result is the right answer.

query.sql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE p.category = 'Electronics'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) = (
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products WHERE category = 'Electronics'
)
ORDER BY c.name;

predict.answer: Priya and Tom. Stationery is the pen and the notebook. Priya already bought both; if Tom also bought one of each, he would have 2 distinct Stationery products too, matching the category's 2. Below, they are added to his order 104.

query.sql:
INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (104, 1, 1), (104, 2, 1);
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE p.category = 'Stationery'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) = (
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products WHERE category = 'Stationery'
)
ORDER BY c.name;

edge.answer:
Take a category with no products, such as 'Toys'.

• The COUNT version returns nobody. Its WHERE keeps only item lines in that category, and there are none, so there are no groups for HAVING to compare with 0.
• The double NOT EXISTS version returns every customer (below). "Is there a Toys product this customer hasn't bought?" can never be yes when there are no Toys products, so every customer passes.

Logically, the NOT EXISTS answer is the correct one: "bought every product in an empty set" is vacuously true, like "all my unicorns are pink". In practice, nobody wants that report, so the honest answer is to ask what the business wants for an empty category, and to handle it on purpose, for example by returning nothing when the category has no products.

query.sql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM products p
  WHERE p.category = 'Toys'
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM orders o
      JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
      WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
        AND oi.product_id = p.product_id
    )
)
ORDER BY c.name;

glossary.definition: An organised store of data that many people and programs can read and change safely at the same time.
A database that keeps data in tables linked by keys, and is queried with SQL.
Database management system: the software that runs a database and answers queries, such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server or SQLite.
Structured Query Language: the language for asking a relational database questions and changing its data. Said "S-Q-L" or "sequel".
A set of rows that all have the same columns, holding one kind of thing — employees, or orders.
One record in a table: one employee, one order. Also called a record or tuple.
One named fact stored for every row, such as name or salary. Also called a field or attribute.
A request written in SQL and sent to the database — usually a SELECT that asks for rows.
Describing the result you want rather than the steps to get it. SQL is declarative; Python loops are not.
The part of the database that decides how to run a query — which index to use, which table to read first. Also called the optimiser; its decision is the query plan.
A popular free, open-source database server, known for following the SQL standard closely. Often called Postgres.
A popular free, open-source database server, used by many websites.
Microsoft's database server. Its SQL dialect is called T-SQL.
A small database that lives inside one file instead of running as a server. It is what runs the examples on this page, in your browser.
What one row of a table or result means: one order, or one product within one order. Mixing grains double-counts totals.
The column (or columns) whose value identifies exactly one row. It must be unique and can never be NULL.
A column that holds another table's primary key, linking each row to a row there — orders.customer_id points at a customer.
A key made of two or more columns together, like (order_id, product_id): neither is unique alone, but the pair is.
A meaningless id, like 1, 2, 3, used as the primary key. A natural key is a real-world value used as a key, such as an email.
A relationship where one row on one side matches many rows on the other: one customer, many orders. The foreign key sits on the "many" side.
A relationship where rows on both sides match many rows on the other: orders and products. It needs a link table.
A relationship where each row matches at most one row on the other side, such as a user and their settings.
A table whose rows pair up keys from two other tables, to store a many-to-many relationship. Also called a junction table.
A foreign key that points back into its own table, like employees.manager_id pointing at another employee.
What kind of value a column holds — a whole number, text, a date — which decides how it compares, sorts and calculates.
A whole-number type: 1, 42, -7. No decimal point.
An exact decimal number type, right for money: DECIMAL(10, 2) holds up to 10 digits, 2 after the point. Also called NUMERIC.
An approximate decimal number type (also FLOAT or DOUBLE). Fast, but cannot hold most decimals exactly, so not for money.
A type for words and other characters. VARCHAR(n) is text of up to n characters; CHAR(n) is always exactly n.
A type for calendar dates. TIMESTAMP (or DATETIME) also holds the time of day.
A true-or-false type. In SQL a condition can also be unknown, when it involves NULL.
Converts a value to another type: CAST('42' AS INTEGER) is the number 42.
Dividing a whole number by a whole number keeps only the whole part: 7 / 2 is 3. Use 7 / 2.0 for 3.5.
A text value. In SQL it goes inside single quotes: 'London'.
The marker for a missing or unknown value. It is not zero and not empty text, and comparing anything to it with = gives unknown, never true.
A separate, sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows by a column's value without reading the whole table — like the index at the back of a book.
The statement that reads data. Also the clause listing which columns or expressions the result should have.
The clause naming the table (or joined tables) a query reads from. The database runs it first.
The clause that keeps only the rows for which a condition is true, before any grouping.
Sorts the result. Without it, the database may return rows in any order at all.
Combines rows from two tables where a condition (usually matching keys) is true, so one result row can hold columns from both.
A temporary name given with AS — to a column (salary + 5000 AS after_raise) or a table (employees AS e) — for the length of one query.
Anything that works out to a value: a column, a number, a calculation like salary + 5000, or a function call.
Words that combine conditions. AND needs both to be true, OR needs at least one, NOT flips true and false. AND is worked out before OR.
A test between two values with =, <> (not equal), <, <=, > or >=. The answer is true, false, or unknown when NULL is involved.
Which part of a condition is worked out first. AND comes before OR, like × before + in maths. Brackets override it.
True when a value equals any value in a list: status IN ('shipped', 'pending').
True when a value is inside a range, both ends included: x BETWEEN 1 AND 5 means 1 ≤ x ≤ 5.
Matches text against a pattern: % is any run of characters, _ is exactly one. ILIKE (PostgreSQL) ignores case.
A symbol in a LIKE pattern that stands for other characters: % for any number of characters, _ for exactly one.
The correct test for a missing value. x = NULL is never true; x IS NULL is.
In SQL a condition can be true, false or unknown. Anything compared with NULL is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true.
Returns the first of its values that is not NULL: COALESCE(amount, 0) turns a missing amount into 0.
NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a equals b, otherwise a. Dividing by NULLIF(x, 0) avoids a divide-by-zero error.
Sort directions for ORDER BY: ASC is smallest first (the default), DESC is largest first. Each column gets its own.
Keeps only the first n rows of the (sorted) result. OFFSET skips rows first. SQL Server uses TOP; the standard is FETCH FIRST.
Showing results a page at a time. OFFSET is simple; keyset pagination ("after the last id I saw") stays fast on deep pages.
An extra sort column used when the first one ties, so the order is the same every time: ORDER BY salary DESC, name.
Removes duplicate rows from a result — comparing every selected column together. COUNT(DISTINCT x) counts different values.
SQL's if-else: CASE WHEN condition THEN value … ELSE value END. Returns the value of the first true WHEN, or NULL with no ELSE.
A function that turns one value into one value, once per row — UPPER, ROUND, a date function. Also called a scalar function.
Functions that change text: UPPER and LOWER (case), LENGTH (number of characters), SUBSTR (cut out a piece), TRIM (remove spaces at the ends), REPLACE (swap text).
ROUND(x, 2) rounds a number to 2 decimal places. Round at the end, after summing.
Functions for dates. SQLite: strftime and julianday. PostgreSQL: DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT and date subtraction. MySQL and SQL Server: DATE_FORMAT, DATEDIFF.
A function that turns many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. All except COUNT(*) skip NULLs.
Counts rows. COUNT(*) counts every row; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts different values.
Aggregates that add up, average, or find the smallest and largest of the non-NULL values. SUM of no rows is NULL, not 0.
Puts rows with the same value in the listed columns into one group; each group becomes one result row. Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
Filters groups after GROUP BY, so it can use aggregates: HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. WHERE filters rows before grouping.
An aggregate over a CASE, like SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), to count or sum only some rows — several totals in one pass.
Turning row values into columns, such as one column per month. In SQL, usually conditional aggregation.
A neater way to aggregate only some rows: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered'). PostgreSQL and SQLite.
The order a query is processed in: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — not the order it is written in.
A join that keeps only rows that found a match on both sides. Plain JOIN means the same.
The part of a join that says which rows match: ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id.
A short name for a table in one query (employees AS e), so columns can be written e.name.
A join that keeps every row of the left table, with NULLs in the right table's columns where nothing matched.
The mirror of LEFT JOIN: keeps every row of the right table. Usually rewritten as a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped.
Finding rows with no match in another table: LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS.
Finding rows that have at least one match, each returned once: EXISTS or IN.
Joining a table to itself under two aliases, to compare rows of the same table — such as employees with their managers.
A join that keeps every row from both tables, with NULLs wherever either side had no match.
Pairs every row of one table with every row of the other (a Cartesian product): 6 rows × 3 rows = 18 rows.
When a one-to-many join repeats the "one" row for each match, so summing a column from the "one" side counts it several times.
A SELECT inside another query, in brackets. It can give one value, a list (for IN) or a whole table (in FROM).
A subquery that returns exactly one value, used wherever a single value can go.
A subquery in FROM, given an alias and used like a table — the way to aggregate an aggregate.
A subquery that uses columns of the outer row, so logically it is worked out again for each outer row.
True if a subquery returns at least one row. NOT EXISTS is the safe way to find rows with no match.
True when a value is not in a list — but if the list contains a NULL it is never true, so prefer NOT EXISTS with subqueries.
Common table expression: a named step written with WITH name AS (…) at the top of a query, used later like a table.
A CTE that refers to itself: a starting query plus a part that keeps adding rows from the previous round, until none are new. Used for trees and series.
Stacks two results on top of each other and removes duplicate rows. UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster.
Set operators: INTERSECT keeps rows found in both results; EXCEPT (MINUS in Oracle) keeps rows of the first not in the second.
UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT or EXCEPT: combines two results vertically. Both must have the same number of columns.
A function worked out over a set of related rows (its window) for each row, written with OVER — without collapsing the rows like GROUP BY does.
The clause that makes a function a window function and defines its window: OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …).
Inside OVER: splits rows into separate windows, one per value — like GROUP BY, but every row is kept.
Numbers the rows of each window 1, 2, 3, 4 with no ties. Add a tiebreaker so the numbering is stable.
Ranks rows; ties share a rank and the next rank is skipped: 1, 2, 2, 4.
Ranks rows; ties share a rank and nothing is skipped: 1, 2, 2, 3. Right for "Nth highest value".
Window functions that return a value from the previous row (LAG) or the next row (LEAD), in the window's order.
A total that grows row by row: SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY date). Also called a cumulative sum.
The average of the last few rows, recalculated at each row: AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
Which rows of the window a row can see, such as ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. With ORDER BY, the default is RANGE up to the current row, which includes ties.
NTILE(n) deals the ordered rows into n buckets of nearly equal size: NTILE(4) gives quartiles.
Returns a value from the first row of the window. LAST_VALUE needs a frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING to really see the last row.
One row's part of the whole, usually as a percentage: 100.0 * x / SUM(x) OVER ().
Defines a new table: its columns, their types and their rules.
Changes an existing table — add, rename or drop a column.
The value a column gets when an INSERT doesn't give one.
The structure of a database: its tables, columns, types and rules — not the data in them.
A rule the database checks on every write — NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK — refusing rows that break it.
A rule that a column must always have a value.
A rule that no two rows may share a value in this column (NULLs usually excepted).
A rule with any condition a row must meet, such as CHECK (price > 0).
A foreign-key option: deleting the parent row also deletes the child rows that point to it. ON DELETE SET NULL blanks them instead.
Adds new rows: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (…), or INSERT … SELECT to copy rows from a query.
Changes values in the rows that match its WHERE — or in every row if there is no WHERE.
Removes the rows that match its WHERE — or every row if there is no WHERE.
Insert a row, or update it if its key already exists, in one atomic statement: INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.
A group of statements that succeed or fail as one: BEGIN, the changes, then COMMIT to keep them or ROLLBACK to undo them.
COMMIT makes a transaction's changes permanent; ROLLBACK throws them all away. BEGIN starts the transaction.
The four guarantees of a transaction: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (rules always hold), Isolated (no interference), Durable (committed means saved).
How strictly concurrent transactions are kept apart: READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. Stricter is safer but slower.
Problems from concurrent transactions. Dirty read: seeing uncommitted changes. Non-repeatable read: a row changes between two reads. Phantom read: new rows appear.
Designing tables so each fact is stored once, to avoid contradictions. Denormalisation copies data back on purpose for faster reads.
Normal forms. 1NF: one value per cell. 2NF: no column depends on part of a composite key. 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column.
When one fact is stored in several rows and an update misses some, so the data contradicts itself.
A saved query you can select from like a table. It stores no rows, so it always shows current data.
A view whose result is stored: fast to read, but only as fresh as its last REFRESH.
Families of SQL commands. DDL changes structure (CREATE, ALTER, DROP). DML changes data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). DCL controls access (GRANT, REVOKE). TCL controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK).
Empties a whole table at once — much faster than DELETE, with no WHERE.
Removes a whole object — DROP TABLE deletes the table with its rows, indexes and rules.
The tree structure most indexes use: values kept sorted in a few levels of pages, so any value is found in a handful of steps.
Reading every row of a table to answer a query. Fine for small tables; slow for big ones. Plans show SCAN or Seq Scan.
How small a share of the rows a filter matches. An index helps most when the filter is selective.
An index that is the table itself, with rows stored in key order (one per table). A non-clustered index is a separate structure pointing to rows.
Shows the plan the database chose for a query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL) also runs it and shows real timings.
In a SQLite plan, a step that jumps to rows through an index or key, instead of scanning everything.
What the database knows about its data — row counts, value spreads — used to choose plans. Refreshed with ANALYZE.
Written so an index can be used: the indexed column stands alone, compared with a value. A function around the column makes it non-sargable.
An index on several columns, sorted by the first, then by the second within it. Also called a multicolumn index.
A composite index on (a, b) helps filters on a, or on a and b — but not on b alone.
An index that holds every column a query needs, so the table itself doesn't have to be read.
An index on the result of a function, such as LOWER(email), so a filter using that function can be fast.
A join method: for each row of one input, look up matches in the other. Fast with a small outer side and an index on the inner.
A join method: build a hash table from one input, then probe it with each row of the other. Good for big equality joins; needs memory.
A join method: walk two inputs sorted on the join key side by side, like a zip.
An unusual input that can break a query: NULLs, ties, duplicates, empty tables, a first row with nothing before it.
OLTP: an app's database, with many small fast reads and writes. OLAP: analytics over lots of history, in a data warehouse.
The pattern for "the highest-paid in each department": rank within each group with a window function, then keep the top ranks.
Finding runs of consecutive values (islands) and the breaks between them (gaps) — streaks, sessions, uninterrupted periods.
The pattern where a few items make up most of the total — often "20% of products bring 80% of revenue".
The share of users who come back and act again within a time window after their first action.
A group of users who started in the same period, such as everyone whose first order was in January.
The middle value when the values are sorted (the average of the two middle ones for an even count). Unlike the mean, extreme values barely move it.
The value below which a given share of the data falls: the 50th percentile is the median. PERCENTILE_CONT computes it in PostgreSQL.
Questions of the form "who did all of these?" — answered by counting distinct matches against the total, or with a double NOT EXISTS.
